Warming to his theme, he said: “I’ll hold that umbrella for me to get wet and for everyone else to stay dry. That’s the position I’m in, and it’s a privileged position.”

Carrick believes all of his squad share his determination – “If you don’t, this is not the place for you,” he said – insisted there were no factions. “It’s not divided. We just need to get back to doing what we do best, and we will.”

Sports.title: Slegers and misfiring Arsenal badly need a result in WSL north London derby
Sports.content:
It says much about Arsenal’s predicament that the team who have conceded 12 goals in two games are not the side whose head coach is under most pressure before a north London derby. Tottenham, four points above their neighbours before Saturday’s meeting, may have been humbled in consecutive Women’s Super League matches but all eyes are on Renée Slegers.

Arsenal are winless in five WSL matches for the first time, and the most decorated club in English women’s football desperately need a turning point. Their failure to beat Birmingham at home last Saturday, dropping points against a promoted side for the second time this season, again demonstrated the team’s inability to convert possession into goals. They increasingly look like a team stuck in Groundhog Day.

The Arsenal hierarchy are understood to remain behind Slegers, but for how long? The answer may hinge on Saturday lunchtime’s result. However much goodwill the Dutchwoman gained for guiding Arsenal to Champions League glory in May 2025, the simple truth is, it is unacceptable for a club with one of the biggest budgets in the world to be 12 points behind the leaders after six games.

That gap is why the draw with Birmingham not only pretty much extinguished Arsenal’s title hopes but also burned a hole in their secondary domestic objective – Champions League qualification. The unthinkable prospect of failure appears a genuine possibility: they are nine points adrift of third-placed London City. Arsenal need a derby win on Saturday but also a winning run to reverse the slide, and there is little evidence to suggest such a turnaround is close.

Arsenal have the worst shot conversion rate in the league (4.1%) and, according to Stats Perform, the third-worst shooting accuracy (30.6%) and third-lowest average xG per shot (0.09) despite averaging over 60% possession. Slegers’s persistence in deploying Alessia Russo – widely regarded as one of Europe’s best No 9s – in the No 10 role has baffled supporters and commentators alike. Russo has scored more WSL goals against Tottenham (eight) than any other player so Saturday’s game may be the perfect moment for that to change.

View image in fullscreen Arsenal’s Alessia Russo and Caitlin Foord wheel away after a goal against Tottenham in February 2025 – however, Russo has not flourished as a No 10 this season. Photograph: Matthew Childs/Action Images/Reuters

Arsenal have struggled against low blocks for a number of seasons, though, so not all fault lies at Slegers’s door. Nonetheless, the 37-year-old was substantially backed in the summer, with Arsenal enjoying perhaps their strongest transfer window in recent memory. So far though they have looked confounded tactically, bruised mentally and lacking the self-belief to grab a game by the scruff of its neck.

Asked if she was surprised to still be in her job, Slegers said: “That’s not something I think about. It’s about, ‘where are we as a group?’ and ‘what are we working towards?’ It’s absolutely not what we expected [our recent results] or what we wanted. But I’m in the here and now, and we are preparing for the north London derby. We have the group together. Everyone is going in the same direction and the fuel and motivation is sky high, because of the fans that will be there for us. That’s where my focus will be.”

Asked how imperative it is that Arsenal climb back up into a Champions League place this season, Slegers added: “Of course that’s in the back of our heads, but what we need right now is to get back to winning ways. We can only do that with the next game in front of us so that’s why the next game in front of us is the most important right now.”

Slegers has maintained after last weekend’s draw that Arsenal will recover when they fix some “details and margins”. Perhaps taking on a Tottenham side who have become only the second team in history to concede six or more goals in consecutive WSL games is the perfect opportunity.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to Moving the Goalposts No topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

“It is a little bit of game intelligence and smartness in moments,” said the Spurs head coach, Martin Ho, insisting he is not worried about his team’s defending in the long-term. “There have been certain aspects that, collectively, players and staff, we were not happy with in certain moments, and we have to make sure we correct them. At the moment we’re getting heavily punished for some small errors with the ball that we’re making.”

The Englishman also only had praise for Arsenal’s qualities when speaking on Friday morning. “If you try and underestimate a team with Arsenal’s quality you’re in for trouble,” he said. Asked about Arsenal’s poor run, Ho added: “Arsenal aren’t a bad side. Their possession stats are probably the highest in the league, alongside Manchester City. Their goalscoring chances and touches in the opposition box are very, very high. They have world-class players.”

Last season’s runners-up do have world-class players but it is high time for them to play like a cohesive team.

Sports.title: Arteta concerned over Saka’s durability as forward faces possible six-week absence
Sports.content:
Mikel Arteta has expressed concern over Bukayo Saka’s robustness after a series of injuries to the forward in the past year and as he awaits further news on how long he will be out for with a thigh issue.

Saka is set for an MRI scan after limping off in the 2-2 draw with Bayern Munich in the Champions League, with Arteta revealing the 25-year-old had “quite a lot of fluid in the area so it was difficult to understand the extent of the injury”. Saka will definitely miss Saturday’s game against Evertonand, it is understood, Arsenal fear it could be a grade-two tear that could potentially keep him out for up to six weeks.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Saka missed a large portion of last season due to hamstring, hip and achilles tendon injuries having also been sidelined by another hamstring issue in 2024-25. In total, he has had 11 different injuries since September 2023 and Arteta insisted that he has been trying to ease his workload as a result. “It’s certainly been different in the last year or so,” the Spaniard said when asked if Saka remains robust enough to start every match. “The demands that we are putting on every player are immense. The amount of games, the intensity of those matches, the international competitions, the times as well between games are getting narrower.

“Bukayo against Lille [in the Champions League last week] didn’t start the game because we knew what was happening. We have to play three times in less than six days. And especially when the games are so demanding, until the last minute you are there, you are chasing the game, you want to win. The necessity is to win every game, so we know that. So we are preparing the players for those scenarios and we do the best that we possibly can.”

Saka missed only three Premier League matches in three seasons between 2021 and 2024 and broke the Arsenal club record by playing in 83 consecutive top-flight games. He is already approaching 300 appearances for the club he joined as a seven-year-old and was rewarded with a lucrative new contract in February that made him one of the highest-paid players in the club’s history.

Asked whether he feared Saka could suffer from burnout having made his Arsenal debut three months after his 17th birthday, Arteta said: “I don’t have that feeling at all but something we have to be very mindful of is to create the right ecosystem around the player to fulfil his qualities. We really need to understand, whenever he comes back, how we are going to manage his load, what he is capable of to sustain having an impact in the team.”

Saka’s absence could hand an opportunity to Max Dowman on Saturday. The 16-year-old has played only nine minutes in the league this season and Arteta feels sure he is ready to make an impact after he became the youngest goalscorer in Premier League history, against David Moyes’s side in March.

“There is something inevitable to go back to that memory and the feeling of the moment. That’s with us, that’s going to stay in that stadium for a long, long time,” said Arteta. “He’s training and every time he’s got a moment to play, he’s showing that he’s a player that is going to impact the game. For sure he’s going to have minutes.”

Sports.title: Football Daily | Mourinho is ready for his clásico return – stock up on popcorn, folks!
Sports.content:
MOU AND WHOSE ARMY?

Football Daily has never had much time for conspiracy theories. Lee Harvey Oswald dunnit, Stanley Kubrick didn’t fake the moon landing, Vinícius Jr doesn’t have a body double and Miranda isn’t a secret traitor. But our Spidey senses picked up when the UK government announced their Be Ready campaign on Thursday night. In case you missed it, or live outside the UK and couldn’t care less about this weird little island, we’ve lifted this from our news story:

“Every Briton is being urged to stock up to nine litres of bottled water and three days’ worth of food in new government guidance designed to ensure that households can survive a weather, cyber or other serious emergency. The Be Ready campaign is aimed at persuading people to stock up with supplies to last 72 hours, amid growing official concern about the impact of the climate crisis, technological dependency and hostile state threats.”

War’s a comin’, in other words, so you’d better buy some tomato soup (10 tins of), mushroom soup (eight tins of, for consumption cold) and ice cream (vanilla, one large tub of). Here’s where it gets interesting. The government released their three-day survival plan on Thursday afternoon, three days before the event most likely to cause World War III: José Mourinho’s first Clásico since 2013. Barcelona meet Real Madrid at the Camp Nou on Sunday and suddenly the government are telling us we may need to hunker down. Coincidence? We think not!

OK, OK. Coincidence? We think so! José may be the most charismatic baddie since Dirty Den’s most recent death, but not even he is capable of starting the geopolitical answer to El Clásico. Sunday’s match will spark a form of global conflict, even if it’s just a load of strangers caterwauling at each other on the internet rather than talking to their children, reading a book or practising any of the gazillion behaviours that would make their lives and the world a better place.

Mourinho’s relationship with Barcelona could fill a book, never mind a teatime email. There is love lost, but it’s decades since it went missing. These days they can’t stand the thought of each other, never mind the sight. There is an argument (NB: Football Daily doesn’t actually want to argue) that Mourinho’s greatest achievement in football, apart from finishing second with Manchester United in 2017-18, was to take a La Liga title off probably the greatest club side of all time. He also drove Pep Guardiola into a sabbatical – but that, and the Realpolitik of the Bernabéu dressing-room, took so much out of Mourinho that he has never been the same since that triumphant 2011-12 season.

The Camp Nou was the venue for Mourinho’s “most beautiful defeat” (you know the one, when not even a good hosing could douse his celebrations) and his most humiliating defeat a few months later. He can’t afford any kind of defeat on Sunday: Madrid are six points behind Barcelona, who have won all nine league games, scoring 39 goals in the process. But Mourinho’s team have scored four goals in each of their last three matches and, even in the absence of the suspended Vinícius Jr , have attacking threats galore. And whatever the result, Mourinho’s post-match press conference will be must-see TV.

The match kicks off on Sunday evening, but only if you take these things literally. For Mourinho, it began the moment he was asked a question about it. He has had the face on all week because, well, wouldn’t you if you were treated like this? Barcelona played 24 hours earlier than Madrid in Bigger Cup, an open goal for conspiracy theorists and performative underdogs. “We’re pushing ahead,” he said. “At the moment, we’re missing out on 24 hours of rest, but we’re moving forward.” So is Football Daily, to the supermarket to get some urgent shopping. We’ll Be Ready for Sunday – not with 72 hours of essential supplies, but with a month’s worth of popcorn.

LIVE ON BIG WEBSITE

Join Scott Murray at 8pm (BST) for red-hot Premier League updates on Ipswich Town 0-0 Nottingham Forest.

QUOTE OF THE DAY

“I’ll hold that umbrella for me to get wet and for everyone else to stay dry. You know, that’s the position I’m in, and it’s a privileged position” – Michael Carrick delivers a near six-minute monologue defending Manchester United’s values in which he veered close to painting a picture of himself as being akin to another former Middlesbrough manager who once held a brolly while watching his team fail.

View image in fullscreen Steve McClaren: a reminder. Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The Guardian

double quotation mark Would it not be much easier all round if the two big clubs in Manchester simply swapped all playing and coaching staff before the next round of fixtures? United would finally get the squad that Bruno Fernandes and Lisandro Martínez clearly feel they deserve, one of serial winners who are worthy of the club’s fine history (and free of the whiners). Meanwhile, City would might get a team that would make them (somewhat) competitive in the lower tiers where they’re surely headed. And a manager who has coached there quite recently. Sure there’d be a few grumbles from the fans, but more importantly in the current football climate, think of all the potential new shirt sales, and the Us-Against-the-World mentality that Enzo Maresca would be able to instil in his team whose own supporters would even hate them. And no-one would even have to move house. It’s a win-win solution. Although, no, it’s United; so probably a win-high-scoring-draw-against-Wycombe solution” – Justin Kavanagh.

double quotation mark Like all right-minded people, I only read Big Website to get my fill of news and information (ahem …). However, I did come across a recent piece in The New Yorker on James Daunt, the chief suit of the US book chain Barnes & Noble (no relation). The billionaire Russian oligarch, Alexander Mamut, asked him 20 years ago how much it would cost to buy Waterstones, and when he was told it would be £40m, he looked pleased and just said, ‘That’s less than Fernando Torres’, before adding, ‘It’s not even half a boat’. Odd reference points these billionaires” – Noble Francis.

double quotation mark May I be the first of 1,057 Daniels to say thank you for the good luck message at the end of Thursday’s Football Daily. It has put a little extra pep in my step today” – Daniel Mee.

If you have any, please send letters to the.boss@theguardian.com. Today’s prizeless letter o’ the day goes to … Justin Kavanagh. Terms and conditions for our competitions, when we run them, are here.

Sports.title: Crystal Palace and Newcastle face off with both in search of season kickstart
Sports.content:
Are the team underperforming?

Conceding 17 goals in seven Premier League matches is not exactly the start Pierre Sage or Crystal Palace’s hierarchy would have hoped for. The transition from Oliver Glasner’s counterattacking 3-4-2-1 formation to the Frenchman’s more aggressive approach has exposed massive weaknesses in defence, culminating with last week’s humiliating defeat at Brighton. Palace fans became used to success under Glasner and they are already looking nervously over their shoulders at the bottom three. Even their league wins under Sage so far – against Fulham and Nottingham Forest – could have ended in defeat. Something doesn’t seem right in south London. EA

There have been so many arrivals and departures on Tyneside in recent months that it’s too early to say. Any team that sold their three best players – Sandro Tonali, Anthony Gordon and Bruno Guimarães in Newcastle’s case – during the summer would expect a degree of disruption. Eight signings were made, with four aged 20 and under and the others aged 24 and under, and only one (Nico González) had Premier League experience. Throw in a change of manager and an almost entirely new backroom staff and playing style three weeks before the season and teething troubles seem almost inevitable. LT

How much pressure is the manager under?

Sage is sailing extremely close to the wind and was warned after the Brighton game that things must improve quickly or he will be shown the door. It is understood that the Palace chair, Steve Parish, has yet to be convinced by the manager who led Lens to the French Cup last season and has demanded improvements in defence. After the creditable Europa League draw with Besiktas in midweek, Sunday’s meeting with Newcastle is crucial to his future. Thomas Frank and Kieran McKenna are likely candidates should Sage get sacked. Ipswich would be due substantial compensation for McKenna despite him leaving Portman Road in the summer, which could be a major hurdle. EA

View image in fullscreen Adam Wharton (centre) looks dejected during Crystal Palace’s defeat at Brighton. Photograph: Robbie Hoad/Every Second Media/Shutterstock

Very little internally but, externally, the honeymoon is over. Newcastle paid Saudi Arabia’s Al-Ahli £9.5m compensation for Matthias Jaissle, convinced that the 38-year-old German and his “vertical football” were ideal fits. David Hopkinson, the chief executive, and Ross Wilson, the sporting director, are very impressed by Jaissle’s management style, particularly his collaborative approach. They appreciate that Eddie Howe’s successor is new to the Premier League, did not have a proper pre-season and is coping with a raft of injuries. All parties remain sufficiently realistic to predict a season of “ups and downs” but Newcastle’s Saudi Arabian owners crave a return to Europe. Many fans believe Jaissle’s football is old-school, rudimentary long ball with a fancy name, and believe his system and team selections have been flawed. They fear he may be a slave to philosophy. LT

How much responsibility does the manager bear?

Palace have looked a shadow of the side that won three trophies in the space of 12 months under Glasner and Sage must take some of the blame. He fell out with Parish after failing to sign several of his preferred targets in the summer, but it was his decision to break up the Adam Wharton-Daichi Kamada axis in central midfield having brought in Quinten Timber on deadline day. While the Dutchman, who missed the game in Turkey due to injury, has provided extra energy and Kamada has excelled in a more advanced role, Wharton has been struggling defensively. Palace looked much more solid when Wharton and Kamada started together against Besiktas – surely Sage will now stick with the partnership that served Glasner so well. EA

Jaissle’s belief in a gung-ho 4-2-3-1 featuring a classic No 10 is serving him badly at Newcastle, where he does not possess a natural attacking playmaker. It is also leaving González, a holding midfielder, frequently overrun and in need of additional support. With Malick Thiaw and, particularly, Sven Botman struggling in central defence, a switch to a more stable 3-5-2 may be sensible. More importantly, changing the philosophy to a more contain-and-counterattack approach would help camouflage the flaws and make the most of the team’s blistering attacking pace. Jaissle’s high-pressing, attack-minded tactics often appear overly high-risk. His critics fear he may prove to be another Ruben Amorim but Newcastle insiders insist Howe’s successor will prove more flexible than he may seem. Newcastle have not kept a league clean sheet for 13 games, equalling a club record, but six of those came under Howe. LT

How much is beyond the manager’s control?

A typically chaotic end to the transfer window left Sage with a bloated squad but insufficient leadership at the back after selling Maxence Lacroix to Chelsea. Axel Disasi’s three-match ban due to a reckless red card against Ipswich, after he arrived on loan from Stamford Bridge along with the promising Italian teenager Honest Ahanor, hasn’t helped. Parish and the sporting director, Matt Hobbs, deserve criticism for not bringing in more experienced replacements, with the latter’s position also thought to be under heavy scrutiny. Sage has also had to deal with unhappy attackers in Ismaïla Sarr and Jean-Philippe Mateta, who made no secret of their desire to leave Selhurst Park in the summer. EA

Quite a lot. Given his late arrival, Jaissle had limited influence over Wilson’s eight summer signings. He has, though, apparently swiftly decided that Aladji Bamba (£34m from Monaco) and Bazoumana Touré (£43m from Hoffenheim) are not ready to be thrown into Premier League combat. Similarly, the fleet-footed £51m former Lille forward Matias Fernandez-Pardo looks as if he is going to need time to adjust. Newcastle’s policy of generally recruiting players under 25 dictates the dressing room is a little light on leadership. Meanwhile iIt is hard to say whether the manager’s high-intensity training bears any responsibility for a lengthy injury list, with Anthony Elanga, Tino Livramento and Jacob Ramsey notable absentees. LT

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

View image in fullscreen Matias Fernandez-Pardo, seen here round

ing Coventry keeper Carl Rushworth but failing to score, will need time to adjust to the Premier League. Photograph: Nick Potts/PA

How important is winning this game?

After seeing positive signs against Besiktas, as Mateta scored on his first start since the opening day, three points on Sunday will be crucial for Sage. Yet while Palace haven’t lost to Newcastle at home since November 2020, Jaissle’s side have had extra time to prepare and will present a difficult challenge. EA

Given that Newcastle are 11th it is far from imperative. And yet after a demoralising 4-1 defeat at Coventry and a 1-0 home reverse against Aston Villa, victory would offer much-needed reassurance regarding the team’s potential and boost player confidence, not to mention quieten the social-media noise surrounding Jaissle and his tactics. LT

Are there any reasons for optimism?

Palace’s summer net spend of almost £40m in profit was the second lowest in the Premier League behind Aston Villa. They also have American owners who are estimated to be worth a combined £10bn. But Parish revealed last month that he is still looking for extra funding for the new main stand at Selhurst Park, with Woody Johnson, Josh Harris and David Blitzer thought to be open to selling their shares after Palace enlisted Raine Group to seek fresh investment in the club. So there is plenty riding on making sure there is no prospect of being relegated. Sage showed at Lens that he is capable of building a winning team and needs time to do that. EA

Yes, quite a few. Jaissle, understandably, does not want to overplay the 18-year-old central midfielder Sean Steur but the summer signing from Ajax is a joy to watch, has a wonderful passing range and looks capable of reaching the top. Lewis Hall, the England left-back, looks to be going from strength to strength and is capable of elevating standards. Despite an undoubted dogmatic streak, Jaissle appears intelligent – and humble – enough to learn from his mistakes and make necessary adjustments. Club insiders cite his refreshing willingness to listen. Newcastle also possess several extremely quick attacking players – and, as coaches rarely tire of pointing out: “If you’ve got pace, you’ve got a chance.” LT

Sports.title: Pascal Gross: the obsessive runner keeping Brighton ‘one step ahead’ after fast start
Sports.content:
Most footballers like to spend their summers unwinding after a long season but not Pascal Gross. Having been part of the Germany squad eliminated in the quarter-finals of Euro 2024, the midfielder entered – and won – a running race.

Gross completed the 8.4km course on Juist, in the East Frisian islands, in 31 minutes and 35 seconds. He is not known as someone who courts attention, and his victory by more than a minute came to light only when a video was posted on social media by a competitor.

Gross was moving from Brighton to Borussia Dortmund after seven years in the Premier League and reported to his boyhood club for pre-season training days later. Running is an obsession for Gross, as it is for his former teammate James Milner, who revealed last month he was training for a marathon after finally hanging up his boots, and that has shown since he returned for a second spell at the Amex in January for a bargain £1.2m.

“I think he’s looking in his free time now: ‘Where can I run a race?’ because he will never stand still,” joked Brighton’s manager, Fabian Hürzeler, after the 35-year-old scored the opening goal in a 3-0 victory over Arsenal last month. “ During the off season he’s never the person who can lay on the beach for several hours and do nothing. He always needs to do something.”

Given that Gross has this season racked up an average distance of more than 11.5km per match and has covered the third-most ground of any player in the Premier League, it is no surprise Hürzeler has compared his compatriot to a good wine: “The older the wine gets, the better it gets.”

That analysis is borne out by the rest of his statistics this season as Brighton have emerged as challengers for Champions League qualification, at the very least, before Sunday’s game at Liverpool. Not only has Gross, the Premier League’s player of the month for September, contributed a combined seven goals and assists, he is in the top five for several other metrics such as big chances created (six), chances created from open play (14) and line-breaking passes leading to a goal (three). In a team who have scored the fourth-most goals (23) in Premier League history after seven games, Gross has been the standout performer.

View image in fullscreen Pascal Gross (in white) up against Jablonec's Matej Polidar in the Conference League. The match finished 0-0. Photograph: David W Cerny/Reuters

“Sometimes he’s just one step ahead than his opponent,” said Hürzeler, who is understood to have been instrumental in bringing back Gross. “He might not be the quickest player, but he can be the quickest in the head and sometimes being the quickest in the head is very helpful. No one expected that it would be this good. But it also shows that he still has this capacity in his body.”

At a club where experience is valued despite Hürzeler being the youngest permanent manager in the Premier League’s history, insiders describe Gross as the perfect role model for some of Brighton’s younger players. Charalampos Kostoulas has scored three goals in his past four league matches and the 19-year-old Greece striker is clearly thriving alongside the man who is approaching 300 appearances for the club. Diego Gómez, the dynamic Paraguayan who scored a goal-of-the-season contender against Crystal Palace that will go down in Brighton folklore, the homegrown talent Jack Hinshelwood and the midfield linchpin Yasin Ayari are others benefiting from his vast experience, as is Hürzeler.

Gross managed 75 Brighton goals and assists after joining from Ingolstadt in 2017 in the summer when Brighton were promoted. His departure for Dortmund, a year after his first Germany cap, was to fulfil a boyhood dream but there was always something drawing Gross – who wears a long-sleeve shirt owing to a grass allergy – back to the club where he is known as the Kaiser.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

“It was really difficult,” Gross said of his Brighton exit. “Only something really special got me out of here. There were a couple of other options [before returning], but Brighton was always the priority. I just stayed in touch with all the lads over the time away. Maybe you watch less of the games or you don’t stay in touch as much any more, it gets less and less. But it never really did.”

Gross retiring from international football after the World Cup has also been to Brighton’s benefit. His status as a club legend was augmented by delivering the free-kick that Palace’s Jaydee Canvot headed into his own net during the 5-0 humiliation on Sunday. That was the third game in a row in which Gross has provided an assist and he has an opportunity to become the oldest player to make it four since Chelsea’s Gianfranco Zola in December 2002.

The trip to Anfield continues a gruelling run of five away fixtures in a row. Brighton drew at the Czech club Jablonec on Thursday in the Conference League and after Sunday they go to Manchester City twice in four days – the first in the Carabao Cup – before heading to Spain to play Getafe. It will test Brighton’s mettle after their spectacular start. Hürzeler can count on Gross – who has started every game in all competitions – to last the course.

Sports.title: Asian Football Confederation backs Gianni Infantino in U-turn on Fifa presidency
Sports.content:
The Asian Football Confederation has endorsed Gianni Infantino for another term as Fifa’s president in a turnaround in its stance from two months ago when it criticised the head of football’s world governing body for a breach of trust.

The AFC president, Sheikh Salman bin Ibrahim al-Khalifa, speaking at the body’s extraordinary congress in Tokyo on Friday, embraced Infantino with a large hug in front of the membership as he delivered his endorsement.

“We affirm our full commitment to supporting you and your leadership as you seek a new mandate as the Fifa president.” Sheikh Salman said. “You’ve visited a lot of countries in Asia. I’ve spoken to a lot of members within this continent. I know your feeling and I think your commitment is clear as well.”

The AFC has 47 member associations. Even if all the members do not follow the direction of Sheikh Salman, those votes could be a key to guaranteeing another mandate for Infantino. The Fifa election is in March and nominations close on 18 November. So far no one is standing against him.

Addressing his remarks to Infantino, Sheikh Salman indicated not every AFC member would go along with the endorsement but that most will. “My feeling is, I’m sure, the feeling of most of my members,” he said. “And I’ve said that to you.”

This is an abrupt turnaround for Sheikh Salman. In August, the AFC joined Uefa and Concacaf – the North and Central American and Caribbean confederation – in saying that Infantino had committed a “fundamental breach of trust”. They wrote an open letter calling for “leadership that serves football, not seeks to command it”.

Infantino apologised last week in Zurich to Fifa’s council – which he chairs – for “mistakes” he made in assembling a now-scrapped $4.2bn plan to sell chunks of the World Cup to private investors. Sheikh Salman referenced the differences with Infantino in his speech but glossed over any details.

“Yes, we had some issues we spoke about in the past,” he said. “But let’s not relate the two things together. I think the last few [times] we met in Zurich you made it clear that there’s a true understanding between us.”

Even before the AFC endorsement the indications were that Infantino was edging toward a simple majority of the 211 Fifa member federations.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

The largest applause came at the end of Sheikh Salman’s address when he repeated his support for Infantino. Fifa’s president took the podium after and acknowledged some errors. “When you do many things, you do – hopefully, as we did, many good things – you do some mistakes as well,” Infantino said.

The largest applause came as he mentioned how, under his leadership, more millions were flowing. “Before I started as Fifa president, each of you, some of you are still [here] and still remember that time … Each of you was receiving $1m every four years. As of the first of January of next year, it will be $25m.”

Sports.title: Mamdani loves Arsenal. He should challenge them to cut ties with the UAE over Sudan | Sasha Lezhnev and John Prendergast
Sports.content:
Like him or not, there is no doubt that New York mayor Zohran Mamdani’s passion for certain issues is electric, and that passion played a large part in him getting elected. But today, two of his biggest passions are on a collision course.

On one hand, Mamdani is now arguably the US’s most high-profile supporter of English Premier League champions Arsenal. A superfan since he was a child, he has put the Gunners into the American spotlight more than anyone since becoming mayor. The Empire State Building gleamed in Arsenal’s red and white when they won the Premier League title. He wrote an essay about what Arsenal’s championship means to him, talks about Arsenal at press conferences and interviews and inaugurated Thierry Henry Way near Times Square in honor of the Arsenal legend.

But another of Mamdani’s passions – standing up against genocide and for human rights – is now presenting a problem for the mayor’s Arsenal fandom. One prominent part of Arsenal’s current image is deeply disturbing, and it presents a major opportunity for Mamdani.

Arsenal’s chief sponsor is Emirates Airlines, owned by the Emirates Group, a state-owned Dubai-based holding company. Emirates is on the front of every jersey, and the team plays at Emirates Stadium in London. The United Arab Emirates has spent more than $1bn sponsoring the team, including expanding its contract through 2033 to more than $100m per season. Arsenal is the UAE’s second biggest sports investment globally.

The trouble is the UAE is also sponsoring a genocidal militia in Sudan, where war has created the world’s largest displacement crisis, with 14 million people, or a quarter of the country’s population, forced to flee their homes, and 21 million people facing acute hunger. The UAE has provided the militia, known as the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), with weapons and killer drones, according to numerous investigations. In fact, the UAE is the RSF’s biggest supplier of weapons and drones.

And therein lies the rub. The UAE is engaging in one of the world’s largest sportswashing campaigns in an attempt to clean up its image, including with Mamdani’s beloved Arsenal. The UAE’s sportswashing isn’t limited to the Gunners. We calculated that the UAE government has spent more than $5.2bn on sponsoring sports teams and leagues around the world, including Manchester City, the NBA champion New York Knicks (a team Mamdani also cheers for), the Emirates NBA Cup and Formula One. There are multiple other football, basketball, cycling, rugby, cricket and UAE-sponsored teams as well.

The good news is that Arsenal’s ownership isn’t blind to abusive sportswashing relationships. Last year, the club announced it was cutting its sleeve sponsor, Visit Rwanda, after the country’s invasion of the Democratic Republic of Congo and the humanitarian catastrophe that ensued as a result. More than 8 million people have been displaced from their homes, as Rwanda has invaded the DRC and commanded the deadly M23 militia that has tortured victims, engaged in extensive sexual violence and enlisted child soldiers. The Arsenal Supporters’ Trust weighed in on the issue, following campaign initiatives such as Gunners for Peace, and the owners changed course.

double quotation mark One prominent part of Arsenal’s current face is deeply disturbing, and it presents a major opportunity for Mayor Mamdani

Now it’s time for Arsenal to tackle their bigger sportswashing sponsor, and Mamdani can play a key role. As one of the world’s most visible Arsenal fans, his voice would have an important impact on the club’s decision makers. The club’s owners are American, Josh and Stan Kroenke, and they have stood up in the past for human rights – for instance, calling for a lifetime ban on former Los Angeles Clippers owner Don Sterling for making racist remarks.

Mamdani could make the Kroenkes and the rest of the Arsenal board aware of the UAE’s sportswashing and call on them either publicly or privately to move on to another sponsor because of the genocidal militia the UAE is sponsoring in Sudan. The club is, after all, awash in cash after winning the league and reaching the final of the Champions League, earning $411m in total, a record for Arsenal. It is now reportedly the most profitable football club in England. So they don’t need the Emirati money.

Importantly, the UAE is not the only game in town for football sponsors – there are viable alternatives. Snapdragon, a Qualcomm tech company, pays approximately the same amount for sponsoring Manchester United as the Emirates pays Arsenal, and automaker Jeep and telecom company T-Mobile pay Juventus and Bayern Munich just a hair under.

Arsenal canceling the deal would also have a meaningful impact on the UAE and on the genocide unfolding in Sudan. The UAE is very sensitive to public image, and a cancelled Arsenal deal would be a major public relations blow. Mamdani’s intervention could have major human rights implications.

Mamdani is passionate about human rights, combating genocide and supporting his favorite team. Urging the club’s leadership to change its sponsor from the UAE would combine all three passions into one and potentially have a positive impact on the world’s deadliest humanitarian crisis. New Yorkers and Arsenal fans alike should encourage Mamdani to weigh in with the club on this important issue.

Sports.title: Tearful Simone Biles struggles to come to terms with quick sale of $1M mansion she shared with NFL star husband
Sports.content:
Tearful Simone Biles struggles to come to terms with quick sale of $1M mansion she shared with NFL star husband

Simone Biles broke down in tears as she said an emotional goodbye to her stunning Texas home where she spent six years alongside NFL star husband Jonathan Owens.

The 29-year-old took to TikTok to share the bittersweet moment with fans after the 3,998sq ft property was snapped up just four days after hitting the market.

'Why the f*** am I boohoo crying? F***,' Biles said through tears as she panned around the empty residence.

'This house will be on the market for the first time and I don't know why I'm boohoo crying. I was here for six years and I feel like there were so many good memories.

'I feel like I grew up in this house. It's made me a real adult so I'm going to miss it. Ugh, I didn't think I'd be emotional about a house', the gymnastics icon added.

Biles walked through the vacant rooms before stepping outside to the spacious backyard before sharing a warm message for the future homeowners.

Simone Biles broke down in tears as she said an emotional goodbye to her Texas home

The 29-year-old took to TikTok to share the bittersweet moment with fans after the 3,998-square-foot property was snapped up just four days after hitting the market

'Whoever buys this house, I hope it brings you as much joy as it did for me', she said.

Biles captioned the video: “I was so excited to put in air fresheners for the potential buyers & showing Jonathan the last look. I just cried instead… anyone else?”

The property was initially listed for $1.275 million before eventually being sold for a fee between $1.08 million and $1.24 million, according to the Houston Association of Realtors.

Spanning nearly 4,000sq ft in a gated community near Spring, Texas, the four-bedroom, 3.5-bathroom estate sits on just over an acre of land.

The luxury residence features a heated backyard swimming pool, an in-home sauna, a dedicated dog-washing station and a custom wine display wall.

Inside, the home boasts a waterfall island kitchen with quartz countertops, a hidden walk-in pantry and an oversized three-car garage.

The property went under contract just four days after the listing went live on September 22, with the sale officially closing on October 15.

The gymnastics icon spent six years in the home alongside NFL star husband Jonathan Owens

Earlier this year, Biles shared a glimpse at the stunning property in a series of online posts

The update comes one month after Biles revealed three masked intruders broke into her Chicago home and stole her luxurious Porsche.

The legendary Team USA gymnast dropped the bombshell news during a TikTok video. It remains unclear when the burglary happened or if the police have made any arrests but Biles confirmed the car was recovered.

'Feel like I need a new car because during our last few months in Chicago, three men in masks came to our house and stole my Porsche,' she said.

'Stole the GTS. But that's another story. If you guys want to know, I'll do a story time on that.'

Sports.title: Michael Carrick's five-minute monologue: Under-fire boss admits Man United have 'lost our way', demands 'humility' from Bruno Fernandes and Co and refuses to say if he'll keep the captaincy
Sports.content:
Under-pressure Manchester United boss Michael Carrick claimed that the club have 'lost our way' in a five-minute opening speech to the media ahead of their crunch clash with Bournemouth.

There is increasing uncertainty surrounding Carrick's future at Old Trafford following United's humiliating 4-1 defeat away at Como in the Champions League on Wednesday evening.

The defeat by the beautiful lakes of Italy extended United's winless run to seven games in all competitions, with the club not having tasted victory since early September.

The 45-year-old is set to take charge of the Red Devils as they take on the Cherries on Sunday and in his pre-match press conference ahead of the match, Carrick spoke from the heart.

'I'll start today. I just want to say a few things, really,' said Carrick. 'Recently, we haven't had a good time. I think that's pretty obvious. So I totally accept what we're going through at the moment.

'We had five months of relative success in a spell where I was happy with a lot of things I was seeing and that we were doing as a team. We haven't done well enough lately. We've had a spell that we're really not happy with.

Michael Carrick gave a passionate near-six minute address to the media on Friday afternoon

'Wednesday was a bad night. It was a bad night for a lot of reasons. It hurt a lot.

'It obviously hurt me to see us play that way, to see how the game panned out. As I said after the game, it was really unacceptable.

'The supporters are a huge part of this football club. They have to make the effort and the time and money they spend, to feel how we all felt on Wednesday was a tough moment.'

During the impassioned speech, Carrick seemingly issued a call to arms directly to his current squad by saying that Manchester United is 'bigger than any single individual', even listing names of legends such as Sir Alex Ferguson and Sir Bobby Charlton when making his point.

And while Carrick is happy to 'hold the umbrella to keep everyone else dry', he also wants his players to step up and reach the levels demanded by the 20-time champions.

Carrick continued: 'We need to respect this football club and respect what it means to be here, respect what it takes to win, what you have to do to win.

'I'm not entitled to be here. Entitlement cannot be at this football club. We're not entitled to win. We've won in the past, we've got an incredible history, but that doesn't mean that you're entitled to just win.

'I'm fully aware of that. It takes hard work, takes a lot of sacrifice. You've got to invest yourself in the football club and you've got to do a lot of things that maybe aren't so nice, but you've got to do it for each other, and you've got to win.

United are winless in seven games after being humiliated by Como in the Champions League on Wednesday

Carrick refused to say whether had had spoken to Bruno Fernandes since his captain questioned the head coach's tactics

'I think it's important we live up to that, and it's important for me to push those values, and it's important for our supporters to feel that moving forward.

'We've had it, we've kind of lost our way a little bit if I'm totally honest, and we will get it back. I'm totally convinced we'll get it back. Respect this football club, respect what it takes, because it's very, very important to me.'

Following the speech, Carrick was asked to address whether he is considering stripping Bruno Fernandes of the club captaincy after the midfielder questioned his tactics following the defeat to Como. He refused to answer directly.

However, Carrick claimed that the dressing room is 'not divided' despite the outspoken nature of Fernandes and Lisandro Martinez in recent weeks.

Martinez was first to break ranks, taking aim at his Old Trafford bosses – and director of football Jason Wilcox in particular – following a 2-0 defeat to Atletico Madrid in the Champions League last week. Fernandes then followed suit to question why United were so passive again.

He said: 'It's a decision from the staff to not press man to man and sometimes leave space behind and try to get the ball, wait for them, but sometimes when you give space to these teams they get confidence.'

Asked if he meant that Carrick got his tactics wrong, Fernandes added: 'That's on the manager and staff to say, not me.

‘Sometimes you have to be more brave under pressure, take the risk of pressing high and making them uncomfortable. As you saw with Como, the centre back was coming to mark me in my own half. We need to do that as a team but we were unable to.

‘A team that plays through the middle with small connections, if you give them too much time and space then they can hurt you out wide.’

Sports.title: Inside Matthias Jaissle's Newcastle struggles: 'Vertical football' philosophy that led to crisis meeting, fan concern at Ruben Amorim echoes, square pegs in round holes and why he wants to copy Hansi Flick's Barcelona blueprint
Sports.content:
It is a good time to play Crystal Palace. That, at least, is the crumb of comfort being nibbled at on Tyneside this week. The rather more uncomfortable truth is that it is also a good time to play Newcastle United.

Just two months in and, unfairly or otherwise, Matthias Jaissle’s future is being measured by some in days and weeks. Not by those inside St James’ Park, nor inside the PIF towers of Riyadh, and not by those on the outside who make allowance for the difficulty of the situation he inherited in August.

Newcastle sold their best players and replaced them with, to be brutally candid, inferior models. It is hard, of course, to upgrade on stars who leave for Barcelona and Arsenal, and what was billed as a brave new era has, in the short term, looked like a backwards stumble.

But Jaissle’s job, as is that of any manager, is to manage what he has, not lament what has been lost. At present, too many square pegs are being hammered into round holes in the hope that they will fit, which they have not. During Saturday’s 1-0 home defeat by Aston Villa, three players started in a position they would not consider their best.

Among them was £51million marquee signing Matias Fernandez-Pardo, who arrived on the promise of reinventing himself as a striker. After three starts without a goal, the 21-year-old was shifted to the wing, albeit the opposite flank to where he spent much of his time at previous club Lille.

Meanwhile, at No 10, in the absence of an actual No 10, midfielders and strikers continue to moonlight.

Just two months in and, unfairly or otherwise, Matthias Jaissle’s future as Newcastle manager is being measured by some in days and weeks

In the defeat against Villa, three players started in a position they would not consider their best. Among them was £51million marquee signing Matias Fernandez-Pardo

In the closing stages, centre back Dan Burn was then parachuted in at centre forward. The last time he did that, England were chasing a World Cup semi-final against Argentina.

Jaissle’s ploy was criticised, but the sobering thought for Newcastle, a club who have spent £175m trying to replace Alexander Isak, is that the Hail Mary was their only prayer.

Mitigation for a head coach, however, only extends into so many matches. Another defeat at Selhurst Park – Newcastle have lost three of the last four – and the trauma of summer will be overtaken by the anguish of today. That means more focus on Jaissle and less on the deeper legacy issues as to why his side are struggling.

As opposite number Pierre Sage has found, when there is no easily reachable body of work to use as a shield against scrutiny, judgment can be quick and unforgiving.

Jaissle, at 38 years old and having landed from Saudi Arabia via a successful period with Red Bull Salzburg in Austria, is learning that harsh reality in the harshest of surrounds.

By any reasonable measure, the young German should be afforded time, patience and understanding. He is bright and, increasingly, likeable.

In the Premier League, however, what you deserve you don’t always get. Supporters, especially those amplified by football’s anger-rithm, demand immediate evidence of competence and progress. In other words, results.

Yet the concern when it comes to Jaissle and Newcastle, among those not governed by such outcome-driven emotion, is that the underlying numbers and observations of the eye are more troubling than a far-from-disastrous league position of 11th.

In the closing stages against Villa, centre back Dan Burn was parachuted in at centre forward, a Jaissle ploy that has been criticised

‘Expected Points’ has Harvey Barnes and his Newcastle team-mates in the bottom three of the Premier League

The manager is not blind to that reality, either. He is aware of his side's critical ball losses and unforced errors ranking too highly in the division. ‘Expected Points’, also, has them in the bottom three.

Jaissle has held meetings with his players over the past fortnight, the first in the wake of last week’s 4-1 defeat by Coventry, when issues over the implementation of his ‘vertical football’ philosophy were addressed. His 4-2-3-1 formation has consistently left them exposed in midfield.

Before that, following another 4-1 loss at Leeds last month, Jaissle determined that the poor performance was not a consequence of his tactical approach.

He felt helpless at Elland Road when his players failed to compete for first balls, never mind second, and were bullied into submission.

Working alongside a dozen analysts in a war room at the club’s training ground, he decided it was no time to abandon his strategy when basic application was more so to blame.

But now that effort is present – few could question Newcastle’s commitment against Villa – the spotlight returns to shape, game-plan and preparation. The basics of a manager, if you like.

That has been the source of debate this week. The doubters have likened the coach to Ruben Amorim or Ange Postecoglou, stubbornly wedded to a style that will likely lead to divorce. Jaissle believes otherwise but says he needs time.

‘We have for sure a lot of potential still,’ he said. ‘This is something I mentioned to some of the club’s decision-makers, that sometimes we still feel in pre-season when we train with the group. We are still implementing the basics for our way of playing. It takes time. The good part is that everyone within the club is realistic and can see that.’

By any reasonable measure, the young German manager should be afforded time, patience and understanding

One of those decision-makers is Jacobo Solis, the Spanish PIF chief and club director who was, unusually, present for Jaissle's press conference on Friday. We understand nothing should be made of that, and Solis is taking the chance to spend time around the club while entry to Riyadh is disrupted.

Solis was raised on La Liga and that is where Jaissle has also looked for some reassurance in recent weeks. Indeed, he has noted an interview with Barcelona midfielder Rodri, who spoke of the intensity and physicality with which they train, a level replicated on a matchday. That is Jaissle’s vision.

He looks at what countryman Hansi Flick is achieving at Camp Nou, with a 4-2-3-1 set-up, and he wants that energy and incision at Newcastle. His conviction is to be admired, but there is a fine line between sticking to your principles and being held hostage by them.

Jaissle has the kindest fixture in the calendar this weekend. But if the gift horse bites, patience will be the first thing to bolt.

Sports.title: Stamp of disapproval! Shocked rugby fans demand lifetime BAN for Welsh player's 'disgusting' violent trample
Sports.content:
Rugby fans have called for a player to be banned from the sport for life for a deliberate act of violence during a semi-professional match in Wales.

The shocking incident occurred during a Super Rygbi Cymru match between Llandovery and Ebbw Vale on Thursday night.

Ebbw Vale lock Curtis Gregory was handed a straight red card late in the first half after being caught deliberately stamping on an opposition player.

During a ruck in the 35th minute, Gregory saw the leg of a Llandovery star and deliberately stomped his boot into the player's knee.

The victim of the stamp appeared to come away unharmed and immediately got up to confront Gregory. A heated altercation followed before the Ebbw Vale player was given his marching orders.

After spotting the incident, the referee said: 'We have a stamp by this player. I did ask the question if anything aggravated it.

Lock Curtis Gregory was red-carded for stamping on an opponent during a semi-professional match between his side Ebbw Vale and Llandovery

'My AR (assistant referee) didn't see anything. It's a stamp on the leg. Red card. Permanent.'

Dyfed-Powys Police have confirmed to Daily Mail Sport that the incident has not been reported to them, and there is currently no investigation ongoing.

A clip of the incident posted on S4C's social media channels displays the reaction from commentators covering the game. Both let out a groan after seeing replays of the incident.

The stamp also left rugby fans shocked and horrified, with many taking to social media to voice their disgust.

One Reddit user posted the clip online and captioned it: 'If anything deserves a life ban, it's this one'.

Another user replied: 'Yup - ban him for life. It was intentional and could easily have resulted in a career-ending injury for his victim.'

Further replies to the clip saw angry rugby fans call Gregory 'disgusting' for the stamp, while a different user backed the call for a lifetime ban by saying that he 'shouldn't be allowed near a pitch again'.

Sports.title: Lewis Hamilton calls for 'free Congo, free Sudan, free Syria, free Palestine' and demands colonialism problems are added to school curriculums in new outburst about 'the west intervening'
Sports.content:
Lewis Hamilton calls for 'free Congo, free Sudan, free Syria, free Palestine' and demands colonialism problems are added to school curriculums in new outburst about 'the west intervening'

Lewis Hamilton has spoken out about concerns surrounding the controversial proposed African Grand Prix in Rwanda, after making clear his desire to compete in the race.

It was announced last week that the sport will return to Africa for the first time since 1993, with a race confirmed in Rwanda from approximately 2032 in a 10-season deal.

Hamilton has long argued that F1 should race on the continent once again, having last held a Grand Prix there in Kyalami, South Africa, more than 30 years ago.

And while the 41-year-old – who may well be 46 by the time the race rolls around – has vowed to carry on racing to complete a long-desired ambition to compete on the continent, the seven-time world champion also voiced his worries regarding Rwanda's human rights record.

Hamilton used his platform to call for Africa to unite amid the proxy war inside Rwanda's neighbouring country, the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC).

'I don't get to choose where we go and naturally there's problems all over the world today,' Hamilton said. 'I've seen many of the stories, but I think we really have to approach it with humility.

Lewis Hamilton has voiced his worries regarding Rwanda's human rights record amid the proposed African Grand Prix

'There's a lot that we don't know. Growing up in England, they never ever taught us anything about Africa. It needs to be on the curriculum: a lot of the problems they have there are still results of colonialism and the west intervening.

'But if you see the people, you see so many designs that are out there today; top brands come from Africa and it's got all the richest resources.

'I really hope, and I still have hopes, that Africa unites. I know there's many people that don't want that to happen because they would be so powerful if they did, but I'm still hopeful that at some stage they will.'

The United Nations and Western governments accuse Rwanda of backing the armed rebel group M23 with weapons and troops to fight a proxy war inside the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC). Rwanda deny supporting the insurgency.

Millions of civilians in eastern DRC have been displaced or killed as the conflict spirals into a humanitarian crisis.

Hamilton believes that more people need to speak up on the ongoing war in the Congo, alongside the ongoing Israel-Hamas conflict, the latest Sudanese civil war and the conflict in Syria.

Hamilton added: 'Of course, going doesn't mean that you neglect the things that are happening there.

'So hopefully many people start to educate themselves a little bit more about what is happening there, what has happened there for hundreds of years and I hope that does spark the conversation.

F1 will return to Africa with Rwanda set to host at an unbuilt track (pictured an artist's impression)

'I guess I'll finish it off with: I think we need to make sure we're pushing to free Congo, free Sudan, free Syria, free Palestine. I think there's a lot of peace that I'm hoping that at some stage we get to.'

Rwanda is a controversial presence in British sport over its human rights record and alleged ‘sportswashing’ with the ‘Visit Rwanda’ brand drawing criticism as a sponsor of Arsenal for eight years, before ending in June. ‘Visit Rwanda’ are now Aston Villa’s main shirt sponsor.

Amnesty International UK’s head of campaigns Felix Jakes said recently: ‘Rwanda is buying into the world's biggest sports to polish its image and deflect from its appalling human rights record.

‘Formula One says sport can be "a positive force for good". That rings hollow if F1 shrugs off who it is partnering with. Formula One must not be a bystander. It should use its influence with the Rwandan authorities to push for change, rather than lend its brand to a PR exercise.’

Sports.title: How John Murtough will supercharge Birmingham City's Premier League mission: Cutting out expensive mistakes, elite contacts book and academy revolution
Sports.content:
If anyone thought Birmingham were scaling back their ambitions after failing to reach the Premier League last season, they should think again today.

As exclusively revealed by Daily Mail Sport, Blues have appointed former Manchester United transfer chief John Murtough as their new director of football.

The remit is wide and yet narrow. He will oversee every area of the club but when the 55-year-old was approached for the job, the priority will have been clear – help us reach the Premier League.

Daily Mail Sport looks at why Blues went for Murtough and what he will be expected to deliver at St Andrew’s...

Promotion plans

Murtough was director of football for three years at Old Trafford and left in April 2024, soon after Sir Jim Ratcliffe took control. He had also been United’s academy manager and director of development.

Knighthead’s plan for Blues is predicated on reaching the Premier League. They have invested heavily in transfers but not always made the right calls, as the summer 2025 recruitment drive proved. High wages were paid to players like Kyogo Furuhashi, who had little impact and left after a year.

John Murtough - Birmingham City's new director of football - is pictured with Erik ten Hag at his Manchester United unveiling

Blues have made some costly mistakes in the transfer window in recent years - including signing Kyogo Furuhashi (right)

During 11 years at Old Trafford, Murtough became known as ‘The Fixer’ and was instrumental in the appointment of Erik ten Hag. While the Dutchman divided opinion, he did deliver the FA Cup and the Carabao Cup – no small achievements in the post-Sir Alex Ferguson era.

Murtough was a driving force behind the women’s team at United. He also overhauled the approach to academy recruitment to target some of the best age-group players overseas. One of those who arrived on his watch was Alejandro Garnacho, who scored 26 goals and had 22 assists in 144 games and was sold to Chelsea for £40million.

Even though Murtough was criticised when players like Antony and Rasmus Hojlund struggled, there are those at United who feel his influence has been missed since his departure.

Birmingham hope to enjoy the fruits of that now. When Knighthead took control three years ago, they spoke of hiring ‘exceptional leaders’. The Americans are convinced Murtough fits the bill.

Recruitment shift?

Nobody would doubt Craig Gardner’s commitment or work ethic, yet his approach to recruitment could be haphazard at times.

Blues are convinced that will change under Murtough. The summer window was overseen by the impressive Joe Carnall, whose reputation in the game is growing, and he would be a strong lieutenant to Murtough.

Carnall is an expert in coding and analytics tools. There are numerous metrics within Blues’ data model, most of which are guarded closely to ensure rivals do not gain a competitive edge. But no player will be signed unless he clears the data checks.

In recent times, Blues under Knighthead have insisted any transfer target should have up to three seasons’ senior football under his belt. They have also prioritised durability and have prioritised players in their mid-20s, although Colombian midfielder Jhon Solis is a notable exception. Solis has only just turned 22 but is already worth at least double the £6.5m Blues paid Girona for him last summer.

It will be interesting to see whether Murtough tries to alter this. Blues believe his vast experience and long list of contacts across the global game will open doors for them. Though Gardner did a fine job as technical director and was admired by Knighthead, Murtough is the kind of guy who can make football’s big players pick up the phone.

Jhon Solis is an exception to Birmingham's transfer rule of recent seasons - but already worth far more than Blues paid for him

Birmingham chiefs will hope there are more good times ahead with Murtough in the boardroom

Academy issues

Birmingham's youth set-up has been one of the top priorities for Knighthead since they took charge. After years of neglect by previous ownership groups, the Americans feel they have been playing catch-up for too long.

While Aston Villa have invested heavily in their academy and West Bromwich Albion’s is admired across the country, Blues have struggled. Blues’ academy was awarded category one status in May 2025 – a significant step forward – but attracting top talent across the region and beyond has still been a challenge.

Of course, Birmingham did produce Jude Bellingham, possibly the finest English footballer of his generation and one of the best on the planet. His younger brother, Jobe, and Jordan James, also made the first team before moving on but Blues want more.

If anyone can rectify that, it is Murtough. During his first spell with Everton’s academy, Wayne Rooney advanced to the first team. He also helped shape the system that delivered Jack Rodwell and Ross Barkley to the senior side. At United, Kobbie Mainoo progressed from a nine-year-old hopeful to a Premier League starter while Murtough was in place. Anthony Elanga and Garnacho also had useful United careers.

In the era of strict financial rules, developing homegrown players is essential – even if they do not establish themselves in the first team. As unromantic as it is, these players can be sold for pure profit with the money reinvested into recruitment.

The best place to implement such plans is the Premier League. Along with boss Chris Davies and his squad, Birmingham are counting on Murtough to take them there.

Sports.title: Wayne Rooney rips into Man United's 'babies' after explosive outbursts from Lisandro Martinez and Bruno Fernandes - and labels captain 'selfish' following public criticism of Michael Carrick
Sports.content:
Wayne Rooney lambasted Manchester United's players in the wake of explosive comments made by Lisandro Martinez and Bruno Fernandes, describing the group as 'selfish' and 'like babies' amid a dismal run of form. Team captain Fernandes openly questioned Michael Carrick's tactics after a woeful 4-1 defeat to Como on Wednesday evening, one week after Martinez criticised the board's transfer strategy after a first limp showing on the road in Europe against Atletico Madrid. Man United legend Rooney admitted that the moment he heard Martinez's comments, he knew it was an 'absolute nightmare' scenario, destined to 'rip the dressing room apart'. 'That was the start,' Rooney explained on the United Stand podcast. 'We've seen it now with Bruno and you're going to see it with more players because they don't want to take responsibility. 'You can say whether Bruno was right or wrong in what he said but you have to take responsibility on the pitch. You have to take responsibility as a group of players. 'These players, they're selfish. They don't care about their team-mates, don't care about the manager, the staff or the fans, they care about themselves. If they're not getting what's right for them, they're like babies and just throw their toys out of the pram and go and deflect the blame on to anyone else but themselves.' Wayne Rooney described Man United's players as 'selfish' and 'like babies' in the wake of their 4-1 defeat to Como Bruno Fernandes appeared to hit out at his manager Michael Carrick's tactics after the loss Rooney added that he believed that Fernandes had made his comments because of his unwillingness to 'face' a personal drop-off in his form this season, instead opting to put 'pressure on someone else'. 'If he looks at himself in the mirror, if Martinez and all of them looked at themselves in the mirror, they'll find what's looking back at them is them, and that's not good enough,' he continued. 'They need to show more.' Fernandes had shrugged off questions of Man United's passivity and instead directed it towards his manager in the aftermath of defeat beside Lake Como on Wednesday. 'It's a decision from the staff to not press man to man and sometimes leave space behind and try to get the ball, wait for them, but sometimes when you give space to these teams they get confidence,' he said. Asked if he meant that Carrick got his tactics wrong, Fernandes added: ‘That's on the manager and staff to say, not me. ‘Sometimes you have to be more brave under pressure, take the risk of pressing high and making them uncomfortable. As you saw with Como, the centre back was coming to mark me in my own half. We need to do that as a team but we were unable to.' When his comments were put to Carrick in his post-match press conference, the former midfielder suggested that there was an issue with his players' willingness to run. ‘We actually were half-pressed man-to-man in the second half and then conceded a goal from that,’ he said. ‘There's a little bit on whatever system you play, whatever tactics you play, but if you don't run – you don't run forward and you don't run back – you aren’t going to win.’ On their performance more widely, the former United midfielder said: 'It was more than disappointing. I think everyone has to take responsibility for that. 'I'll 100 per cent take responsibility for the overall team and performance; that stops with me and I accept that. But as a supporter of this club for so long and I care so much about this club, to see a performance like that is unacceptable.' Man United were outplayed on a dreadful rainswept Champions League night on Wednesday His team-mate Youri Tielemans admitted that the squad had been lacking effort in every area, and outplayed by Como. 'It's a combination of everything: tactical, technical, effort. We need to try do better at everything,' he said after the match. 'It's the same message as we've had the last few weeks. We can be here and talk about it, but we have to show it on the pitch. We can only apologise to the fans who travelled, the fans who watched us from home and support us. They're disappointed and we're disappointed. 'The only thing we can do is try to show something on the pitch, which we haven't done over the last few weeks.' Man United have three days before facing their next opponents Bournemouth in Premier League action this weekend and Rooney implored his former team-mate to 'come out fighting' amid widespread speculation that his days in the dugout might be numbered. Giving his own advice, he told Carrick he should show players 'there's no more Mr Nice Guy'. 'There are certain things you've got to do to protect them players, but you have to come out fighting for yourself because those players will drag you down and it's going to be you who's going to lose your job over it,' he stressed. Man United's civil war is not limited to the dressing room: Daily Mail Sport reported on Thursday that there are growing tensions between director of football Jason Wilcox and director of recruitment Christopher Vivell over the next manager of the club - should Carrick be replaced. Vivell is understood to be pushing hard for Julian Nagelsmann to be the leading candidate, with the 39-year-old out of work following a disastrous World Cup in charge of Germany. Chelsea assessed Nagelsmann as a potential manager when Vivell was technical director in west London and his admiration remains. But sources have suggested that Wilcox, who is Vivell’s boss in the chain of command, prefers a Premier League proven manager, with Eddie Howe, Fabian Hurzeler, Unai Emery and Antonio Conte, who have all come up on a shortlist, a tick in that category. Hurzeler does not have a release clause in his Brighton contract and so would require enormous compensation. There is well-placed scepticism as to whether any move would even be remotely possible, regardless of how well liked he is inside Old Trafford. Carrick is set to be in charge at least until after Man United's pre-Premier League weekend press conference, which is set to take place on Friday. After facing the Cherries at Old Trafford on Sunday, Man United will also play host to Roma at the beginning of next month, after a test away at Chelsea. A final home match against Aston Villa will come before the next two-week international break in November.
