World.title: SA Explained | eNCA/MarkData 2026 Election Poll: Is Cape Town's DA Majority Safe as Johannesburg Fragments? | 23 October 2026
World.content:
A City Can Be Well Run and Still Leave People Behind

South Africa's local elections are testing more than political loyalty. They are exposing difficult questions about what good municipal government should deliver, who benefits from it, and how residents judge the results.

A city can collect revenue, maintain roads, manage its finances and earn relatively favourable ratings from residents while still struggling with crime, exclusion and unequal access to opportunity. Conversely, a city can promise a more inclusive future while failing to keep basic infrastructure functioning. Neither picture tells the whole story of good governance.

That tension emerges from the latest eNCA/MarkData local government election survey. In Cape Town, 60.5% of respondents described the municipality as either very well or averagely well run. In Johannesburg, the corresponding figure was 29.2%. These are perceptions reported by surveyed residents, rather than independent audits of municipal performance, but the contrast raises a larger question: what exactly should South Africans expect from a functioning city?

The difference between running a city and making it fair

Cape Town's proposed N2 security wall illustrates the complexity. The survey found that 69.6% of respondents supported the proposal, while 19.9% opposed it. The City has presented the project as a way to improve safety along a dangerous transport corridor. Critics have questioned its implications for communities living alongside the highway and whether it addresses the deeper conditions that allow violence to persist.

Both safety and the equitable use of public space are legitimate matters for public scrutiny. Residents travelling along the route should be able to reach their destinations without fear of attack. Residents living alongside it should also have a meaningful voice in decisions affecting their neighbourhoods. A physical barrier might address particular risks, but its effectiveness, consequences and alternatives must be examined rather than assumed.

The disagreement also reveals how difficult it can be to define public value. A project could be welcomed by road users and opposed by neighbouring communities without either response capturing every practical consequence. That is precisely why public consultation, clear evidence of effectiveness and transparent spending decisions matter.

The infrastructure question Johannesburg cannot escape

Johannesburg presents a different accountability problem. The survey found that 68.7% of respondents assessed the municipality as either not well run or extremely badly run. Residents' dissatisfaction is not itself a technical assessment of the city's infrastructure, but the underlying importance of water, electricity, roads and sewerage is difficult to overstate.

The Auditor-General has previously identified inadequate preventative maintenance and infrastructure-management failures affecting Johannesburg's water and

electricity services. Problems of this kind are rarely solved by changing a political slogan. They require functioning procurement, competent management, realistic budgets, preventive maintenance and sustained oversight.

A broken water pipe offers an unusually clear test of political accountability. Residents need to know who is responsible for the repair, whether funding exists, when the work will happen and how the city will prevent the same failure from recurring. When these answers are missing, distrust becomes a practical consequence of institutional weakness.

Beyond the politics of comparison

Cape Town and Johannesburg should not be reduced to a contest over which city is better. Their different survey results invite scrutiny of what each municipality delivers, but also of what remains unresolved. A comparatively favourable performance rating does not settle questions about spatial inequality. Widespread dissatisfaction does not, by itself, identify which political arrangement will repair a failing service.

South Africa's Constitution places local government within a democratic framework that requires accountable institutions and representation of communities. The real test comes between elections, when councils must turn political decisions into public services.

Better municipal government therefore needs two measures of success: whether the administration works, and whether the benefits and burdens of that administration are distributed fairly. Reliable water, safe roads, transparent spending and meaningful consultation are not competing ambitions. They are parts of the same public obligation.

The question facing South Africa's metros is not simply who controls the council chamber after the ballots are counted. It is whether residents can experience the difference in the streets, homes and neighbourhoods where local government is supposed to matter most.

World.title: UPDATE: Case against 'pastor', wives postponed
World.content:
JOHANNESBURG - The case against self-proclaimed pastor Caiphus Mkhawane and his two co-accused has been postponed.

The trio appeared in the Atteridgeville Magistrate's Court on Friday.

They face charges related to the rape of a 43-year-old mother and the murder of her four-month-old baby.

READ | Baby murder case raises questions over accountability of religious leaders

According to reports, the woman accompanied Mkhawane and one of his wives to the Hennops River for a ritual, where she was allegedly raped.

The baby was allegedly abducted and killed as part of a plan to cash in on a funeral policy.

The matter will return to court on 29 October to allow for accused number one, Ntsako Makhubela, to undergo a mental evaluation.

World.title: Dressed to kill: Haircuts cap menacing look of Japan's yakuza
World.content:
TOKYO - At a barbershop in Tokyo, yakuza gangster Tekisasu glances in the mirror at his meticulous new cut and thanks the hairdresser for the weekly trim crucial to his mobster trade.

Japan's yakuza operate an organised crime empire worth billions of dollars and have long dominated the country's drug rings, gambling dens and sex trade.

From precise haircuts to sharp suits, many mobsters try to project an image of menace and wealth, and barbers play a key role in crafting it.

"The yakuza are all about vanity," said Tekisasu, whose moniker means "Enemy Stabber", in an exclusive interview that took months to set up.

"The neater someone's appearance, the better his reputation becomes," the 44-year-old active gangster allied to a major clan told AFP.

"Say you want to sell someone on a deal... they won't take you seriously if your punch perm is all in shambles," he said, referencing his ultra-short, tightly curled style.

For Tekisasu and his fellow mobsters, barbershops also represent a break from the violent lifestyle they have chosen and an intensifying crackdown by authorities.

World.title: Marquez tops incident-packed opening practice for Australian MotoGP
World.content:
PHILLIP ISLAND - World champion Marc Marquez topped the timesheets in an incident-packed first practice at the Australian MotoGP on Friday ahead of Raul Fernandez and Jack Miller who both took nasty tumbles.

The Spanish Ducati rider clocked a last-gasp blistering lap of 1min 27.985sec around the waterfront Phillip Island circuit -- which is hosting its final MotoGP -- in warm but windy conditions.

Championship leader Jorge Martin, who is two points clear of Marquez with five rounds of the season left, came seventh on his Aprilia.

Marco Bezzecchi, who won last week in Indonesia and is third in the standings, was fourth, also on an Aprilia.

Marquez's fastest time put him 0.048 ahead of last year's Australian grand prix winner Fernandez, who skidded off at Turn 7 and barrel-rolled across the gravel mid-way through the session.

Iker Lecuona, standing in for the injured Fermin Aldeguer at Ducati-Gresini, also suffered a fall at the same corner, bouncing off a tyre wall.

Both men walked away uninjured.

Home hero Miller was another to crash out at high-speed, this time at Turn 2, just seconds after setting the fastest time. He gave the thumbs up afterwards to signal he was okay.

Brad Binder, meanwhile, suffered a big engine failure on the main straight, pulling off with white smoke billowing from his KTM.

Phillip Island has been a staple on the calendar since 1997, but the Australian race is moving next year to a street circuit in Adelaide.

The second practice session, from which the top 10 riders go straight into Saturday's second round of qualifying, gets underway at 3:00 pm (0400 GMT).

World.title: Reclaiming the walls in a former Salvadoran gang hotspot
World.content:
SAN MARCOS - In El Salvador, walls that were once plastered with gang graffiti now feature tableaux of birds, flowers and landscapes, as artists reclaim public spaces from vanquished crime gangs.

A few years ago, Colonia 10 de Octubre district in the town of San Marcos, about 10 kilometres from the capital San Salvador, was a no-go zone.

Only people given the nod by the brutal Mara Salvatrucha (MS-13) gang dared to enter this warren of small houses, where bodies of murder victims were dumped on the street and extortion was rife.

Armed with spray cans and paintbrushes, Patricia Vega, Marcela Alvarenga, and Elizabeth Guardado are giving a makeover to one of the many communities where President Nayib Bukele has cracked down on the country's "pandillas" (gangs) since 2022.

The women, two of whom teach art, were invited to help reinvent the district by a collective that promotes social inclusion through urban art.

Vega told AFP she grew up in fear of places like Colonia 10 de Octubre, named after the date of a 1986 earthquake that killed approximately 1,500 people in El Salvador, because of their brutal turf wars and violence against women.

World.title: Pentagon, Lockheed announce agreement for 850 F-35 jets over 10 years
World.content:
WASHINGTON - The Pentagon and Lockheed Martin on Thursday announced a 10-year agreement for the production of 850 F-35 warplanes, underscoring Washington's long-term commitment to the high-tech stealth aircraft.

The two sides did not specify a value for the agreement, which comes as the Pentagon seeks to strike multi-year deals to expand American weapons production and boost the US defense industrial base.

The announcement "cements (the plane's) role as the free world's key frontline fighter for years ahead," Lockheed Chairman, President and CEO Jim Taiclet said on a call with investors.

F-35s -- which Washington's forces have used in combat during the US-Israeli war against Iran -- come in three versions that can cost more than $100 million per plane.

The "framework agreement," which the Pentagon said would "modernise and expand" the F-35 program, still requires congressional approval and funding.

"We have fundamentally changed how we stabilise the American defense industrial base to produce at speed and scale," top acquisition official Michael Duffey said in the Pentagon's announcement.

"By aligning financial incentives with actual performance, we are ensuring our warfighters are equipped with the lethal capabilities they need to fight and win," Duffey said.

The F-35, a joint project between the United States and a number of allies, is one of the world's most advanced military aircraft. There are more than 1,375 F-35s based around the world, according to Lockheed.

The deal, if approved, would give Washington a "predictable, affordable, and resilient" fighter jet program, Lockheed said, pointing to billions of dollars in expected savings thanks to "long-term pricing and industry volume discounts."

- 'Greater certainty' -

In exchange for the Pentagon's 10-year commitment, Lockheed Martin will fund $7 billion in projects supporting the F-35s, the Pentagon said.

"With the greater certainty that comes from the US government's transformative approach to F-35 production and sustainment, we can make the upfront investments needed to expand capacity, improve efficiency, and build a more resilient supply chain," Lockheed's Taiclet said in a statement.

"That's good for the taxpayer, good for our suppliers and, most importantly, good for the United States and its allies," he added.

In addition to the F-35s themselves, the agreement also covers "initial spares, 10 years of modification kits and sustainment, and international customer orders," Lockheed said.

There is significant international interest in the aircraft, with the United States recently announcing the approval of a $24.3 billion sale of 48 of the stealth planes to Saudi Arabia last month.

Turkey, which was expelled from the F-35 program in 2019 over its purchase of a Russian air defense system, recently expressed confidence that it would regain access to the jets -- a move that is strongly opposed by Israel.

Lockheed said the F-35 program will support more than 315,000 jobs and generate nearly $80 billion in economic activity in the next 10 years, "strengthening the nation's industrial base and providing long-term stability for suppliers."

The company on Thursday announced better-than-expected earnings for the third quarter, once again benefiting from higher activity levels across all of its segments.

Lockheed shares surged more than seven percent in Thursday trading, closing at $590.2.

World.title: LIVESTREAM | AKA, Tibz murder trial continues
World.content:
DURBAN - The murder trial of seven men accused of killing rapper Kiernan “AKA” Forbes and his friend, celebrity chef Tebello “Tibz” Motsoane, continues.

Some of the footage shows accused number four, Mziwethemba Gwabeni, following Forbes from the airport to a hotel while driving different vehicles.

World.title: Ruto hands over COMESA chairmanship, pushes for levy to fund regional programmes
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

President Ruto and Zimbabwean President Emmerson Mnangagwa during the handover of the Common Market for Eastern and Southern Africa chairmanship at the bloc’s 25th Summit of Heads of State and Government in Harare, Zimbabwe, on Thursday, October 22, 2026. [PCS]

President William Ruto has handed over the Common Market for Eastern and Southern Africa (COMESA) chairmanship to Zimbabwean President Emmerson Mnangagwa.

Ruto took over the one-year chairmanship from Burundi’s President Évariste Ndayishimiye at the 24th COMESA Summit in Nairobi on October 9, 2025.

His tenure focused on using digital technology to deepen regional integration, expand trade and promote inclusive growth.

He handed over the role on Thursday, October 22, during the 25th Comesa Summit of Heads of State and Government in Harare, Zimbabwe, where he urged the regional bloc to fast-track a market levy to finance its programmes and institutions.

“We cannot be ambitious in our plans and timid in our financing. Every programme we agree upon must be matched by the resources to deliver it. Otherwise, our communiqués will promise what our budgets cannot pay for,” Ruto said.

He urged the Comesa Secretariat to fast-track Article 168 of the COMESA Treaty, which provides for the Comesa Market Levy, as the organisation seeks sustainable and predictable financing.

The treaty establishes the levy to generate resources for financing the bloc’s activities.

Ruto said officials from finance ministries, central banks and other relevant agencies would meet to consider a draft COMESA Resource Mobilisation Strategy aimed at strengthening member states’ ownership of regional programmes and finding new ways to raise funds.

He called on member states to make financing central to their discussions, warning that the bloc’s institutions and integration agenda would depend on their ability to fund agreed commitments.

“Can we finance what we commit, and deliver what we finance?” he asked.

Ruto also urged African countries to channel more of their domestic financial resources into African institutions rather than leaving funds in foreign accounts while development projects lack capital.

He said Africa holds more than $4 trillion in domestic financial assets, arguing that regional financial institutions could mobilise more of these resources to support trade, infrastructure and development.

Ruto named the Trade and Development Bank (TDB), the African Trade and Investment Development Insurance (ATIDI) and ZEP-RE among the institutions that could mobilise capital for regional priorities.

He urged African governments to place more reserves with these institutions, finance more projects through them and support their bonds and guarantees.

The outgoing Comesa chairperson said the bloc needed stronger regional value chains and more trade among member states as global supply chains faced disruption and protectionism returned.

“Regional integration is no longer a dream we discuss. It is an economic and strategic necessity,” he noted.

Ruto said Comesa’s economic growth rose from 5.6 per cent in 2024 to 6.4 per cent in 2025, while inflation fell from 31 per cent to 13.2 per cent.

Exports among member states increased by 10.5 per cent to $14.7 billion, their highest level between 2020 and 2025, while exports to global markets rose by 6 per cent to $212 billion, he said.

He argued that African countries needed to process more raw materials locally instead of exporting them and importing finished products.

“To every partner who seeks our minerals, our markets and our young workforce, our offer is clear: invest with us, process with us, build with us,” Ruto added.

He called for partnerships based on mutual benefit and equal treatment, saying African countries should have a greater role in determining how their resources and markets contribute to economic development.

World.title: Judge certifies fresh bid to jail Sakaja, Charles Kerich over Sh76.7m debt as urgent
World.content:
Nairobi Governor Johnson Sakaja. [File, Standard]

The High Court has certified as urgent a fresh application seeking to have Nairobi Governor Johnson Sakaja, former Finance Executive Charles Kerich and two other county officials jailed over an alleged breach of a court-approved payment plan in a Sh106.7 million legal fees dispute.

Justice Francis Gikonyo certified the application by Kwengu & Company Advocates seeking to reinstate a three-month jail sentence previously imposed on Kerich and hold Sakaja, current Finance County Executive Committee Member Ibrahim Auma Nyangoya and Chief Officer for Finance Asha Abdi accountable for the alleged failure to pay Sh76.7 million.

World.title: Kenya confirms third Ebola case
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Kenya has confirmed a third case of Ebola involving a 65-year-old woman who is a close relative of the first two patients.

The Ministry of Health, in a statement, said the woman developed a fever, sore throat and malaise while in quarantine, prompting her isolation and testing.

Her samples tested positive for Ebola at both the National Virology Reference Laboratory and the Kenya Medical Research Institute (KEMRI).

According to the Health Director-General Patrick Amoth, the patient has been transferred to an infectious disease unit, where she is receiving supportive care and being monitored.

“Having been in quarantine, she was diagnosed early and is currently receiving supportive care, improving her chances of recovery while limiting the risk of further spread of the disease,” the statement read.

The second patient, on the other hand, is in stable condition and responding well to supportive care.

The latest case brings the number of confirmed Ebola infections in Kenya to three.

According to the Ministry, of the 130 contacts identified so far, 127 had been traced and placed in quarantine, with efforts ongoing to trace the remaining three.

World.title: Motorists, households face fresh fuel price hikes
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

EPRA attributed the price increases to the escalating conflict in the Middle East. [FIle, Standard]

The Energy and Petroleum Regulatory Authority (EPRA) has increased fuel prices, raising the cost of super petrol by Sh12.93 per litre, diesel by Sh9.90, and kerosene by Sh28.49.

The new prices, effective from October 15 to November 14, 2026, will see motorists in Nairobi pay up to Sh226.96 per litre for super petrol, Sh227.76 for diesel, and Sh219.85 for kerosene.

EPRA Director-General Edward Mwirigi Kinyua attributed the price increases to the escalating conflict in the Middle East, which has disrupted petroleum supply chains and driven up the cost of importing fuel.

The rise in kerosene prices is likely to hit low-income households that rely on the fuel for cooking and lighting.

Meanwhile, higher diesel prices could raise the cost of transporting goods and operating public service vehicles, potentially driving up fares and commodity prices.

Diesel is a key fuel for the country's freight transport sector and a significant portion of public service vehicle operations, meaning the increase could have a ripple effect across the economy.

The latest review comes after EPRA maintained pump prices during the September 15 to October 14 pricing period, despite a decline in the cost of importing petrol.

World.title: Oburu Oginga to leave hospital soon - ODM
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

ODM SG Catherine Omanyo criticised bloggers spreading unverified information about the veteran politician.

ODM Secretary General Catherine Omanyo has dismissed social media reports about the health of party leader Oburu Oginga, saying he is recovering well and is expected to be discharged from hospital either today or tomorrow.

Omanyo criticised bloggers spreading unverified information about the veteran politician, accusing them of exploiting his health condition to attract online attention and increase engagement.

“It's unfortunate what I've been reading on social media. Those people who are seeking to have more likes or viewers, they will be disappointed because he's up, he's well, he's fine. In fact, he's headed home either today or tomorrow,” she said.

Omanyo insisted that the reports had exaggerated his situation, dismissing claims of his death and assuring the public that he was doing well.

She noted that health conditions could fluctuate, saying Oburu's position as ODM party leader had made his well-being a subject of heightened public interest.

“Everybody, everybody, including you and me, our health is not static. You can be under the weather any time. It's just that he's a party leader, and it makes breaking news,” Omanyo said.

She urged social media users to exercise restraint when discussing the health of public figures, warning against spreading unverified reports, particularly claims of death, before confirmation from credible sources.

Her remarks come amid growing speculation on social media about Oburu's health, with some users circulating unverified claims about his condition.

World.title: Kenya declares Ebola a formidable epidemic disease, sets new rules
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Health Cabinet Secretary Aden Duale, who declared Ebola caused by the Bundibugyo virus a formidable epidemic disease under the Public Health Act. [File,Standard]

Kenya has declared Ebola virus a formidable epidemic disease, introducing new rules governing screening, isolation, quarantine, contact tracing and the handling of bodies.

Health Cabinet Secretary Aden Duale issued the declaration through a legal notice published in the Kenya Gazette on Monday, October 12, under Section 35 of the Public Health Act.

The declaration follows Kenya’s confirmation of its first imported case of Bundibugyo Ebola virus disease on October 6, after a Kenyan citizen who had been living in the Democratic Republic of Congo travelled through Uganda to Nairobi. The patient died despite receiving supportive treatment.

The case prompted health authorities to trace people who may have come into contact with the patient and strengthen screening at points of entry.

In an update on October 12, the World Health Organization (WHO) said Kenya had listed 127 contacts, with 94 in quarantine, and screened more than 665,000 travellers at points of entry.

WHO also supplied protective equipment and testing materials worth about US$70,000 to support the response.

The government published two legal notices on October 12. Legal Notice No. 203 declares the disease a formidable epidemic, while Legal Notice No. 204 establishes the Public Health (Ebola Disease) Rules, 2026.

The regulations provide for screening at points of entry, medical assessment, isolation, referral, quarantine and monitoring.

They also assign responsibilities to transport operators, health facilities, medical practitioners and laboratories.

Health authorities will conduct investigations and contact tracing, while designated health facilities will manage suspected and confirmed cases. The rules also provide for the inspection and decontamination of premises.

The regulations cover the safe and dignified disposal of bodies, burial procedures, record-keeping, transportation and repatriation. They also address public communication, media houses’ responsibilities in public sensitisation and assistance from enforcement agencies.

The rules provide for offences and penalties, although the Gazette extract does not specify the penalties for individual violations.

What the declaration means

Bundibugyo virus disease is a form of Ebola that spreads through direct contact with the blood or other bodily fluids of an infected person or contaminated materials.

Contact with the body of someone who has died from the disease can also expose people to infection during unsafe burial practices.

Symptoms can include fever, fatigue, muscle pain, headache and sore throat, followed by vomiting and diarrhoea. The incubation period ranges from two to 21 days.

WHO says no approved vaccine or specific treatment currently exists for the Bundibugyo strain, making early detection, isolation, supportive care and contact tracing central to controlling its spread.

The health agency has advised against travel or trade restrictions on Kenya, Uganda and the Democratic Republic of Congo based on the information available.

The new rules establish a legal framework for managing the disease, from identifying suspected infections and monitoring contacts to caring for patients and preventing exposure during burials.

World.title: Mo Salah achieves milestone for Trabzonspor unattained in 13 years in European competitions
World.content:
Egyptian international Mohamed Salah maintained his fine form for Trabzonspor, converting a penalty against Scottish side Hearts in the UEFA Conference League.

The goal marked his 10th in all competitions for the Turkish club and snapped a 13-year drought for Trabzonspor in European play.

According to Turkish news outlet Haberler, Salah’s strike was the club’s first successfully converted penalty in a European fixture since August 2013, when Polish midfielder Adrian Mierzejewski scored from the spot against Albania’s FK Kukësi.

Summer move to Trabzonspor

Following a high-profile departure from Liverpool in mid-2026, Mohamed Salah completed a headline transfer to Turkish Super Lig club Trabzonspor, quickly becoming the cornerstone of their domestic and European campaigns.

Rapid impact

Upon his arrival in Trabzon, Salah established himself as the team’s primary attacker and designated spot-kick taker, hitting double digits in all competitions within his first few months at the club.

European context

Trabzonspor qualified for the 2026/27 UEFA Conference League group phase, making Salah’s clinical penalty against Hearts a key moment in restoring the club’s offensive reliability on the continental stage.

World.title: CBE Governor explains reasons for Egyptian pound’s historic drop against US dollar
World.content:
Central Bank of Egypt (CBE) Governor Hassan Abdalla reaffirmed the bank’s commitment to a flexible exchange rate policy in his first comments following the Egyptian pound reaching a historic low against the US dollar.

The Egyptian pound closed at 55.35 per dollar in commercial bank trading on Thursday, a record low that surpassed the previous historic peak of LE 54.75 reached last April following the US-Iranian military escalation.

Speaking during the panel session titled “Foreign Currency Resources and Debt Management” at the Egypt 2026 Forum, Abdalla stated that the exchange rate moves dynamically in response to shifting economic conditions surrounding Egypt, emphasizing that such fluctuations are completely normal given current circumstances.

Abdalla called on the public to understand currency movements in light of surrounding regional and global developments, stressing that what would actually be concerning is a fixed exchange rate despite changing conditions. He also urged the public not to give in to unwarranted anxieties regarding currency fluctuations.

The governor emphasized the resilience and capability of the Egyptian banking system to navigate rapid international and regional developments.

World.title: Madbouly outlines 3 energy scenarios amid surging global oil prices
World.content:
Mostafa Madbouly, Prime Minister, clarified the reality of statements attributed to him regarding power cuts, affirming that circulating reports claiming the announcement of power load shedding for 6 to 8 hours daily are inaccurate. He noted that his remarks during an earlier session at the Egypt 2026 Forum were confined to reviewing potential scenarios for dealing with rising global energy prices, without announcing the implementation of load shedding.

In his intervention to outline the features of the National Economic Transformation Program at the Egypt 2026 Forum on Thursday, Madbouly explained that presenting these scenarios aimed to illustrate the challenges facing the energy sector and the available alternatives to address them. He emphasized that the state chose in the current phase to bear the financial burden resulting from higher prices to avoid placing additional burdens on citizens.

The Prime Minister indicated that the forum provided an opportunity to clarify facts to the public and respond to inaccurate information circulating on social media, aligning with President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi’s emphasis on discussing various issues and explaining their dimensions to citizens. The Prime Minister stated that the world is facing major challenges in the energy sector due to current economic and international developments, which affect developed and developing nations alike.

He explained that the state budget for the current fiscal year was built on an estimated oil price of $75 per barrel, whereas the price currently exceeds $110, imposing additional pressure on the budget and the costs of providing the fuel and gas necessary to operate the energy system.

Madbouly added that his earlier remarks simply outlined three options for managing global energy price hikes:

World.title: From approval to abstention: How Egyptian parties stand on Saudi military mandate
World.content:
The House of Representatives held two important sessions on Sunday and Monday of this week regarding the request from President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi for parliamentary authorization to send military forces to the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia to participate in its defense. Despite the House convening in urgent sessions over the two days, no official decision was issued—whether of approval or rejection—regarding the President’s request.

During Monday’s session, the House of Representatives decided to continue the secret session designated for discussing the authorization of the President to send armed forces to the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia next Monday to vote on the decision.

Ahead of the anticipated session next week, what are the positions of political parties and MPs regarding this request?

Political party positions

Several political parties issued statements defining their positions regarding the President’s request:

Al-Adl (Justice) Party: The party’s political bureau released a statement revealing its decision to authorize its parliamentary bloc to vote in favor of the President’s request regarding sending armed forces outside the state’s borders.

Wafd Party: Issued a statement confirming its approval to authorize the President to take all necessary measures to support and defend the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia in light of current regional developments.

Egyptian Social Democratic Party: The political bureau directed its parliamentary bloc to abstain from voting on the decision to authorize the deployment of forces to support Saudi Arabia, citing considerations related to Egyptian national security, economic costs, and the potential risks of regional escalation.

Al-Nour Party: Galal Morra, First Deputy Head of Al-Nour Party, confirmed in an official statement that Egyptian national security extends to its Arab surroundings and that the stability of Arab nations is a fundamental pillar of Egypt’s security. He noted that recent developments in the Straits of Hormuz and Bab al-Mandab demonstrate how closely regional security is linked to Egypt’s strategic and economic interests, stressing the necessity of defensive coordination and Egyptian support for Saudi Arabia whenever needed based on shared responsibility for regional stability.

Positions of individual MPs

During the parliamentary sessions on the matter, some MPs expressed rejection of the authorization while others abstained:

MP Maha Abdel Nasser: Announced her rejection of the authorization and called for a diplomatic solution, asserting that the proposed mandate presented to Parliament is open-ended and ambiguous, and that she refuses to grant an open mandate.

MP Mohamed Abdel Alim Dawood (Wafd Party), MP Mahmoud Sami (Egyptian Social Democratic Party), and MP Diaa El-Din Dawood: Expressed reservations regarding the decision.

Finalizing the decision

The House of Representatives will hold a session next Monday, during which it is expected to finalize its decision regarding the authorization to send armed forces to the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia. The vote will be conducted by roll call, and approval requires a two-thirds majority of members.

World.title: In talks with Turkey, Egypt holds firm on Mediterranean sovereignty
World.content:
Badr Abdelatty, Minister of Foreign Affairs, International Cooperation, and Emigrants, met with Hakan Fidan, Minister of Foreign Affairs of Turkey on Friday, in Istanbul on the sidelines of the Quad mechanism meetings with the three European nations.

The two ministers discussed developments in Libya, where Minister Abdelatty emphasized Egypt’s firm stance supporting Libya’s unity, sovereignty, territorial integrity, and stability, as well as its keenness to support Libyan state institutions in a way that safeguards the interests of the Libyan people and fulfills their aspirations.

The Foreign Minister also reiterated Egypt’s categorical rejection of ratifying the 2019 Memorandum of Understanding regarding the delimitation of maritime jurisdiction zones in the Mediterranean.

He stressed the importance of respecting the principles of international law of the sea and the provisions of the 1982 United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS) concerning the designation of the Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ) and the continental shelf, in accordance with the principles of justice and equity among states.

For his part, the Turkish minister affirmed his understanding of Egyptian concerns regarding developments in Libya, noting the importance of continued consultation, coordination, and joint action to address these concerns and support efforts to achieve security and stability in Libya.

World.title: Why did the Netherlands close its embassy in Cairo?
World.content:
The Dutch Embassy in Cairo announced on Thursday, the closure of its building to the public until further notice, in a step it described as a precautionary measure following demonstrations taking place around the embassy premises.

This development comes in the context of protests witnessed outside the embassy in recent days following the arrest and detention of Egyptian national Ahmed Nasser in the Netherlands.

Why has public service been suspended at the Embassy?

Dutch public broadcaster NOS reported that Dutch authorities arrested Nasser in The Hague following police reports and complaints filed by Egyptian activist Anas Habib—the activist who gained notoriety for locking the gates of the Egyptian embassy in The Hague—alleging threats, intimidation, and suspected physical assault.

The decision to close the Dutch embassy building in Zamalek, Cairo to the public—which halts public consular services like visa processing and in-person consular appointments—was made by the Dutch Ministry of Foreign Affairs purely as a security and precautionary measure.

Cause of closure

The closure was prompted by days of ongoing demonstrations and protests outside the embassy building in Cairo. Protesters gathered to demand the release of Egyptian citizen Ahmed Nasser, who was detained by Dutch authorities in the Netherlands.

Safety concerns

During the demonstrations, the embassy had to be evacuated for security reasons. To ensure the physical safety of embassy staff, visitors, and the public, the Dutch government decided to suspend in-person consular operations until further notice.

World.title: Massive strikes hit Kyiv hours after Putin agrees to fresh peace talks
World.content:
Russia attacked the Ukrainian capital of Kyiv in a massive missile attack overnight into Thursday, hours after President Vladimir Putin said the Kremlin was ready to resume trilateral peace talks next month.

At the request of US special envoy Steve Witkoff during their three-hour meeting on Wednesday, Putin said he would be willing to resume talks with Ukraine and the United States after November 10. But the latest diplomatic push – during which Witkoff controversially called Putin a “humanitarian” because he freed a detained American citizen – was followed by an attack on Ukraine involving 21 missiles and 210 drones.

US President Donald Trump said on Wednesday that his administration is “the closest we’ve been” to settling the war in Ukraine. The first explosions hit Kyiv three minutes before he made those comments.

The large-scale strikes killed two people and injured 34 others, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said Thursday. Ukrainian officials said central Kyiv was also hit with a cluster warhead.

“Russian ‘humanitarians’ have launched three waves of ballistic strikes against Kyiv since this evening,” Zelensky said. “This means there has been no real change in its attitude toward everything that is happening.

“When Russian ballistic missiles are the response to negotiations, real pressure must be applied on Russia to take other steps – steps to stop the killings,” he added, calling for a rapid delivery of air defense missiles.

Firefighters try to extinguish a fire after a Russian missile attack in central Kyiv, Ukraine, on Thursday. Efrem Lukatsky/AP

None of the ballistic missiles that hit Kyiv were intercepted, according to the Ukrainian Air Force, which comes as the country faces a critical shortage of US-made Patriot defense missiles. Air raid sirens continued to blare in Kyiv on Thursday, with warnings of further incoming ballistic missile attacks.

A separate Russian attack hit the central market in the city of Lozova, Kharkiv region, killing at least two people and injuring dozens more as they were shopping on Thursday, according to the mayor.

Meanwhile in Russia, Moscow’s mayor said that 630 drones flew toward the region overnight, in an attack that injured two people in the rural Voronovo area. Most of those were intercepted.

Despite the positive comments on potential future negotiations, there are no indications so far that Russia has budged on any of its maximalist positions.

Russia’s previous demands amount to near-total victory – calling for Ukraine to give up the entire eastern Ukrainian Donbas region, which is now mostly under Russian occupation. Moscow has also called for Ukraine to dramatically reduce the size of its military and pledge to never join NATO.

Ukraine skeptical about fresh trilateral talks in November

According to a post-meeting briefing by Putin’s aide Yury Ushakov, the Kremlin would like to discuss the establishment of a “security framework” for both Russia and Ukraine following the end of the conflict, without offering further details on what Russia would demand as part of that framework.

The next trilateral round could take place in Abu Dhabi, the capital city of the United Arab Emirates (UAE), Ushakov said in response to a question on Russian state news channel Russia 24.

Zelensky said on Wednesday that he would like the meeting to happen “no later than the beginning of November.”

“Russia said many times it is ready for a meeting and then things changed and got canceled,” Zelensky added. “Let’s see what happens this time.”

The meeting in St. Petersburg came a day after Witkoff’s summit with Zelensky in Norway. The US envoy described the meetings with both leaders as “constructive” in a post on X later Wednesday, and said the discussions would continue with the trilateral talks.

“While there is still important work left to do, President Trump remains committed to seeing this war end and achieving a comprehensive, durable peace,” he wrote.

Russian President Vladimir Putin and US special envoy Steve Witkoff meet inside the Constantine Palace in St. Petersburg Wednesday. Obtained by CNN

During the latest talks, Putin also expressed interest in the topic of restoring economic cooperation with the United States and the possibility of a meeting with China to discuss Ukraine. That follows recent moves by the Trump administration to waive sanctions on Russia and strike a deal on diesel exports.

Speaking to media after the meeting, Russian presidential envoy Kirill Dmitriev said there was “no question” that US-Russian economic cooperation would continue, and added that a recently-announced diesel deal between the two countries would go ahead despite European criticism.

A key outcome of the meeting was Witkoff announcing that Russia had released 74-year-old American prisoner Stephen Hubbard, who had been detained in the country for more than four years. A video obtained by CNN after the meeting showed the freed American detainee speaking with Witkoff at the airport in St. Petersburg.

Putin, Witkoff and translators sat around a large round table as they also discussed a wide range of issues including Russia’s willingness to help resolve the war in Iran, potential Russian fertilizer exports to the US and Hubbard’s release. The meeting continued behind closed doors, and Kushner, Trump’s son-in-law who has also been involved in the peace negotiations, joined remotely given he has the flu.

The US and Ukraine made “meaningful progress” in the Norway talks on Tuesday, a US official previously told CNN, adding that the two sides are now in “strong alignment” on what the next steps will be.

“Discussions covered key elements of a comprehensive peace framework, including long-term security guarantees for Ukraine, a post-war economic and prosperity plan, and a broader European security architecture designed to create lasting stability,” the US official said.

But Kremlin aide Ushakov poured cold water on those discussions, saying that while Witkoff had highlighted to Putin “certain new approaches and developments in the positions taken by the Europeans and Kyiv… in truth, these contained little of actual value for resolving the Ukrainian crisis.”

Ukraine and its allies have reiterated the key red lines set by Kyiv for any peace negotiations, including the need for future security guarantees – to ensure Russia doesn’t invade again – and a rejection of any demands to give up territory it controls.

In an Fox News interview on Wednesday, Zelensky repeated a long-held position that Ukraine would accept a ceasefire deal that involves a freeze along the current frontline – something that would involve retaining only about 75 percent of Ukrainian land – and would then ask allies for meaningful security guarantees.

Zelensky also said that Ukraine also wants trilateral negotiations involving Trump, Putin and himself, but the process would be “better with Europeans.”

“I always said that we are open to negotiate in any format, any topics, but don’t speak about us without us, please,” he said, balking at the prospect of any Russia-China-US negotiations.

A European official in Oslo told CNN: “I think plans – or lack of – isn’t as much of a problem as getting Russia to treat any plan seriously.”

This story has been updated with additional developments.

World.title: Meta ordered to pay $25 billion in New Mexico case over Cambridge Analytica scandal
World.content:
New York — A New Mexico judge ordered Meta to pay $25 billion after the company was found to have misled users about its privacy practices in a case related to A New Mexico judge ordered Meta to pay $25 billion after the company was found to have misled users about its privacy practices in a case related to the Cambridge Analytica scandal

The Wednesday ruling marks one of the largest-ever legal penalties for a tech giant — and just the latest court loss for Meta this year.

The company, then known as Facebook, disclosed in 2018 that the private information of as many as 87 million Facebook users was improperly obtained by political analytics firm Cambridge Analytica. The firm used that information to build profiles of American voters.

New Mexico sued Facebook in 2021, accusing it of mishandling state residents’ personal information and deceiving those users about its policies in connection with the incident.

A jury found in September that Meta had violated the state’s Unfair Practices Act more than 43 million times. State District Court Judge Francis Mathew criticized the company for what he described as a “coherent strategy designed to mislead the public” in his Wednesday penalty decision.

“Facebook’s misrepresentations about users’ control of their data were not isolated incidents, but rather a systematic pattern of deception at the core of Facebook’s business model,” Mathew wrote.

After Wednesday’s penalty decision, Meta said it will appeal the decision and has accused New Mexico’s attorney general of conflating privacy and speech issues.

“This ruling, and the Attorney General’s approach to this enforcement, makes it all but impossible to do business in the state of New Mexico,” Meta Chief Legal Officer C.J. Mahoney said in a statement. “At its core, this lawsuit seeks to impose a tax on speech to enforce new rules for what people can say online. We are confident we will prevail on appeal.”

Meta’s legal battles threaten to strain its business, though court penalties and settlements remain relatively small compared to the company’s earnings so far.

The company reported earnings for the quarter ended in September on Wednesday, including lower quarterly profits than Wall Street had expected. It attributed the miss to a charge from the $18 billion multistate settlement it agreed to in August to resolve claims that its platforms have addicted and harmed young people.

New Mexico was not a party to that settlement, which also resolved the participating states’ outstanding claims related to Cambridge Analytica.

Meta posted income from operations of nearly $13 billion during the quarter, compared to nearly $23 billion that it said it would have earned without the settlement.

Meta CFO Susan Li said on a call with analysts following the earnings report that the company is monitoring “active legal and regulatory matters that could significantly impact our business and financial results,” including additional youth-related trials set for later this year and next.

Meta was also ordered to pay nearly $1 billion in a separate New Mexico case earlier this year over claims that its platforms addicted and harmed young people. Meta, along with YouTube, also lost a case in March in Los Angeles brought by a young woman with similar addiction and harm claims. The companies plan to appeal.

Meta earnings

Still, Meta’s business continues to grow at a strong clip thanks in large part to its investments in artificial intelligence. The company posted sales growth of 26 percent year-on-year to more than $64 billion in the quarter.

Meta’s stock (META) jumped more than three percent in after-hours trading following the report on Wednesday.

Meta launched its Muse AI personal assistant app in September. The app quickly rocketed to the top of app stores and has gained more than 10 million users, according to the company. It also launched its latest foundation model, Muse Wonder, last month.

Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg presents the Muse Charm at the company’s headquarters in Menlo Park, California, on September 23. Carlos Barria/Reuters

The company said Wednesday that its AI investments are boosting its core advertising business “through stronger engagement, better recommendations, and more efficient monetization.” Its average price per ad, a key metric for the company, jumped 14 percent year-over-year in the September quarter.

Across the industry, tech companies face questions about their heavy spending on AI infrastructure. Meta’s capital expenditures during the quarter reached nearly $35 billion, up 80 percent from the year-ago quarter. And the company narrowed its full-year capital expenditure guidance to between $135 billion to $145 billion, the upper end of the range it had previously provided. Meta declined to provide spending guidance for next year.

But investors are signaling they’re willing to give Meta some leeway, given the success of Muse, said Jesse Cohen, senior analyst at Investing.com.

“The market has shifted from punishing Meta for spending to rewarding it for having a compelling product story,” Cohen wrote in emailed commentary.

World.title: Liberia: Judge Cites Evidence in Finding NSA Staff Peter Bon Jallah Guilty of Statutory Rape, Kidnapping
World.content:
Criminal Court E Acquits Him of Gang Rape; Orders Pre-Sentence Report Before Sentencing

By Gerald C. Koinyeneh

Monrovia — Assigned Circuit Judge Wesseh Alphonsus Wesseh Sr. has found 63-year-old Peter Bon Jallah, a staff member of the National Security Agency (NSA), guilty of statutory rape and kidnapping, but not guilty of gang rape in a case involving a 16-year-old boy.



In a verdict delivered Friday, October 23, Judge Wesseh said he had reviewed the evidence presented by both parties and considered the arguments advanced during the trial before determining that the prosecution had established sufficient grounds to convict Jallah on two of the three charges.

The judge framed his decision around three central questions: whether the prosecution’s evidence justified a conviction for gang rape, statutory rape and kidnapping.

He answered the first question in the negative, acquitting Jallah of gang rape, but answered the other two in the affirmative, finding him guilty of statutory rape and kidnapping.

Following the verdict, Judge Wesseh ordered Jallah remanded at Monrovia Central Prison pending the submission of a pre-sentence and behavioral report by the Bureau of Probation Services at the Ministry of Justice.

The judge directed the clerk of court to communicate with the probation authorities to ensure that the report is made available as soon as possible to assist the court in determining the appropriate sentence.

Judge Identifies Three Decisive Questions

In his ruling, Judge Wesseh said the court had examined the facts and circumstances contained in the evidence presented at trial before identifying three issues that were decisive to the case.

On the gang rape charge, the judge concluded that the prosecution’s evidence did not provide sufficient and reasonable grounds to convict Jallah. He consequently declared the defendant not guilty and acquitted him of that charge.

However, on statutory rape, the judge found that the evidence presented by the prosecution provided sufficient grounds for conviction.

He reached a similar conclusion on the kidnapping charge, finding Jallah guilty on that count as well.

The ruling represents a split decision in a case that involved allegations of repeated sexual abuse of a minor and the alleged confinement of the complainant for several days.

Indictment Details Alleged Repeated Abuse

According to the indictment summarized in the court’s verdict, Jallah and two unidentified men were indicted by the Montserrado County Grand Jury during the February 2026 Term of Court for gang rape, statutory rape and kidnapping.

The indictment alleged that Jallah and the two other men acted individually and jointly in sexually abusing the complainant on multiple occasions.

It further stated that the complainant, who was 16 at the time of the alleged incidents, lived in the Airfield Shark Community in Monrovia and regularly visited Jallah’s residence to perform domestic work for which he received compensation.

The indictment alleged that on November 29 and December 24, 2025, Jallah lured the boy to his residence in the Sharks Community of Airfield Sinkor, where he allegedly sexually assaulted him.

The most serious allegations concerned an incident said to have occurred on January 1, 2026, after the boy participated in a community football league at the Kpelle Town football field.

According to the indictment, the boy encountered Jallah near his residence after the game. Jallah allegedly offered to purchase football boots for him and instructed him to return home to bathe before accompanying him.

The indictment alleged that the two subsequently travelled by car to a building in the Camp Johnson Road area of downtown Monrovia, where the boy was allegedly held for three days and sexually abused by Jallah and the two unidentified men.

It further alleged that on January 3, 2026, at about 10 p.m., the boy was concealed at the back of Jallah’s vehicle and abandoned along 15th Street in Sinkor.

The complainant was reportedly rescued by private security guards, who alerted his parents. His mother and other relatives subsequently took him to the John F. Kennedy Medical Center for medical examinations.

These details formed part of the allegations contained in the indictment and should not be interpreted as separate findings by the court unless expressly established in the judge’s ruling.

Case Faced Procedural Delays

The court’s verdict also outlined the procedural history of the case, which experienced several delays before proceeding to a full trial.

The case was initially before Criminal Assizes Court “A” for Montserrado County before being transferred to Criminal Court “E” for evidentiary proceedings and a full trial.

Jallah was arraigned on June 18, 2026, and pleaded not guilty to the indictment. He subsequently elected to be tried by a judge without a jury.

The trial was delayed after the prosecution filed a motion seeking a change of venue. Following the denial of that motion, the prosecution petitioned the Chamber Justice for a writ of certiorari, but the petition was denied and the case was ordered to proceed.

The proceedings encountered another setback when the judge previously presiding over the matter could not continue taking evidence after the regular sitting of the court expired.

On August 5, 2026, the case was reassigned for trial.

According to the written verdict, the prosecution presented 13 regular witnesses and six rebuttal witnesses, while the defense called eight regular witnesses and three subpoenaed witnesses from the Ministry of Gender, Children and Social Protection, Orange GSM and the John F. Kennedy Medical Center.

The prosecution’s witnesses included the complainant, police investigators, medical personnel and Rwandan forensic examiner Pascal Bavugirije.

The defense witnesses included Jallah himself and several other individuals who testified on his behalf.

The number of witnesses listed in the written verdict differs from earlier accounts that referred to 12 prosecution witnesses, making the court’s official record the appropriate reference for the final tally.

DNA and Medical Evidence Featured at Trial

The prosecution relied in part on forensic findings linking Jallah’s DNA profile to biological material recovered from four clothing exhibits.

However, testimony attributed to the forensic examiner indicated that the findings could not establish precisely when or how the biological material was deposited.

The defense challenged the prosecution’s interpretation of the evidence, pointing to alleged inconsistencies in the complainant’s account and limitations in the medical and forensic findings.

Medical evidence also featured prominently in the proceedings. Earlier accounts of the trial referenced a John F. Kennedy Medical Center report that reportedly found no visible signs of anal trauma, while the parties disputed the significance of the medical and forensic findings.

The precise weight the court assigned to each item of evidence should be established from the complete written ruling and trial record. The verdict provided identifies the court’s conclusions on the three charges but does not detail its assessment of every witness or exhibit.

Prosecution and Defense Clash in Final Arguments

During final arguments on Thursday, October 22, prosecution lawyer Cllr. Calvin H. Momolu urged Judge Wesseh to convict Jallah, maintaining that the evidence presented during the trial supported the charges.

Defense lawyer Cllr. Wilfred Sayeh argued that the prosecution had failed to prove its case to the required legal standard. The defense questioned the police investigation and challenged the interpretation of the medical, forensic and testimonial evidence.

The judge adjourned the proceedings until Friday morning to review the evidence and arguments before delivering the verdict.

In reaching his decision, Judge Wesseh found the prosecution’s evidence sufficient to convict Jallah of statutory rape and kidnapping, while concluding that it did not warrant a conviction for gang rape.

The two other men named in the indictment were not brought under the court’s jurisdiction and were not tried alongside Jallah in these proceedings.

Defense Plans Appeal

Following the verdict, defense lawyer Cllr. Sayeh announced plans to appeal the ruling to the Supreme Court of Liberia.

The planned appeal would give the defense an opportunity to challenge the lower court’s decision before the country’s highest court.

In the meantime, Jallah remains ordered remanded at Monrovia Central Prison while the Bureau of Probation Services prepares the report requested by Judge Wesseh.

The report is intended to assist the court in determining the sentence to be imposed following the guilty verdicts.

The case now enters the sentencing stage before the anticipated appeal, with the court having found Jallah guilty of statutory rape and kidnapping but acquitted him of gang rape.

— Acquits NSA Staff of Gang Rape; Defense Announces Supreme Court Appeal

By Victoria Wesseh

Following the verdict, Judge Wesseh ordered Jallah’s remand at Monrovia Central Prison. However, the court had not announced the sentence at the time of reporting.

Defense lawyer Cllr. Wilfred Sayeh has announced plans to appeal the ruling to the Supreme Court of Liberia, setting the stage for another legal battle over the verdict.

Prosecution Presented 12 Witnesses

During the trial, prosecutors presented 12 witnesses, including the complainant, police investigators, medical personnel, and Rwandan forensic examiner Pascal Bavugirije.

The prosecution also relied on DNA findings that linked Jallah’s DNA profile to biological material recovered from four clothing exhibits.

However, the forensic examiner reportedly testified that the findings could not establish when or how the biological material was deposited.

Jallah had pleaded not guilty to all charges, while his defense challenged the prosecution’s evidence, citing alleged inconsistencies in the complainant’s account and limitations in the medical and forensic findings.

Defense Challenges Evidence, Plans Appeal

During Thursday’s final arguments, prosecution lawyer Cllr. Calvin H. Momolu urged the court to convict Jallah, arguing that the evidence presented during the trial supported a guilty verdict.

Defense lawyer Cllr. Sayeh countered that the prosecution had failed to establish the allegations beyond a reasonable doubt. The defense questioned the interpretation of medical and forensic findings, as well as aspects of the police investigation.

The competing arguments centered on witness testimony, medical findings, forensic evidence, and whether the prosecution had sufficiently established the elements of the charged offenses.

With the guilty verdict on two charges and the defense’s announced intention to appeal, the case is expected to proceed to the Supreme Court, where Jallah’s lawyers will seek a review of the lower court’s decision.

World.title: Liberia Poised to Surpass 2026 Intellectual Property Registration Target
World.content:
The Government of Liberia, through the Liberia Intellectual Property Office (LIPO), has announced that it is on track to surpass its annual intellectual property registration target after recording 526 registrations by the end of the third quarter of 2026.

Speaking at the Ministry of Information’s regular press briefing on Thursday, LIPO Director General Hon. Garmai Koboi noted that the Office had achieved 95.6 percent of its annual target of 550 registrations — expressing confidence that the current pace of registrations would push the year-end figure beyond the projected benchmark.

According to Hon. Koboi, trademarks accounted for the overwhelming majority of registrations, with 483 recorded during the period, followed by 40 copyright registrations and three industrial designs.

Of the total, Hon. Koboi further disclosed that 174 of the registrations were by Liberian-owned businesses and foreign nationals with established business operations in the country.



“With 526 applications recorded against an annual target of 550, we have achieved 95.6 percent of our FY2026 intellectual property registration target, leaving an outstanding balance of just 24 applications, representing 4.4 percent of the annual target,” Hon. Koboi added. “This performance reflects the work we are doing to strengthen intellectual property awareness and engagement among businesses, entrepreneurs, and other key stakeholders through targeted outreach, capacity-building initiatives, and stakeholder collaboration.”

According to Hon. Koboi, the uptake in registration is down to LIPO’s ongoing efforts to make intellectual property services more accessible, particularly to entrepreneurs, creators, and small businesses seeking to protect and commercialize their innovations, brands, and creative works.

“These achievements reflect the progress we are making toward building a stronger and more inclusive intellectual property ecosystem in Liberia,” the Director General said. “By supporting enterprise development, promoting creativity and innovation, strengthening intellectual property protection, and expanding access to IP services for SMEs and creators, we are seeing a lot of uptake in our registration and use of the IP system.”

Highlighting LIPO’s other achievements, Hon. Koboi pointed to the implementation of the Business and Intellectual Property Management Clinic (BIPMC), undertaken in partnership with the United Nations Industrial Development Organization (UNIDO) through its GROW-2 Project.

The initiative, according to LIPO and UNIDO, reached 142 entrepreneurs across Lofa, Bong, Nimba and Margibi counties, providing practical training, business advisory support and technical guidance on intellectual property identification, registration and management.

At the closure of the clinic, 90 intellectual property applications were filed for the first time by enterprises in these counties, of which 39 resulted in the issuance of intellectual property registration certificates to applicants who satisfied the legal and regulatory requirements under the Liberia Intellectual Property Act of 2016.

The project, according to Hon. Koboi, forms part of a broader national effort by the Government to integrate intellectual property protection into business development, particularly in agriculture, food processing, fashion, manufacturing and other sectors where entrepreneurs increasingly rely on brands, creative designs and product differentiation to compete in the marketplace.

Speaking also, Hon. Koboi noted that LIPO, in collaboration with the World Intellectual Property Organization (WIPO), has expanded the 2nd edition of the Intellectual Property Management Clinic (IPMC) to 40 SMEs in four counties, providing specialized one-on-one mentorship support to 40 small and medium-sized enterprises across Montserrado, Nimba, Bong and Lofa counties.

The initiative provides training and technical advisory support to participating businesses in order to help them strengthen their intellectual property management practices, minimize infringement risks and identify opportunities for business growth and market expansion.

“These projects support the government’s commitment under the ARREST Agenda to its 2029 vision of developing a robust intellectual property ecosystem, as they expand access to intellectual property protection services for businesses and creators while equipping them with the knowledge and practical guidance needed to understand, protect, and effectively manage their intellectual property assets,” Hon. Koboi noted.

Meanwhile, Hon. Koboi has noted that one of the greatest achievements for the office this year has been the successful completion of the national stakeholder validation of Liberia’s National Intellectual Property Policy and Strategy (NIPPS), describing the exercise as an important step toward establishing a coordinated framework for intellectual property development.

The document is intended to strengthen coordination among public institutions and other stakeholders while positioning intellectual property as a tool for innovation, enterprise development, creativity and economic diversification.

The completion of the validation exercise represents a key milestone in Liberia’s efforts to establish a more structured national approach to intellectual property development, although further steps will be required before the framework becomes fully operational.

The LIPO Director General has also disclosed that the institution is preparing to digitize its intellectual property registration services through the Intellectual Property Administration System (IPAS), with technical assistance from WIPO. The planned introduction of the system is expected to modernize the administration of intellectual property applications, streamline registration procedures, and improve the efficiency of service delivery.

In a separate development, the LIPO Director General has appealed to the Liberian Senate to give attention to outstanding international instruments submitted by the President for ratification, emphasizing their potential importance to the country’s agriculture, tourism and creative sectors.

Hon. Koboi noted that the ratification of relevant instruments could strengthen Liberia’s ability to benefit from international intellectual property protection frameworks, particularly in areas involving geographical indications and the protection of products associated with specific geographical origins.

“We also want to appeal to the Senate to look at all outstanding instruments submitted by the President for ratification,” Hon. Koboi noted. “These instruments are very cardinal to our agriculture sector, for example, looking at our potential geographical indications, including our Liberian coffee, the tourism sector, our local government and the creative industries.”

Geographical indications are intellectual property protections used to identify products whose qualities, reputation or other characteristics are linked to a particular geographical origin.

World.title: Liberia’s Supreme Court Weighs Whether Parliament Defied Its Order in Expelling Outspoken Lawmaker
World.content:
MONROVIA, Liberia — Liberia’s Supreme Court on Thursday reserved judgment in a case that could determine whether the country’s House of Representatives defied a court order when it expelled one of its most outspoken members, Yekeh Kolubah, in April.

By Victoria G. Wesseh

The case turns on a narrow but consequential question: was the House leadership legally served with a Supreme Court order instructing it to halt proceedings against Kolubah before it voted to remove him? If it was, the vote may have been taken in breach of a binding judicial directive. If not, the House may have been free to act.



How the Dispute Began

Kolubah represented District 10 of Montserrado County, which includes the capital, Monrovia, and was long one of the Legislature’s most combative voices. The disciplinary case against him followed a controversial statement he made about the Makona River boundary dispute, one that many considered provocative, even offensive.

Kolubah was formally notified on April 9, 2026, to appear before the House Committee on Rules, Order and Administration on April 13. He and his lawyers walked out of a later committee hearing after it refused to grant them an additional five days and access to evidence.

His lawyers then asked the Supreme Court for a writ of prohibition, an order used to stop a body from exceeding its authority. Associate Justice Yussif D. Kaba granted the petition on April 16, summoning House leaders to a conference on April 20 and ordering them to stay all further proceedings pending its outcome. The directive was addressed to Speaker Richard Nagbe Koon, Deputy Speaker Thomas Fallah, the House Chief Clerk, the Sergeant-at-Arms and everyone acting under their authority.

The next day, the House went ahead. Kolubah was expelled by the full House on Friday, April 17, after a resolution was signed by 49 of the chamber’s 73 members, the two-thirds majority the Constitution requires. The resolution said he was removed for acts and utterances deemed unpatriotic and detrimental to the country’s sovereignty and territorial integrity.

The Service Dispute

The House says it was never properly served. Its lawyers cited Rule 26.5 of the House rules, which names the Sergeant-at-Arms as the only officer authorised to receive court orders on behalf of the House. Court records show the Supreme Court Marshal instead served the documents on a receptionist and a computer operator attached to the offices of the Speaker and the Chief Clerk.

That argument has already succeeded once. In May 2026, Justice Kaba dismissed Kolubah’s follow-up complaint, known as a bill of information, for improper service, reportedly finding that the House had not been properly served with the writ and stay order. Kolubah appealed to the full five-member bench, which heard arguments on Thursday.

Jonathan Massaquoi, who leads Kolubah’s legal team, told the justices that the validity of service should be judged by Liberia’s Civil Procedure Law, not by the House’s internal rules for handling correspondence.

He cited Section 3.38(9), which states: “Personal service upon a subdivision of the government subject to suit or upon a municipal corporation shall be made by reading and delivering the summons to the chief executive thereof.”

On that basis, the petitioners argued that delivering the order to the office of the Speaker, the House’s presiding officer, was sufficient. A court officer identified as Joshua B. delivered the document there, they said, and a receptionist acknowledged receipt and signed for a copy.

Whether the provision covers the House at all is an open question. It refers specifically to “a subdivision of the government subject to suit” or “a municipal corporation,” and the Court must decide whether a branch of the national Legislature falls into either category.

Did the House Defy the Court?

The justices must weigh the wording of the order, the Marshal’s report of service, the receptionist’s acknowledgment and the legal standing of the office that received it.

Even a clear answer on service may not end the dispute. If the Court upholds the dismissal, it will not necessarily have examined or endorsed the disciplinary proceedings; and a win for Kolubah on service would not automatically prove the expulsion unconstitutional.

Other questions hang over the vote itself. A Bomi County lawmaker has denied backing the expulsion, raising questions about whether the House reached the legally required majority. A media adviser to Speaker Koon also told FrontPage Africa the expulsion took place on April 22, not April 17, before abruptly ending the conversation. A later date could matter, because it would fall after the scheduled court conference.

The case has become a test of the balance between Liberia’s branches of government. Critics have likened it to the recent standoff over former Speaker Fonati Koffa, which tested the limits of legislative authority. Prominent lawyer Tiawan Saye Gongloe has said the Court’s options include voiding the expulsion, holding House leaders in contempt, or ordering Kolubah’s reinstatement pending a hearing that satisfies due process.

The Court did not say when it would rule.
