A southern Michigan school district has voted to restrict participation in girls' sports to biological females, approving a new policy in a 4-2 school board vote amid the ongoing national debate over transgender athletes competing in women's and girls' athletics.

"The Board of Education approved a new policy with a vote of 4 yes and 2 no with one board member absent," Andrew Shaw, superintendent of Monroe Public Schools, told Fox News Digital in an email Wednesday.

"As the superintendent it is my role to implement the policies established by the Board of Education," he added. "The policy that was approved is for Monroe Public Schools only and does not impact any visiting school."

EDUCATION DEPARTMENT RESCINDS BIDEN TITLE IX RULE, RESTORES TRUMP-ERA REGULATIONS

The policy, titled "Girl's Athletic Participation and Facilities Use," addresses participation in girls' athletics and access to facilities. A copy of the proposed policy obtained by Fox News Digital states that participation in girls' athletics at Monroe Public Schools would be restricted to biological females, with eligibility tied to documentation on a student's birth certificate.

The policy reads, "Participation in girl's athletics at Monroe Public Schools shall be restricted to biological females as documented on the birth certificate at the time of birth. Access to and use of girl's athletic facilities (locker rooms) shall follow the same restriction."

The decision comes as school districts across the country continue to grapple with questions surrounding transgender student participation in girls' sports and access to sex-separated facilities.

The new policy announcement also comes after Briley Lechner, a varsity volleyball player at Monroe High School in Monroe, Michigan, and her father, Sean, filed a federal lawsuit on Oct. 9, announced by the Thomas More Law Center, raising Title IX and constitutional claims against Monroe Public Schools, the Michigan High School Athletic Association and school officials over the alleged incident.

COLORADO SCHOOL PARENTS SOUND ALARM AFTER DAUGHTERS WERE CUT FROM VOLLEYBALL TEAM WHILE TRANS ATHLETE PLAYS

BLUE STATE SCHOOL DISTRICT ACCUSED OF DEFYING SUPREME COURT, HIDING GENDER TRANSITIONS FROM PARENTS

Briley Lechner said she filed a lawsuit after she unknowingly shared a locker room with a transgender athlete.

"What's very scary is that the day that this happened, I had no clue that there was a boy on the other team," Lechner told Fox News Digital in an interview on Oct. 15.

The lawsuit from the Thomas More Law Center "alleges that school officials knowingly concealed from the Monroe High School girls' volleyball team and their parents that the September 9, 2025, match with Ann Arbor's Skyline High School would involve a biological male (transgender female)," according to the legal group.

In a statement, Briley Lechner told Fox News Digital, "Our family loves and respect everyone, regardless of our differences. This has always been about my privacy, my safety, and fair play. Nothing more, nothing less."

She added, "Every female athlete deserves to have her rights respected and protected. Boys do NOT belong in girls’ locker rooms or girls’ sports. Every girl deserves to feel safe, respected, and protected, both in the locker room and on the court. We should NEVER have to fight for that."

WOMEN WHO FACED BIOLOGICAL MALES IN GIRLS SPORTS AND LOCKER ROOMS SPEAK OUT AHEAD OF WASHINGTON STATE VOTE

Sean Lechner, her father, told Fox News Digital, "The new policy may be watered down, but it's an incremental victory for my daughter and every female athlete. It's shameful it took nearly a year to get here but we still have work to do. Who's to say they can't change it again? Regardless of how some try to twist the narrative, this has ALWAYS been about my daughter's privacy, safety, and fair play. Nothing more, nothing less!"

He continued, "Since our lawsuit was announced, my daughter and I have received even more harassing and threatening messages. But at the heart of everything I'm doing is something simple — being a father, being a parent, and loving my daughter enough to stand beside her when she needs me most."

He added, "To all parents....put aside your differences, bring faith, common sense, and respect back into our homes. Our children are God's most precious gifts. Love them. Cherish them. Protect them. One day, your daughter may look you in the eyes and ask, 'Why didn't you stand up for me when I needed you?' I never want my daughter to ask me that question. I want her to know her father stood beside her and never backed down. No amount of hate or threats will silence us. I will never stop standing up for my daughter."

World.title: Chicago's 12-language ballots make elections 'harder to monitor,' Illinois GOP chair warns
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Chicago voters can cast ballots in 12 different languages this election, an expansion that Illinois Republican Party Chairman Bob Grogan warns is making an already complicated election system harder to independently monitor.

Grogan told Fox News Digital the proliferation of versions in languages such as Tagalog, Gujarati and Urdu creates additional challenges for election judges and party observers tasked with ensuring voters receive accurate ballots. He also questioned how many voters need some of the translations, arguing that many immigrants who speak those languages also speak English.

"It's a solution in search of a problem," Grogan told Fox News Digital. "It's big city virtue signaling."

TRUMP ADMIN SUED OVER ALLEGED ILLEGAL COLLECTION OF SENSITIVE VOTER DATA FROM 47 STATES

Chicago voters can cast ballots in 12 different languages: English, Spanish, Chinese, Hindi, Korean, Tagalog, Polish, Gujarati, Urdu, Ukrainian, Arabic and Russian.

Section 203 of the U.S. Voting Rights Act requires the Chicago Board of Elections to make materials and ballots available in certain precincts for Spanish, Chinese and Hindi speakers, a spokesperson for the elections agency told Fox News Digital. The Board includes the other non-English languages to "maintain uniformity with the languages used by the Cook County Clerk's office under a county ordinance, so that all voters throughout Cook County are afforded equal voting opportunities," the spokesperson added.

But Grogan, a former DuPage County auditor for 12 years, said he has "a fair number of Gujarati friends ... and everyone in their family speaks English."

"Gujarati — it's from India, and English is an official language in India," Grogan added.

TRUMP ADMIN'S PROPOSED 'ENGLISH-ONLY' HEAD START RULE DRAWS FIRE FROM LOS ANGELES MAYORAL CANDIDATE

Data provided to Fox News Digital by the Chicago Board of Elections shows that some of the less commonly used language options accounted for only a handful of ballots cast during the March primary. Just nine ballots were cast using the English-Gujarati option, while 15 used English-Urdu, 10 used English-Arabic and 25 each used English-Russian and English-Ukrainian, according to the Board's figures.

Other translations were used more frequently, including 4,474 English-Polish ballots, 2,183 English-Chinese ballots, 664 English-Hindi ballots, 352 English-Korean ballots and 100 English-Tagalog ballots.

Grogan also questioned why language requirements can change substantially across county lines, noting that Chicago offers touchscreen ballots in 12 languages while nearby DuPage County offers fewer language options.

"You can have a Gujarati population in Peoria," Grogan said. "You would think that there would be some more uniformity to all of that as well."

SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER

Beyond questioning the need for some of the translations, Grogan raised a broader concern about oversight, arguing that election judges and party observers cannot independently scrutinize ballots written in languages they do not understand.

However, the Chicago Board of Elections pushed back, telling Fox News Digital that it has in-house staff who help translate ballots and signs and assist multilingual media ahead of elections. It also said voters are allowed to bring "interpreter[s] to assist them in understanding and casting their ballot" under certain conditions.

When asked about multilingual judges, the Board noted that of the 7,218 election judges assigned for November's general election as of Thursday, 810 are multilingual candidates. Those multilingual judges include speakers of Spanish, Chinese, Hindi, Urdu, Gujarati, Polish, Korean and Tagalog, according to the Board.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Pressed on whether he believes the additional languages create an election security vulnerability, Grogan said the risk depends in part on how widely the translated ballots are used.

Overall, the Board's figures show 7,857 multilingual ballots were cast during the March primary, representing about 1.85% of the 424,564 ballots cast citywide.

"I think it certainly makes it harder to monitor," Grogan said. "If there is one ballot cast in that language, that's a very small vulnerability you have. If all of a sudden we have 10,000 in some very small, poorly understood language, then that increases the risk."

Fox News Digital asked the Chicago Board of Elections how many languages are available for mail-in ballots but did not receive a response in time for publication.

World.title: Ex-FBI officials arrested in Hunter Biden laptop probe as testimony comes under scrutiny

The Department of Justice charged two former FBI officials with lying to Congress about their involvement in FBI investigations into Hunter Biden, including matters involving his laptop.

Former FBI officials Nikki Cole Floris and Bradley Benavides, according to the DOJ, falsely denied involvement in the investigations into former President Joe Biden’s son when speaking to Congress. Both surrendered Friday on arrest warrants, according to the DOJ.

"Lying to Congress by anyone strikes at the heart of our democratic system, but when senior FBI agents lie to Congress believing they are above the law, it’s time to bring the hammer of justice down on them," U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro said of the charges.

"When senior officials entrusted with safeguarding our nation’s security choose deception over duty, they undermine the very institutions they swore to uphold. Today’s action makes clear that no one is above the law, and we will hold accountable all who obstruct the truth."

FBI CO-DEPUTY DIRECTOR ANDREW BAILEY RESIGNS AFTER YEAR IN ROLE

The Justice Department claims to possess evidence that shows Benavides discussed the laptop story with others in the FBI, contradicting his testimony that he learned about the story from Wikipedia. Similarly, the department says that it has evidence Floris discussed Hunter Biden with members of the FBI’s Foreign Influence Task Force (FITF), despite testifying to the contrary.

A statement of facts filed by the DOJ points to 2023 testimony that Floris gave to the House Judiciary Committee where she denied any involvement in the investigation into Biden's son. She answered in the negative to questions about whether there was "ever a discussion at the FITF about Hunter Biden" or if she had "any involvement in the Hunter Biden investigation."

Contrasting these statements, the DOJ pointed to email logs purporting to show that Floris discussed Hunter with colleagues at the bureau.

Benavides, meanwhile, told lawmakers that he read the Wikipedia page on the laptop story when asked where he learned "that there was an ongoing criminal investigation related to the laptop." The DOJ says emails it has obtained show he was in contact with the team working the investigation into Hunter Biden and that he met with the team prior to a meeting with lawmakers.

"Nikki Floris is a patriot. She served our nation as a dedicated FBI intelligence officer for nearly 20 years. Yet today, the DOJ has accused her falsely of a crime on the say-so of politicians, not on the facts. It’s no coincidence the government is filing these nonsense charges now, years later, on the eve of an election," her attorneys said in a statement.

Floris served as the deputy assistant director and functional head of FITF while Benavides was the task force's section chief.

Republican Sens. Chuck Grassley and Ron Johnson previously accused Floris and Benavides of participating in a 2020 FBI briefing about Russian disinformation that the senators alleged was intended to undermine their investigation into Hunter Biden's foreign business dealings.

Claims that Hunter Biden’s laptop was part of a Russian disinformation operation fueled controversy ahead of the 2020 election. But the FBI later authenticated the laptop during Biden’s 2024 federal gun trial, when prosecutors introduced it as evidence.

World.title: DOJ charges two former top FBI officials who were frequent targets of Trump allies
World.content:
WASHINGTON — Two former FBI officials who have come under withering criticism from allies of President Donald Trump have been charged with allegedly lying to Congress over the investigation into former President Joe Biden’s son Hunter Biden.

A court docket shows that Nikki Floris, the former deputy assistant director of the FBI’s Counterintelligence Division, and Bradley Benavides, another FBI official, were facing one count of the rarely-charged criminal offense which can be difficult to prosecute.

Hunter Biden was investigated, charged and eventually convicted of gun and tax crimes, before his father pardoned him shortly leaving office.

U.S. Attorney for the District of Columbia Jeanine Pirro said in a social media post that Floris and Benavides had surrendered Friday morning. She alleged that the duo lied about their roles in the Foreign Influence Task Force and “about their roles in the FBI’s Hunter Biden investigations.”

Attorneys for Floris said in a statement that Floris was “a patriot” who “served our nation as a dedicated FBI intelligence officer for nearly 20 years” and was charged so the administration could “push a false narrative for a shot at political points.”

Deputy Assistant Director for Counterterrorism at the FBI Nikki Floris testifies before the House Judiciary Committee hearing on Capitol Hill on Oct. 22, 2019. Susan Walsh / AP

Attorneys Margaret Donovan, Chris Mattei, Mary Dohrmann and Kyle R. Freeny said in a statement that the “DOJ has accused her falsely of a crime on the say-so of politicians, not on the facts. It’s no coincidence the government is filing these nonsense charges now, years later, on the eve of an election.”

An attorney for Benavides was not listed yet on the court docket.

The case was brought through a criminal complaint. They have not yet been indicted by a federal grand jury in D.C., where grand jurors have been skeptical of cases brought during Trump’s second term. Earlier this year, federal grand jurors rejected an attempt to indict six sitting Democratic members of Congress over a video Trump criticized.

Flores was the FBI’s security lead for the 2020 presidential election, which Trump has falsely claimed was stolen. A mob of Trump supporters violently broke into the U.S. Capitol on Jan. 6, 2021, in a failed effort to stop the certification of Democrat Joe Biden as president. They beat and bloodied law enforcement, shattered windows and broke through barriers.

She joined the FBI as an intelligence analyst in 2005, working on the director’s daily briefing staff and helped produce intelligence documents. She was promoted in 2017 to the department’s counterterrorism division.

Benavides is a former colleague of Floris who focused on election security, foreign influence and Chinese intelligence threats.

Floris has also been under criticism from Republicans over emails in which she discussed intelligence work that were obtained by Congress and declassified in July by Trump.

Republicans have alleged that FBI officials buried what they describe as a credible report on China’s efforts to influence the election in an effort to protect then-FBI Director Christopher Wray.

Intelligence officials and her legal team have said the pullback was a standard administrative move for a report that may have been unverified or had flawed intelligence.

World.title: Russian diesel tanker heads to the U.S., the first since Trump’s deal with Putin
World.content:
A tanker loaded with diesel fuel set sail Friday from Russia for the United States, the first shipment since President Donald Trump agreed to a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin to release more fuel into the global market.

Trump eased some sanctions on the Kremlin two weeks ago and has since waived more, reversing years of American policy despite Moscow’s ongoing illegal invasion of Ukraine in an apparent bid to lower prices ahead of the midterm elections.

The ship’s departure for the U.S. was confirmed by the Kremlin. The tanker, a Malta-flagged ship named Agioi Fanendes, left a port in Russia’s Primorsk today, according to MarineTraffic tracking data reviewed by NBC News. The ship listed New York as its destination.

President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin in Anchorage, Alaska, in 2025. Andrew Harnik / Getty

Energy Aspects, a market intelligence firm, said that it had confirmed with its industry sources that the ship loaded up 298,000 barrels of diesel in Primorsk.

The firm said that currently the ship plans to unload that fuel in New York. It is expected to arrive Nov. 10.

The ship’s expected arrival would put it just after the midterm elections. Trump’s Republican Party is on edge for potentially heavy losses in House and Senate seats its candidates are defending, driven in part by blowback from consumers facing soaring energy prices.

Trump and his administration have scrambled to try to bring down those prices, which have increased in the wake of supply shocks stemming from the Iran war launched by the U.S. and Israel, and the Russia-Ukraine war.

Trump has taken a number of steps to warm ties with the Kremlin and pressure Kyiv to agree to end the war, drawing outrage from Ukraine and its bipartisan backers in Congress.

“I believe there have already been reports from the Ministry of Energy that the first tanker has departed for its destinations and that further shipments will continue on a regular basis,” Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said early Friday.

Crude oil was headed for a third straight weekly gain. Brent, the most important global oil benchmark, traded around $114 per barrel, less than $13 away from its highest point this year.

Since the start of the year, the average price of diesel fuel has soared from $3.55 per gallon to $6.32, an unprecedented rise of 78%.

Energy Aspect’s analysts said the impact of the cargo’s arrival would likely be “limited.”

Diesel’s sky-high price has troubled economists more than the jump in the price of regular gasoline because, “the cost of diesel gets into just about everything,” as KPMG chief economist Diane Swonk told NBC News in an August interview.

“Everything from … running a farm … cost of food, but also everything across the economy that’s shipped gets that extra fee tacked onto it,” she said.

Currently, U.S. daily diesel demand is about 3.8 million barrels, meaning that Friday’s shipment would satisfy not even a full day’s worth of usage.

“Global distillate markets have tightened sharply,” Bank of America’s head of global commodities, Francisco Blanch, wrote in a recent note, adding that it signals “an acute scarcity of refined products.”

Diesel is a distillate fuel, produced by refining crude oil.

“Geopolitical disruptions are exacerbating that shortage as attacks on shipping around Hormuz make energy flows more difficult and costly, while attacks on Russian refining capacity further restrict product availability,” he wrote.

Russia has historically been one of the world’s largest exporters of diesel.

In September and for some of October, the Kremlin restricted the export of diesel fuel amid a Ukrainian campaign of attacks on its energy infrastructure. It lifted those export restrictions after Putin’s diesel deal with Trump.

Easing sanctions on Russia to open up some previously-blocked diesel supplies was just the latest in a number of policy levers pulled by Trump.

In just the last few weeks, the president has also signed an order allowing more widespread use of an off-road variety of diesel. The administration also pressured European allies, particularly Germany and France, to urgently release some of their diesel reserves.

The administration has also reportedly pushed for a fresh release of crude and diesel reserves, though the International Energy Agency has rebuffed that request.

Experts say that even with all this put together, Trump’s actions will do little to help ease prices, which have continued to trend higher.

“Policy intervention can provide temporary relief, but there is no silver bullet for diesel,” Blanch wrote.

World.title: Etsy to restrict AI-generated content in effort to combat seller slop
World.content:
Etsy announced new restrictions Thursday on AI-generated content on its platform, saying it threatens the integrity of its sellers’ work and leaves buyers exposed to fraud.

Among the new stipulations:

Patterns, recipes, or any other item that involves a buyer “putting in effort to achieve a finished product” cannot be created using AI.

Sellers must include at least one unaltered photo of the actual item against a real background.

Bot-generated listings are banned.

AI-generated art can still be sold on the platform as long as merchants “Play a clear role in what they create and are transparent about the process,” Etsy said in a note to sellers.

“Our marketplace only works when buyers and sellers trust each other,” Etsy Vice President of Customer Operations James Ossman wrote in a blog post.

“Sellers need clear guidance and confidence that their creativity and craftsmanship will be represented fairly; buyers need to understand what they’re buying and the human involvement behind it. We know we have work to do to uphold this standard on Etsy.”

Etsy hosts more than 5 million entrepreneurs, most of whom are women who run one-person businesses out of their homes, according to an annual company report.

That distinguishes it from other major e-commerce platforms like Amazon and eBay, though it commands a fraction of those platforms’ revenues. As of 2024, Etsy hosted $10.9 billion-worth of goods’ sales, compared with about $75 billion for eBay and more than $700 billion for Amazon.

Some buyers responded positively to Etsy’s announcement.

“I can’t explain how infuriating it has been to purchase a crochet pattern, only to open the PDF and realize it’s fully AI-generated, doesn’t make sense, and definitely doesn’t match what the finished product should be,” creator Kara Lynne said on X.

The dawn of advanced AI has led to an explosion in AI-generated sales content — and a growing backlash from consumers against what they see as AI slop.

A recent social media trend among cafes and restaurants saw owners pledging not to use AI after egregious examples of AI-generated food images in the wild were shared on social media.

Major platforms are responding to the growing discontent. Many, including Facebook and Instagram, now work to append labels to images or videos created via AI.

Others, like LinkedIn, have added buttons allowing users to report AI-generated content.

Snap has banned wholly AI-generated content from its recommendation algorithm, while Spotify recently announced it had removed 50 million AI-generated tracks from its platform.

Ossman said Etsy would add a function similar to LinkedIn’s that makes it easier for users to report listings that include misleading AI imagery.

He also said Etsy would be using technology to identify misleading imagery and fraudulent listings, with the goal of expanding removals of illicit listings in the coming months.

“We’re actively working to address the questions AI raises for our marketplace,” Ossman said in the post.

“This work is hard, and we don’t have every answer today. But I believe this is an important moment for Etsy, and that these initial steps are putting us on the right path.”

World.title: Trump hopes to flatter Putin into negotiating on Ukraine
World.content:
WASHINGTON — In recent weeks, President Donald Trump has taken measures that strengthen Russia’s position and may rehabilitate Russian President Vladimir Putin’s soiled reputation in the international community.

Trump returned to office vowing to swiftly end the Russia-Ukraine war, proclaiming last year that he was on “nobody’s side” except “humanity’s side.” But the neutral posture he said he has adopted is peeling away.

A specific strategic goal underlies Trump’s overtures to Putin, foreign policy experts said. The idea is to entice him to come to the negotiating table and end a war that is now in its fifth year. Whether it will work is another question.

Trump’s lead negotiator in the Russia-Ukraine war, Steve Witkoff, called Putin “a humanitarian” in St. Petersburg on Wednesday upon the release of retired American teacher Stephen Hubbard, whom Russia had detained since 2022. Even Republican lawmakers balked at the remark.

00:43 Witkoff thanks Putin for release of retired American teacher 00:00 00:00

“I would describe Putin as a warmonger, a thug. He’s certainly not a humanitarian,” Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, who is in a tough fight for re-election, said Wednesday.

“He is the aggressor in the war against Ukraine,” she added at a campaign stop at a factory in Norway, Maine.

Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., who isn’t running for re-election following public disagreements with Trump, was blunter. “WTF, Steve? Look up the definition of ‘humanitarian,’” he posted on social media.

Freedom House, a nonprofit that works to expand freedom and democracy, describes Russia as an authoritarian country where power is “concentrated in the hands of President Vladimir Putin.” The Kremlin “manipulates elections and suppresses genuine dissent,” the group says.

Trump tends to see diplomacy through the prism of personal relations, and he has made no secret of his regard for Putin. When he hosted Putin for a summit meeting in Alaska last year in a futile attempt to end the war, the U.S. rolled out a red carpet. A picture of Trump and Putin standing side by side hangs in the White House’s Palm Room.

By contrast, Trump has stepped up his on-again, off-again criticism of Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy. As he left the White House on Monday for a campaign trip, he said Zelenskyy “is a man that should have had this war settled a long time ago. I think it’s time for somebody else to negotiate on behalf of Ukraine.”

Blandishments are a tool Trump is using to get Putin to strike a deal, said Robert O’Brien, who was White House national security adviser in Trump’s first term. Not much else has worked.

“We thought we could get the war settled two years ago, but Putin has been intractable in not coming to the table. President Trump is using cordiality to get Putin to negotiate,” O’Brien said in an interview.

“There’d be no hope of getting Putin to engage in talks, with the U.S. as the mediator, if he viewed Trump as 100% aligned with Ukraine in this situation,” he added.

Michael Kimmage, a foreign policy expert at the Brookings Institution think tank, said the Trump administration’s “theory of the case is that by distancing themselves from Ukraine and by flattering the Russians, they can accomplish something at the bargaining table.”

He doesn’t expect the gambit to succeed, though.

“In the absence of a clear agenda coming from the White House and in the absence of very serious forms of leverage over Russia — which the Trump administration has shied away from — progress at the negotiating table is very difficult to imagine,” he said.

Asked about Trump’s warmer attitude toward Putin in recent weeks, the White House pointed to his comments at a roundtable on cybercrime when he was asked about Witkoff labeling the Russian leader “a humanitarian.”

Trump responded: “I guess you could say for that particular purpose — for the purpose of allowing a man who was thinking he was going to be in prison for life out.”

He went on to add that the U.S. is negotiating with Russia to end the war in Ukraine and was complimentary towards Russia for having “not gotten involved with Iran.” Trump said that some “stupid people” were critical of his position and “the last thing I want to do is upset an apple cart where we’re getting close to settling a war.”

Ending the war between Russia and Ukraine was one of Trump’s signature promises in the 2024 campaign. He had confidently predicted he’d get it done on his first day back in office, but he has since conceded that the problem is more stubborn than he’d envisioned.

As Trump works to broker a peace deal, one of his recent gestures to Putin is to treat him as a statesman, rather than a global outcast.

Trump thanked Putin on Oct. 9 after they reached a deal in which Russia agreed to release hundreds of thousands of tons of diesel fuel into global markets. Trump said the move would ease energy costs, but relief at the pump hasn’t happened yet. Since then, the average price of a gallon of diesel has risen 4 cents a gallon, from $6.26 to $6.30.

Trump invited Putin to attend the G20 international summit meeting at his Doral golf resort in Miami, and he said this week that he’s open to a trilateral meeting with Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping to discuss nuclear weapons.

A summit meeting alongside the leaders of the world’s two largest economies would be a boon to Putin, whom the West has ostracized since Russia invaded Crimea in 2014. World leaders expelled Putin from an elite international organization called the G8 after that attack.

“There’s no question that Trump has been trying to reintegrate Putin into polite society,” said Brett Bruen, who was director of global engagement in the Obama White House.

At the G20 summit at Trump’s golf club in December, Putin would be “the shiny object that Trump would dangle in front of the world press corps as purported progress toward peace,” Bruen said.

A question Europeans are asking is what sort of peace deal does Trump visualize. Would it be fair to Ukraine or carve up the country at Putin’s behest, they ask? If Ukraine ceded territory to Putin as the price of ending the war, that would only embolden him to threaten more states, a European official said.

Marko Mihkelson, chairman of Parliament’s Foreign Affairs Committee in Estonia, which borders Russia, said in an interview: “If you reward aggressors” and signal that they can “achieve their goals through aggression, then that doesn’t stop them from continuing.”

Faced with a war in Iran that he started and a war in Europe that he can’t stop, Trump is advised by a thinning inner circle. A senior aide, press secretary Karoline Leavitt, left the White House over the summer. Sen. Lindsey Graham, R-S.C., one of Trump’s confidants and a Russia hawk, died unexpectedly in July.

Two months later, Trump signed a bill named after Graham that sanctioned Russian officials and parts of the country’s economy.

Trump waived those sanctions last week — which Graham might have warned against in their many phone calls and golf games.

“Lindsey Graham is rolling over in his grave,” Sen. Mark Warner, D-Va., told reporters Wednesday.

World.title: Buttigieg endorses independent Seth Bodnar in Montana Senate race
World.content:
Former U.S. Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg has endorsed the independent candidate in the Montana Senate race, Seth Bodnar, over the Democratic nominee, Bodnar's campaign announced Friday.

"The best leaders I've served with, in uniform and in government, care more about getting the job done than about who gets the credit, and Seth is one of them," Buttigieg, a potential 2028 presidential candidate, said in a statement. "Seth and I don't agree on everything, but he has spent his adult life serving this country and the next generation, from the Army Green Berets to the University of Montana, and he'll bring that same character to the Senate on behalf of all Montanans."

File: Seth Bodnar at the Murray Hotel while campaigning for the Senate on May 8, 2026, in Livingston, Montana. William Campbell / Getty Images

Bodnar said he was "honored to have Secretary Buttigieg's support, and proud that people across the political spectrum are joining this campaign."

He says that if he's elected senator, he will not caucus with Democrats or Republicans, remaining independent. Bodnar, 47, a retired U.S. Army Green Beret who graduated first in his West Point class, is a Rhodes scholar and was until recently the president of the University of Montana. He's running against Democratic nominee Alani Bankhead and Republican nominee Kurt Alme.

Montana is considered a solidly GOP state, with far more voters who have cast ballots for Republican candidates than Democrats. Bodnar's resume and platform of independence, affordability and fighting corruption appear to be winning some support with Montanans, and as a result, Bankhead has faced calls to drop out of the race to give him a better shot at victory. With both on the ballot, they are likely to split the support of those who are not voting for Alme.

Republican Sen. Steve Daines' abrupt decision to not seek reelection shortly before the March filing deadline opened the vacancy.

President Trump held a rally in Montana last week to get out the vote for both Alme and congressional candidate Aaron Flint. Vice President JD Vance is also expected to hold a rally in Montana next week.

World.title: 2 ex-FBI officials charged with lying about Hunter Biden laptop probe
World.content:
Washington — Two former senior FBI officials are facing criminal charges for allegedly making false statements to Congress during testimony in 2023 about the bureau's investigation involving Hunter Biden's laptop.

Nikki Floris, 46, a former intelligence analyst in charge in the bureau's Washington Field Office, and Bradley Benavides, 56, the former deputy assistant director at the FBI's Counterintelligence Division, each appeared in court on Friday in Washington, D.C., where they were presented with a copy of a criminal complaint charging them with one count each of lying to Congress about their roles on the Foreign Influence Task Force during the 2020 election, specifically the FBI's Hunter Biden investigations.

A statement of facts prepared by the FBI and filed with the complaint alleges that Floris made false statements to Congress on July 19, 2023, and Benavides allegedly did the same that September. Their alleged false statements pertained to "their awareness of involvement in the FBI's investigations into Hunter Biden," it said.

"The evidence further establishes probable cause to believe that Floris and Benavides made these statements for the purpose of concealing [the Foreign Influence Task Force's] engagement with and communications about the Hunter Biden investigations and impeding the congressional investigation," it said.

The decision by the U.S. Attorney's Office in D.C. to charge the pair in a criminal complaint stemming from three-year-old allegations is highly unusual, and both their defense attorneys and the magistrate judge who presided over Friday's hearing and unsealing raised questions about the decision.

"The alleged conduct happened years ago. The government has had the information about this for years," said Ron Safer, an attorney for Benavides. He asked Zia Faruqui, the magistrate judge at Friday's hearing in the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia, to immediately schedule a preliminary hearing "as soon as humanly possible" to review whether there was adequate probable cause that a crime was committed.

The politically charged case was also unsealed just about two weeks before the midterm election — a fact that may raise questions by DOJ veterans about the timing of a case involving testimony to Congress that occurred more than three years ago.

Faruqui said he thought the manner in which the case was charged seemed "strange" and he rejected a request by prosecutors to delay the preliminary hearing for two weeks or more.

He ordered the parties to return at 11 a.m. on Tuesday.

"This is the Sword of Damocles hanging over their heads," he said. "This will follow them for the rest of their lives."

Former President Joe Biden's son Hunter has long been a target of President Trump and his allies.

Hunter Biden was extensively investigated by the FBI over his business dealings in Ukraine with the energy company Burisma, and the contents of his laptop after he left it at a repair shop in Delaware.

Former Attorney General Merrick Garland eventually appointed a special counsel to handle the investigations. Hunter Biden was tried and convicted on three felony gun charges. He pleaded guilty in a separate criminal case to three felony tax offenses and six misdemeanor tax offenses.

He was pardoned by his father shortly before his father left office, and was never charged with wrongdoing in connection with the allegations involving his overseas business dealings.

The charges

The criminal complaint unsealed on Friday said an FBI unit chief told investigators in October 2026 that Floris and Benavides both had oversight roles into the various Hunter Biden probes.

The complaint focused on an FBI counterintelligence operation by the Foreign Influence Task Force known as "Round River," which, it said, was focused on collecting "derogatory informant reporting on, among other things, Hunter Biden, to flag the reporting as Russian disinformation."

Floris served as the deputy assistant director of the FITF from mid-2019 through mid-2022, while Benavides served as its section chief from mid-2019 through the 2020 election, it said.

"Witness accounts and contemporaneous documents from December 2019 through September 2021 show that Floris and Benavides knew about and were actively involved in the FBI's investigations of Hunter Biden. FITF hosted classified briefings for the agents and prosecutors on the Hunter Biden case in which Floris and Benavides were active participants," the complaint said.

When Floris later testified to the House Judiciary Committee in July 2023, the complaint alleged she lied about her involvement in the Hunter Biden investigation and the role of the Foreign Influence Task Force.

In one exchange cited in the complaint, she was asked: "Did you have any involvement in the Hunter Biden investigation?" to which she responded, "I did not," the complaint said.

In another exchange cited, it said she was asked: "Was there ever a discussion at the FITF about Hunter Biden?"

"No. At least not with me," she responded, adding: "And again, there's a whole team below me, so whether or not conversations happened, I don't know, but I personally did not have any conversations."

In the September 2023 interview with Benavides before the House Judiciary Committee, the complaint said he told investigators he only learned some of the details about the investigation into the Hunter Biden laptop from Wikipedia when preparing for the hearing.

"When did you learn that there was an ongoing criminal investigation related to the laptop?" it says he was asked.

"The Wikipedia page," he said.

When pressed whether he had any knowledge about the matter during his time at the FBI, the complaint alleges he said, "No."

The complaint also cited a congressional staffer who was present for both interviews. That staffer told investigators the testimony from both officials appeared to be "materially untrue."

An FBI employee also later told investigators that he personally spoke with Benavides about the laptop and discussed reviewing its contents.

"Floris testified that she had no involvement in the Hunter Biden investigations. In reality, she was in frequent communication with the case team for over a year during which she both sent and received information about Hunter Biden," the complaint said.

"Benavides' testimony followed a similar pattern," it added.

Floris' attorneys said in a statement that she has been falsely accused of a crime and raised concerns about the timing of the charges.

"Nikki Floris is a patriot. She served our nation as a dedicated FBI intelligence officer for nearly 20 years. Yet today, the DOJ has accused her falsely of a crime on the say-so of politicians, not on the facts. It's no coincidence the government is filing these nonsense charges now, years later, on the eve of an election," they said.

"The government's reasons for charging Nikki are as transparent as they are unjust: to push a false narrative for a shot at political points. It's another sad day for the DOJ, but we look forward to Nikki's day in court."

World.title: House hunter discovers deceased body in vacant home
World.content:
Florida resident David Hammersley and his family were fleeing from the hurricanes that plagued Florida and decided to tour homes in Kentucky. While house hunting on Sept. 26, 2022, their realtor showed them a rural 2-acre lot with a main house, a detached garage, and a cottage in Burkesville, Kentucky — a town known as the fishing capital of Kentucky.

"The house was immaculate. No furnishings in it. You can eat off the floor," Hammersley told correspondent Peter Van Sant in "The Mansion Above Dale Hollow Lake," an all-new "48 Hours" airing Saturday at 10/9c on CBS and streaming on Paramount+.

Hammersley was impressed with the property, including the sight of a Dodge truck found inside the detached garage.

"And I started to salivate over the possibility of that being part of the deal," he said.

The cottage, right, on the Kentucky property that became a crime scene. CBS News

As Hammersley and his family approached the cottage at the far end of the property, they were overpowered by a stench radiating from the cottage.

"It had to be something like a dead raccoon, in my opinion," Hammersley said.

Hammersley and his father-in-law proceeded to investigate, and within moments they stumbled across a horrific scene.

"I saw a man on the floor, his arm outstretched, obviously dead, from gunshot wounds," Hammersley told Van Sant.

They immediately contacted the authorities, who identified that man as Michael "Mike" Harding, a California transplant who resided across the Kentucky border in Tennessee. He had been missing for over a week.

An autopsy revealed that Harding had been shot four times — twice in the head and twice in the torso. Authorities found his phone at the crime scene and lead investigator BJ Burton from the Kentucky State Police examined it to see if it could answer their questions.

"Once you start looking through the text messages and phone calls, it becomes very obvious early on that he was lured to the house," Burton told Van Sant.

Investigators learned Harding had been contacted by a realtor named James Fraser requesting a repair service because Harding worked as an HVAC technician. However, they discovered the number used to contact Harding came from a prepaid cellphone.

"It was pretty evident early on that this is a burner phone," Burton said.

Burton also discovered Harding was going through a contentious divorce with his wife Julie Harding, a captain with the California Highway Patrol. The two were living in separate places — he was in Tennessee and she was in California.

"I feel like he was blinded by love. He truly loved her ... So, I thought he found his dream girl. But to me personally, I just, I didn't like her," Mike Harding's daughter, Heather Cavalieri, told "48 Hours."

Mike and Julie Harding Preston and Crystal Cleary/Cumberland County Justice Center/CHP

Friends and family of Mike Harding told authorities he feared Julie Harding. They got access to her call log and learned that in the months leading up to his murder, Julie Harding had around 194 calls with a man from Houston. His name was Thomas O'Donnell and he was a former car salesman now living in Napa, California.

They also determined that the prepaid phone and O'Donnell's phone were located together a few weeks before Mike Harding's death.

"And the first thing you notice is ... the phone is first turned on when it's in the Houston, Texas, area," Burton said. "I don't think Mr. O'Donnell got out here by accident. The only connection that he had to Michael Harding was through Julie Harding."

On Dec. 8, 2022, just two months after Mike Harding was found dead, authorities arrested O'Donnell for his murder. For Julie Harding, two days after O'Donnell's arrest, she was found dead at the Tennessee home where Mike Harding had been living. An investigator determined she had died by suicide.

Burton believes Julie Harding may have feared she would lose hundreds of thousands of dollars in their divorce, so she conspired with O'Donnell to kill her estranged husband. O'Donnell pleaded not guilty to the murder charge and would face trial three years after his arrest. A Kentucky jury found him guilty, and he was sentenced to life in prison with the possibility of parole after 20 years.

World.title: Trump administration to push for new labels on seafood
World.content:
The Trump administration intends to push for new labels on seafood sold at grocery stores to give consumers a better idea of where products originated, two U.S. officials told CBS News.

However, the "U.S. Caught Seafood" label, proposed by the Food and Drug Administration, wouldn't be mandatory.

President Trump was expected to mention seafood during his pitch to voters in Florida on Friday afternoon. He is stumping in Fort Myers for Senate candidate Ashley Moody and gubernatorial candidate Byron Donalds before spending the night at his Mar-a-Lago resort in Palm Beach.

The White House has prepared economy-related perks to roll out in each of the states he visits in the final campaign blitz before the midterm elections.

Most seafood eaten in the U.S. is imported, government data shows. About 80% of the seafood Americans ate in 2023 came from abroad, according to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration. U.S. commercial fishermen caught seafood valued at $5.1 billion in 2023, while the U.S. imported $25 billion worth.

The Trump administration was also preparing $5 billion in loans targeted at the fishing industry so that it can buy new equipment, according to U.S. officials. The loans would be through the U.S. Department of Agriculture.

World.title: DOJ sues to block Alaska Senate certification if Sullivan loses
World.content:
The Trump administration is suing to block certification of the Alaska Senate race if incumbent GOP Sen. Dan Sullivan does not win reelection — but would have won if votes for the other GOP Alaska Senate candidate, Daniel J. Sullivan, were counted for the incumbent.

The government alleges that candidate Daniel J. Sullivan deliberately sought to confuse voters by running with the same ballot name and party affiliation as incumbent senator, potentially diverting votes — and benefiting Democratic challenger former Rep. Mary Peltola.

Sen. Sullivan, Daniel J. Sullivan and Peltola and another Republican, Gerald Heikes, are on the general election ballot, which will be decided by ranked-choice voting.

In their court filing Friday, the Justice Department argued that allowing Daniel J. Sullivan to be on the ballot "threatens to mislead Alaskan citizens who want to vote for Senator Sullivan" and said that some of his supporters "likely will inadvertently vote for Daniel J. Sullivan." The department said that the senator's other supporters "likely will be confused as to how to rank the three Republican candidates as to defeat Peltola" and "might not rank Senator Sullivan at all."

Although Alaska courts permitted Daniel J. Sullivan to remain on the ballot, the Justice Department argues that certifying an election result impacted by this confusion would violate the National Voter Registration Act.

The DOJ complaint asks the federal court to block certification if Sen. Sullivan loses, but would have won had the other Sullivan's votes been counted for him, pending an investigation into voter intent.

Alaska voted to change its election system in 2020, and first implemented ranked choice voting in 2022. Its move away from party primaries was an attempt to curtail polarization. The state has seen unusual election outcomes in the past, notably in 2010, when Sen. Lisa Murkowski won her reelection bid on a write-in campaign, after her defeat in the GOP primary.

World.title: Gunmen kill at least 7 in attack on Jordan church, authorities say
World.content:
Gunmen carried out a deadly attack on a church in southern Jordan during a funeral Friday, authorities said. At least seven people were killed in the shooting, the kingdom's interior minister said.

Mazen Al-Faraya said at a press conference that 34 other people were wounded in the rare attack on Christians in the majority Sunni Muslim kingdom. The interior minister said a group of extremists carried out the shooting.

Jordan's King Abdullah II vowed the "harshest retaliation" against the attackers.

"Every Jordanian life is precious, and we will strike with an iron fist against those who dare to threaten our nation," he said on social media.

People and security forces gather outside a Greek Orthodox Church in the village of Hammoud in Jordan's Karak governorate following a shooting on Oct. 23, 2026. AFP via Getty Images

Assailants stormed the compound of a Greek Orthodox church in the village of Hammoud in Karak governorate before opening fire, the public security directorate said in a statement. Karak, home to a significant Christian community in the Muslim-majority kingdom, is 110 miles south of the capital, Amman.

The gunmen got out of a vehicle and opened fire during a funeral procession, the directorate added, saying a manhunt was underway for the perpetrators.

Footage aired by state broadcaster Al-Mamlaka showed the moment of the attack. In the video, two gunmen are seen dressed in casual clothes and brandishing pistols, with a third carrying a long gun, before they open fire on the church from an entrance on the street and charge forward.

Minister of Government Communications Mohammed Al-Momani said security forces were investigating the attack.

Security forces are seen after an attack on a Greek Orthodox church in Jordan's Karak governorate, Oct. 23, 2026, in a screengrab from video footage. Al Arabiya via Reuters

An eyewitness told Al-Mamlaka that a vehicle arrived carrying the gunmen, who fired continuously for five minutes before fleeing the scene.

Between 150 and 200 people were in and around the church at the time, the witness said, adding most of the victims were aged between 50 and 70.

Lebanese President Joseph Aoun, the Arab world's only Christian head of state, called the shooting at the church a "heinous terrorist attack."

He said that it "reaffirms once again that terrorism has no religion and no homeland, and its aim is to strike at coexistence and spread strife," according to a presidency statement.

In 2016, gunmen ambushed police in a series of attacks in Karak, including at a Crusader castle popular with tourists, killing 10 people, including seven officers, and wounding dozens. Jordanian security forces killed the gunmen after a long standoff.

World.title: Ex-FBI employees charged with lying to Congress over Hunter Biden inquiries
World.content:
Ex-FBI employees charged with lying to Congress over Hunter Biden inquiries

toggle caption i Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images

The Justice Department has charged two former FBI employees with making false statements to Congress in connection with the bureau's investigations into Hunter Biden.

Bradley Benavides, 56, and Nikki Floris, 46, each face a single criminal count stemming from testimony before lawmakers in 2023. They were charged by complaint, which means prosecutors have yet to secure an indictment from a grand jury.

The laptop of Hunter Biden, former President Joe Biden's son, was the subject of intense scrutiny after The New York Post reported weeks before the 2020 presidential election that the device was abandoned at a Delaware repair shop in 2019, and then obtained by President Trump's former personal lawyer Rudy Giuliani.

Sponsor Message

Republicans have long accused the FBI of mishandling the laptop and the investigations into the younger Biden. Hunter Biden was convicted of federal gun charges and later pleaded guilty to separate tax offenses.

In a statement on X, the U.S. attorney for Washington, D.C., Jeanine Pirro, said Floris and Benavides "allegedly lied to Congress about their roles in the FBI's Hunter Biden investigations, with one claiming they only learned about it from Wikipedia — despite evidence showing their involvement in helping shape the public narrative about Hunter Biden's laptop right before the election."

Benavides and Floris both appeared in federal court in Washington, D.C., on Friday morning before Magistrate Judge Zia Faruqui.

Faruqui noted that both of the defendants have "sparkling backgrounds" in federal law enforcement and were longtime dedicated public servants. He also noted that charging them by criminal complaint for conduct that is "quite old" is unusual.

Benavides and Floris are due back in court for a preliminary hearing on Tuesday.

The Post reported Hunter Biden's laptop showed wrongdoing by then-Democratic nominee Joe Biden, who subsequently won the election. Some of the data on the laptop was later ascertained to belong to Hunter Biden. House Republicans subsequently launched an impeachment inquiry into President Biden, focusing on Hunter Biden's business dealings at the time his father was vice president. But no evidence has ever been presented that Joe Biden financially gained from his son's business activities.

Sponsor Message

President Joe Biden signed a full and unconditional pardon for his son in December 2024, shortly before leaving the White House.

World.title: Will a macaque eat a grape sitting on a pile of poo? A study on germaphobia
World.content:
Will a macaque eat a grape sitting on a pile of poo? A study on germaphobia

toggle caption i Stephan Kaufhold

In the very early days of COVID-19, millions who'd rarely thought twice about germ avoidance became germophobes.

Some folks wiped down groceries before stuffing them into the refrigerator. Others let mail quarantine outside for days lest it harbor stray viruses. With the hindsight that SARS-CoV-2 spread primarily through the air, these sorts of precautions seem extreme. But in the moment, they were perhaps reasonable ways of avoiding an unknown pathogen.

Around this same time, a different virus hit a macaque sanctuary in Texas. New research suggests the monkeys responded in similar ways as humans did to COVID-19 — by being extra germophobic.

Sponsor Message

Humans are far from the only animals to avoid possible sources of disease. Scientists have found that critters as diverse as monkeys and nematodes (aka roundworms) can sense and steer clear of feces, for instance, which can harbor harmful bacteria.

"Something that has been less studied is the question of how flexible this avoidance is," says Stephan Kaufhold , a cognitive scientist at UC San Diego. He wanted to see if experiencing an outbreak could make individual monkeys even more wary of picking up pathogens.

The outbreak in the Texas sanctuary, home to over 100 macaques, offered Kaufhold and his colleagues an opportunity to put that question to the test.

Grape expectations

In 2020, macaques in an enclosure at the sanctuary started getting sick with an HIV-like virus called SRV.

Once a monkey gets infected through bodily fluids, the disease "can take a rapid progression, where about three to four weeks after you initially get infected, you might die," says Kaufhold. Many monkeys died, while others developed chronic immunodeficiency.

Sanctuary staff quickly started separating monkeys quickly, ultimately creating two groups — those who'd experienced the virus, either by getting sick themselves or witnessing others get sick, and those who hadn't experienced the outbreak.

To see if those different histories made the monkeys more germophobic, the researchers presented individuals with two tasty treats — grapes.

Sponsor Message

"They get a fantastic diet at the sanctuary, but not grapes every day, so grapes were definitely a treat," says Kaufhold.

One red grape was presented on a non-descript, clean-looking piece of wood. The other was on top of macaque poop, encased in epoxy. "Basically not to make the animals eat off actual feces," says Kaufhold. "It did look quite gross, feces with a glossy wet look. Definitely worked also in triggering disgust in humans."

From 2022 to 2024, the researchers presented monkeys with this choice in nearly 200 trials. Among monkeys who didn't experience the outbreak, 79% ate the poop-plated grape. But only 47% of the outbreak veterans ate it, researchers report in the journal Royal Society Open Science.

Essentially, those who'd been oblivious to the outbreak were more likely to throw caution to the wind and eat the poop-plated grape than those who'd lived through it.

"I was surprised," says Kaufhold. "I think it's pretty clear evidence that something is going on." Kaufhold thinks that something might be a heightened sensitivity to disgust.

"If you think about disgust, the evolutionary origins most likely are to try to protect the body from contamination because there are pathogens and parasites that we ideally would want to avoid," he says. Becoming more easily disgusted after a devastating outbreak could pay off if it means avoiding infection, of whatever cause.

Of course, scientists can't know whether macaques are actually experiencing disgust. "But the possibility that things like disgust are influencing the behavior of other species, and especially species like primates, it's definitely a possibility worth considering," says Andrew MacIntosh , a biologist at the Wilder Institute who wasn't involved in the study but has done similar experiments with macaques.

"It seems plausible that past exposure to outbreaks could make individuals more cautious or risk averse," he says, but he thinks more evidence is needed to show that. For example, the experiment was carried out several years after the outbreak, enough time for other factors to influence these behaviors, he says.

Sponsor Message

MacIntosh also points out that the fecal avoidance experiment bears little connection to how the initial outbreak spread, through bodily fluids transmitted through scratches or bites. "The mode of transmission of that virus has really nothing to do with fecal contamination," he says.

Kaufhold doesn't think that's a problem.

"We're not claiming that macaques had any sort of understanding of the mechanism of viruses, it just seems to be an increased caution," he says. People didn't initially know how SARS-CoV-2 spread either, he says, but many went to great lengths to avoid infection. Those impulses may have been shaped not by paranoia, but by evolution, as a way of staving off sickness in an uncertain world.

For stories about life in our changing world, subscribe to NPR's Global Health newsletter.

World.title: Authorities investigating whether first Kenya and Nigeria Ebola cases crossed paths
World.content:
Authorities investigating whether first Kenya and Nigeria Ebola cases crossed paths

toggle caption i Tony Karumba/AFP via Getty Images

JOHANNESBURG – The first Ebola patient confirmed in Nigeria may have crossed paths with the first Kenyan Ebola patient at a Ugandan airport, health officials said Thursday.

Nigeria announced its first case of Ebola in more than a decade on Tuesday. Nigerian health authorities said the patient is the Ugandan-born wife of a diplomat based in Abuja who had vacationed in Uganda in September and returned to Nigeria earlier this month.

She is being treated and 44 people she had close contact with have been quarantined, Dr. Wessam Mankoula, head of emergency preparedness and response at the Africa Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, told a press briefing on Thursday.

Authorities are now investigating what the source of her exposure was.

Nigeria, Africa's most populous country, is the fourth on the continent to record an Ebola case during the current outbreak, but it's the first in West Africa and the furthest away from the epicenter in the Democratic Republic of Congo.

Sponsor Message

Congo's current Ebola outbreak began in May in the country's east. It has become the fastest spreading on record. At least 4,600 people have died and about 9,700 have been infected in Congo.

Neighboring Uganda initially recorded about 20 cases but was declared Ebola-free in August.

The first case in Kenya was recorded in early October and since then eight other cases have been confirmed in the east African nation.

The first Kenyan patient, who has since died, travelled from Congo to Kenya, via Uganda.

Officials are now investigating whether that person crossed paths with the Nigeria case at the Entebbe International Airport in Uganda – as they were there on the same day.

Dr. Mankoula said the center was probing whether there had been "some sort of interaction between the two cases at the airport."

Ebola is spread through direct contact with an infected person's bodily fluids or contaminated items. It causes severe fever and can be deadly. However, generally people are not considered infectious until they start showing symptoms.

World.title: Military reinforcements move to Mideast. And, millions of Americans vote early
World.content:
Military reinforcements move to Mideast. And, millions of Americans vote early

Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for all the news you need to start your day.

Today's top stories

Heavier fighting in Iran could resume in the coming weeks as military reinforcements arrive and some U.S. personnel leave the region. This shift comes as a person briefed on the U.S. and Israel's war planning told NPR that the countries were preparing plans for a possible attack on Iran after the U.S. midterms. Iran said it is prepared.

toggle caption i Atta Kenare/AFP via Getty Images

🎧 There are clear signs of preparations for a possible attack, NPR's Greg Myre tells Up First. The U.S. is deploying a third aircraft carrier to the Middle East, and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth recently visited Israel to meet with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. President Trump will likely consider military action after Nov. 3 to avoid a spike in oil prices before the midterm elections. In response, Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said that Iran is ready for both diplomacy and war. While the U.S. and Israel possess the power to inflict heavy damage, Iran shows no signs of making significant concessions, Myre says. Instead, it demands formal control over the Strait of Hormuz and the withdrawal of U.S. troops from the region.

Sponsor Message

Although Election Day is more than a week away, almost 21 million Americans have already voted, either by mail or early in-person voting, according to the University of Florida's Election Lab.



🎧 That number of votes so far is a lot and is an increase of about 2 million since yesterday, according to NPR's Saige Miller. In key battleground states, early voting is significantly higher compared to the last midterm election. While the early voting data should not be overinterpreted as a predictor of final results, it shows Democrats voting at higher rates than Republicans, Miller says. Unaffiliated voters are also participating early. Democrats are generally more likely to vote early, and Republicans are more likely to turn out on Election Day, Miller says.
