While the early voting data should not be overinterpreted as a predictor of final results, it shows Democrats voting at higher rates than Republicans, Miller says. Unaffiliated voters are also participating early. Democrats are generally more likely to vote early, and Republicans are more likely to turn out on Election Day, Miller says. ➡️ A federal judge in California is limiting the Department of Homeland Security's pre-election field operations. The agency says they aim to identify noncitizens who allegedly voted illegally in nine states.

The agency says they aim to identify noncitizens who allegedly voted illegally in nine states. ➡️ The NPR App has all of NPR's election coverage in one place — from the biggest stories across the country, to the issues that matter close to home. Browse headlines, playlists, podcast episodes, videos and more, all on the 2026 Election tab.

Trump must sit for a deposition in his $10 billion defamation case against the BBC, a federal magistrate judge ruled. Trump is required to comply with court rules or face sanctions, the judge said yesterday. The case centers on a Panorama broadcast from late October 2024, which allegedly edited the president's Jan. 6 speech to make it appear he incited a violent siege of Congress. Trump has described the broadcast as false, misleading and defamatory under Florida law.



Sponsor Message

🎧 It's unclear if Trump will sit for a deposition after he previously canceled for "matters of national importance" and suggested January as an alternative, NPR's David Folkenflik says. The case initially focused on the economic harm the broadcast posed to Trump's brand and financial prospects. Although the BBC apologized for the splicing, it now seeks to understand Trump's mindset during his testimony, as he may have intended to encourage violence. BBC attorneys say more than 200 defendants from Jan. 6 said Trump's speech motivated them. The BBC is actively pursuing details about how Trump has profited since regaining the White House, most likely to assess the extent of the damage he faces, Folkenflik says.

Deep dive

Julianna Conley/NPR

Trump promised to lower grocery prices in his second term. While some individual items have gotten cheaper since he returned to office, overall grocery prices have risen, driven by factors such as increased labor costs, tariffs and higher energy prices due to the conflict with Iran. Specific issues facing a single crop, animal species or geographic region can cause the price of one item to rise well above inflation, while lowering the price of another. NPR analyzed five everyday food items — ground beef, eggs, coffee, butter and chocolate chip cookies — to better understand the math behind grocery store prices.

🍔 Ground beef prices have skyrocketed, reaching $6.79 per pound last month, which is an 85% increase over the past decade, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics. This surge is largely due to weather and financial pressures on producers.

🥚 Prices for eggs fell to $2.27 per dozen last month. Outbreaks like the avian flu can cause significant price fluctuations. In March 2025, the average dozen reached a record high of $6.23.

🧈 In September, a pound of butter averaged $3.96 — down 17.3% from last year. U.S. butter production has surged as dairy farms expanded their herds and boosted milk supply for popular items like Greek yogurt. This has resulted in an oversupply of butter.

🍪 Chocolate chip cookie prices hit a record $5.35 per pound this January, and last month dropped by 20 cents. The price spike is partly due to factors affecting the sweet treat's ingredients, such as higher flour costs driven by the war in Ukraine.

☕ The U.S. imports 99% of the coffee it consumes. Severe weather and climate change have affected harvests, and the price of coffee is still 44% higher than it was two years earlier, despite Trump removing tariffs on the product.

Sponsor Message

Read more about why these prices have fluctuated here.

Weekend picks

toggle caption i Karen Almond/Metropolitan Opera

Check out what NPR is watching, reading and listening to this weekend:

🍿 Movies: A new film version of Jane Austen's Sense and Sensibility focuses on the Dashwood family's two oldest sisters, Elinor and Marianne, who face financial insecurity due to laws that disadvantage widows and daughters.

📺 TV: Actor Sharon Horgan stars as Alex, a 50-year-old divorcée who finds herself at multiple personal and professional crossroads in HBO's new show Youth.

📚 Books: Barbara Trapido's Brother of the More Famous Jack follows Katherine Browne, who is determined to escape her stiflingly conventional upbringing and create a life with fewer constraints.

🎵 Music: NPR's New Music Friday host Stephen Thompson breaks down the best albums released today, including Anderson .Paak and Cordae's Heavy Is the Crown and Fenne Lily's Win Win. Listen to a playlist of the best songs from the new albums.

🎭 Theater: Missy Mazzoli's music brings George Saunders' Booker Prize-winning novel, Lincoln in the Bardo, to life in a stage adaptation at the Metropolitan Opera House in New York. Mazzoli is the first woman composer to have a world premiere on the Met stage.

3 things to know before you go

toggle caption i Karl Bushby

British adventurer Karl Bushby set out from Chile with the goal of walking an unbroken path to his hometown in England. After 28 years, he has returned to the U.K. and plans to return to his mother's home in Hull by Nov. 1. At least four Trump merchandise stores closed this year as the MAGA Mall reports sales fell 30% from his presidential election years. In this week's edition of Far-Flung Postcards, NPR's Carrie Kahn recalls feeling the rare power of nature at Iguazú Falls on the Brazil-Argentina border. A rain-soaked October brought near-record water volumes crashing over the cliffs.

This newsletter was edited by Suzanne Nuyen.

World.title: Why Meta is charging to post more hyperlinks
World.content:
Why Meta is charging to post more hyperlinks

You're reading a newsletter from The Indicator from Planet Money. Once a week, we curate our favorite stories and insights on business, finance, economics and why they matter. Subscribe here to get it in your inbox every Friday.

Outside of Atlanta, two gas stations got into a price war. The Atlanta TV station WSB-TV reported that, over the course of a day, prices dropped from $2.54 down to $1.44, $1.39 and eventually down to just 97 cents. When drivers took notice, the traffic jam began and police intervened. BUT while it was happening, one driver said she only spent $15 to fill up her truck. It usually costs $90. "Look at God, baby! Look at God!" she said.

In our team's Slack, co-host Wailin Wong responded to the low prices, "make it up on volume!?" Jeff Guo wrote, "how is this real." But like, actually. How is this real?

Coming up:



Why Facebook is charging you to post hyperlinks

How fake data centers can still drive up electricity costs

How one man is dealing with a rental car agency

News We're Watching

Why websites make it hard to leave

What To Know: Social media sites don't love it when users leave. If you've ever used Instagram, it's not the easiest place to post links. You need to include them in bios, or through a special button on stories. Well now, if you run a Facebook page, you can only post TWO hyperlinks for free per month. $49.99/month will get you a Meta One Advanced plan, allowing you to include eight hyperlinks in posts or reels. With the $499/month Max plan, you can post an unlimited amount. Ashley Gullen, who runs a game design company, posted on Mastodon, a decentralized social media platform, "Facebook achieving absurd new heights of enshittification" in response to the news. This isn't totally unique. Nieman Lab did a whole study finding that posting links hurts news publishers on X.

toggle caption i Tony Avelar/AP Photo

Why are companies doing this?: Attention is money for social media sites. They want to keep you inside their walls! David Evans, managing director at BRG, a consulting firm, wrote a simple explanation as to why platforms want you to stay on their site: "Attention platforms use content to get consumers to spend time on their platform and sell marketers the ability to expose these consumers to messages."

Sponsor Message

Even FAKE data centers could be driving up electricity costs - The Wall Street Journal

What To Know: Developers are desperate to get their data centers up and running. They need it to help power their precious AI and whatever other computing is needed. BUT, developers won't just say, "This is the only location we'll accept for this project." No, they'll put out requests to all sorts of locations for their centers. The problem is, utilities are still considering data centers that likely WON'T GET BUILT in their electricity forecasts. Energy research firm Wood Mackenzie estimates that only a mere 23% of data-center requests are considered "high confidence," according to The Wall Street Journal. The rest are speculative!

How this affects YOU: Electricity costs could rise even if the data centers don't get built. Hoowwwwww does that work now? Because utilities are still planning for expected demand. They can't just suddenly integrate a wildly power-demanding data center without new substations or transmission lines. It's possible for the utility to pass on some of those grid investments onto consumers, even if the data centers never come to pass. Some power markets also set prices based on future demand so… There are lots of ways these projects could mess with your electricity bill.

Sponsor Message

Another oil reserve gets tapped - U.S. Department of Energy

It's your weekly update on diesel prices! This week, the Trump administration has found a NEW way to try and lower prices, which seems to be a core issue ahead of the midterms. This time, the U.S. Department of Energy has authorized an exchange from the Northeast Home Heating Oil Reserve. It would release roughly a third of the reserves for heating oil. The Chief Energy Advisor for Gulf Oil thinks it won't make a difference on prices.

toggle caption i Screenshot of a post on X by @tomkloza/X

What's interesting, this reserve has only been tapped ONCE, and that was after Hurricane Sandy. According to the DOE's history, that's the sort of thing it was meant for. "The intent was to create a buffer large enough to allow commercial companies to compensate for interruptions in supply during severe winter weather." Here, the DOE will loan out up to 315,000 barrels of heating oil in hopes of lowering prices. It's called an exchange because borrowing entities, like a regional heating oil retailer, would be required to replace the same volume at a premium ahead of next year.

Today's Indicator

Why Oracle's debt load could be your problem

If you HAVEN'T listened: We keep hearing about the AI boom that's propping up the U.S. economy. Well, Oracle is a part of that story. The enterprise software company has moved into building out data centers to serve the AI industry. Now, they have a huge deal with OpenAI worth $300 billion over five years. Here's the problem. Oracle has been spending freely with the assumption that this OpenAI deal will deliver. But what if it doesn't? Oracle already has $169 billion in total debt and a growing credit risk. They're one link in an interconnected chain of enormous tech companies. If that link breaks, it could spell trouble for the economy.

Listen to the full episode

Sponsor Message

If you HAVE listened: Lindsay Tyler, credit analyst, explains in the piece that Oracle is making a bet on data centers. "The analogy might be you have 10 apartments, you've pre-signed leases with, for those 10 apartments, and you're thinking, 'Should I build another floor?'"

On the surface, this doesn't seem plausible. Isn't computing demand insatiable right now? Yeah, right now. But…



AI is getting so much more efficient to run. Research from Epoch AI found "the cost of achieving a given level of AI performance has fallen about 47% per quarter since 2023, or 13× per year."

The chips powering these AI models "have a useful lifespan of one to three years due to rapid technological obsolescence and physical wear."

Some economic historians like to compare the AI buildout to the railroads, but this one is different. Rails last longer than one to three years. The cost of shipping does not plummet 13x per year. And maybe Oracle is at the center of these economic forces colliding: a railroad-type investment boom building castles made of sand.

Rest of the Week

We can inflate away the national debt… at a cost

Piercing the American taboo of talking about income and class

Can a "Moneyball" system work for campaign funding?

Listener Mailbag

Context: Last week, we ran an episode full of consumer rage stories. One included a story about someone charged for damage to a rental car that was impossible to disprove. Stay to the end for a surprising twist.

Listener Jim Zerefos sent in a response from Colorado.

I share the frustration of the person who complained about dubious damage claims from a rental car company. I've been fighting Alamo for nearly a year now over a $1,600 damage claim. Alamo sent me photos of very minor damage taken AFTER our rental, but never provided photos from BEFORE our rental. [The car] had some 23k miles so seems possible (likely?) the scratches occurred some time before our rental.

Sponsor Message

My spidey sense here smells a scam: "rental companies now scan cars for damage and so are trying to find scapegoats for all prior damage"? Alamo's reaction to me (and my insurance company) has been to ignore us - never sending the "before" pics and never acknowledging that's an issue. They just keep sending us invoices. They now are threatening collection action and have banned me from renting from the Alamo rental family (as if I would). So, the story on the broader scam? Or story on which credit cards still offer primary rental damage coverage (which we THOUGHT we had)?

By the way, here at The Indicator, we reached out to the car rental company and they responded in a statement through a spokesperson from Enterprise Mobility: "Customer satisfaction is our top priority, and we are always open to further conversations with customers regarding damage claims. Our team is actively reviewing this matter through our escalation process and will reach out to the customer to share an update today."

And we already have an update: Jim tells us Alamo has since dropped the claim and will make no further collection efforts. Alamo's "risk" department instructed the Cleveland manager to drop the claim, according to Jim.

Jim's response: "Sad to see that you got more action in a day than my insurance company and I got in nearly a year."

In Our Spare Time

Co-host Wailin Wong is reading Under Story

This fall has yielded a bumper crop of big new fiction releases. My favorite from the last couple of weeks of reading is UNDER STORY by Chloe Benjamin. This novel is about a fungi expert who goes to Antarctica after a family tragedy. She's hoping to anonymously wash dishes at a research station. However, a strange light phenomenon and the arrival of her physicist ex-husband pull her back into the scientific world. This was an exciting, imaginative, and beautiful story about grief, family, parallel universes, trees, and mushrooms. (Bonus rec: This book also makes for a good pairing with Emily St. John Mandel's new novel, Exit Party.)

World.title: Israel orders closure of West Bank after soldiers kill 2 men behind an alleged attack
World.content:
Israel orders closure of West Bank after soldiers kill 2 men behind an alleged attack

toggle caption i Mahmoud Illean/AP

HEBRON, West Bank — Israeli soldiers shot and killed two men who the military said had launched an attack near the city of Hebron in the occupied West Bank on Friday morning. At least five people were injured, including some critically.

The army said it prevented a "terror attack against Israeli civilians" and that the gunmen carried an M16 rifle and a handgun. It did not elaborate on the target of the alleged attack. There was also no word on the identities of the two dead and those injured.

A few hours later, Israel ordered the army to prepare for a full closure of the West Bank. The office of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said it instructed security forces to immediately cordon off the city of Hebron and prepare to fully close all of the West Bank, starting Friday.

Sponsor Message

The deadly shooting comes as Israeli voters will decide next Tuesday whether to grant Netanyahu yet another term as prime minister — or usher in a new era of Israeli politics. The election comes three years after the Hamas-led attacks on Israel that triggered the war in Gaza.

Israel's government has warned of potential attacks by the country's "enemies" in the lead-up to the election.

Netanyahu holds an emergency meeting

Following the shooting, Netanyahu held an emergency meeting of his Security Cabinet and officials from top military and security agencies. He blamed Hamas, saying the militant group was "planning a major attack aimed at murdering innocent civilians."

"Our brave soldiers thwarted this attack with courage and determination," he said, without elaborating on what the planned attack entailed.

"I commend them for their actions and wish our wounded a speedy recovery," he added but did not say if the wounded were soldiers or civilians.

Earlier Friday Israel's far-right national security minister Itamar Ben-Gvir, known for extremist views, said that the attack shows that Israel needs to restrict the Palestinians' freedom of movement in the West Bank.

"The lives of the residents of Judea and Samaria, of the settlers, the lives of the soldiers, the lives of the police officers, the lives of our fighters are a million times more important than freedom of movement," he said, using an Israeli reference to the West Bank.

Sponsor Message

Ahead of the anniversary of the Oct. 7, 2023 Hamas-led attack that triggered the war, Netanyahu said the Palestinian militant group could attack Israel in a bid to influence the outcome of the elections. He did not provide evidence to back up the claim.

The injured are evacuated to a hospital, medics say

Emergency responders said five people were injured, some critically, and were being evacuated to hospitals in Israel. A statement from the responders said gunfire was still ongoing as they arrived at the scene of the attack near the Yehuda Junction in the morning.

Two men in their 20s had gunshot wounds to their lower limbs, one was unconscious and seriously injured, the responders said.

"We arrived at a difficult scene while shooting was still taking place in the area," said Tzuriel Edri with the response team.

An investigation was underway, authorities said.

Also Friday, the army said soldiers and Israeli security and intelligence agencies conducted dozens of operations in the West Bank and apprehended dozens of people, including those affiliated with Hamas and Islamic Jihad militant groups. It also said it had located weapons, including M16 rifles and submachine guns.

Closures of the West Bank, such as the one ordered Friday, are growing more common in the territory. It's the fourth time in the past month that Israel has imposed restrictions across the area, shutting gates and checkpoints connecting Palestinian villages to major roads.

Meanwhile, Israeli roads in the territory remain open to Israeli drivers, including settlers, who can still travel through the area but may face delays.

World.title: Hacking attempts rise after flaws found in program affecting 70 percent of websites
World.content:
Hacking attempts rise after flaws found in program affecting 70 percent of websites

toggle caption i Yong Teck Lim/Getty Images

A few months ago AI caused global alarm after autonomous agents were found to have cheated on evaluations and then tried to cover it up, in what became known as the "Hugging Face hack."

This week, AI and hacking are back in the spotlight with AI technology credited to have helped prevent a global cybersecurity crisis.

Cyber-security firm Wiz Research, using OpenAI technology, announced on Wednesday it had discovered security flaws in a computer programming language that helps run some 70 percent of the world's websites.

OpenAI called the bug "one of the most impactful vulnerabilities in recent memory." Wiz Research warned that its "successful exploitation could allow attackers to take control of affected servers, steal sensitive data, and deface the websites running on them."

Sponsor Message

Corporations and governments from the U.K. to Japan are now rushing to prevent hackers from capitalizing on the flaws.

The flaws were discovered in a major programming language called PHP, short for Hypertext Preprocessor. Wiz Research calls PHP "the backbone of the web," saying the technology has underpinned much of the internet since the 1990s.

"These findings rank among the most severe vulnerabilities discovered in PHP, and arguably in software history," the firm said, adding that before publicly disclosing the flaw, teams had worked on building a solution that's now available to websites to protect themselves.

As countries scrambled to prevent cyberattacks, numerous websites and pages were taken offline in the past few days. The U.S. National Security Agency warned organizations using PHP to "maintain heightened awareness" over the coming weeks. The U.K.'s National Cyber Security Center called on organizations to "take immediate action" to update their websites to the latest fixed or patched version.

Dozens of British and Finnish government services were taken offline this week. In France many local government sites were also briefly taken down. China's Industry Ministry urged entities to review security gaps.

In Japan, Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi put out "an urgent request for everyone to take action," adding "If it is difficult to apply the fix patch promptly, temporarily suspending websites and similar measures can be considered an effective way to reduce risk."

Sponsor Message

Matthew Prince, the head of the cybersecurity firm CloudFlare, said his organization saw tens of thousands of attempts to exploit the flaw in the first 45 minutes of its discovery. That's now in the millions, Prince said on Thursday.

Wiz Research said the flaws in PHP had been present for decades.

"But demonstrating their exploitability required an exceptionally complex chain of steps, at the edge of what human researchers could practically achieve," the organization said. The AI models have "substantially reduced that barrier, turning a longstanding flaw into an exploit. "

World.title: Amid Trump's assaults on DEI, how one university is elevating Black students
World.content:
Amid Trump's assaults on DEI, how one university is elevating Black students

toggle caption i Andri Tambunan for NPR

Catch up on what you missed with our Education newsletter, sent weekly.

When Zyearre Amoah was a student at Sacramento State in 2023, there were times when he felt like the only Black student.

"There were African-American students on our campus," he recalls. But at a sprawling state university with more than 30,000 students, "it just felt like we had to look for each other."

Amoah graduated in 2024, just as his university was launching its Black Honors College, a school within a school with a special focus on Black history, life and culture. He's now a staff member at the BHC, as it's called, helping recruit students.

Sponsor Message

"Unfortunately I didn't have the luxury to be part of it as a student," he says, but the university's effort to elevate, and celebrate, the scholarship of Black students has changed how he perceives his alma mater.

"Black students on our campus are actually showing their faces," he says, laughing. "That is really helpful for everyone here. We're finding each other relatively easier. "

The initiative at Sacramento State, formally known as the California State University, Sacramento, began just months before the Trump administration began its widespread assault on diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI) programs on college campuses. In the last two years, dozens of colleges and universities have rolled back or eliminated such offerings to avoid accusations of racial discrimination that have led to loss of research funding and other sanctions.

"Historically, the campus struggled to create an environment of success" for Black students, says Luke Wood, Sac State's president, who helped create the BHC. "So we created an intervention that was designed to meet their needs while also serving any student who was interested in being part of it."

Wood sees this as a vital part of his, or any university's, mission. "I think that more institutions could be easily doing the same."

Sponsor Message

An 'elite, specialized experience'

There are more than 800 students currently enrolled in the BHC, and while the majority of them identify as Black, African, African-American or mixed race, Wood insists it's not exclusive and that it complies with federal and state laws.

"It's nondiscriminatory because you can be a white student, an Asian student or Latino and be in the Black Honors College," he says, "and we have non-Black students who apply who want to have an elite, specialized experience."

toggle caption i Andri Tambunan for NPR

All of the college's courses are taught from a Black studies perspective. A math class, for example, also includes stories of famous Black mathematicians.

Faculty are chosen based on their track record of educating Black students. Among the criteria are low withdrawal and failure numbers for those students.

Now in its third year, women make up a majority of the BHC's enrollment, according to the college's dean, Boatamo Ati Mosupyoe. That's the case on most U.S. campuses . She says one of her priorities is to change that. To do so, she plans to provide more male role models and mentors: not just to convince more men to enroll, but to support them when they do.

A climate of disappearing diversity programs

Following the Supreme Court decision in 2023 banning affirmative action , the Trump administration has launched civil rights investigations targeting programs that single out a specific race — such as a scholarship program for Black students or an office designed to celebrate multiculturalism.

In September, the Treasury Department proposed a new rule that would strip private schools and colleges of their tax-exempt status if they provide help to students based on their race.

At President Trump's State of the Union address in February, he declared, "We ended D-E-I in America!"

Around the country, many students have felt increasingly isolated, and let down, as diversity programs have disappeared.

Sponsor Message

"I was pretty sad just at the fact that our university would comply with those federal guidelines," says Hayden O'Neill, a senior at the University of Michigan. She was part of a scholarship program that was shut down last year.

"It definitely feels disheartening," she says, "I don't feel as comfortable as I thought I would at a school like this."

O'Neill is one of the many students around the country who say that understanding their identity – especially as it relates to their race – is a high priority in college. And while O'Neill feels like she is losing some of that opportunity, students in the Black Honors College say they're being given that chance.

A strong sense of belonging

The bell above the door to the Black Honors College headquarters – housed on the first floor of Sac State's library – rings often:

A sophomore arrives to meet with an advisor. A first-year student has a question about tuition. Over in the corner, a professor has come to ready his notes before class. It's a hub, a home within a home.

On a recent day, one of the students in the office is Naomi Thrower, a junior majoring in Deaf Studies and American Sign Language.

She wanted to attend a historically black college, but California doesn't have any. So, she says, Sacramento State with its BHC felt like the closest alternative.

Growing up in the East Bay, she had what she calls a very multicultural experience, going to school with kids of all different races. While she gained a lot from that, she also felt she was missing a deep understanding of Black culture and identity.

"The kids used to bully me in middle school and say I was whitewashed," Thrower says. "So when it came time for college, I wanted to be surrounded by students who looked like me and also had that same academic drive."

Sponsor Message

She runs a natural hair business on campus as a side hustle, and says it has helped her develop a creative expression. "In high school, when I'd say I have to do my hair, my friends wouldn't understand it's an all day thing. They'd be like, 'Why does it take so long to wash and brush out your hair?'"

But when she made friends in the honors college, it seemed everyone understood. "Two of my friends helped me take down my hair. We detangled it, washed it. We were just listening to music and hanging out, and that was the community that I was longing for, just someone who understood."

She and others NPR talked with often quoted the saying, Ubuntu, which comes from South African philosophy. It describes an interconnected way of living, often translated as, "I am because we are."

Many students said this concept is central to their educational experience.

And at Sacramento State, Wood says, the efforts to build that identity and sense of community are paying off: Enrollment of Black students is up – and those students are doing better – with more of them re-enrolling, and graduating.

This story was produced with support from the Education Writers Association's Reporting Fellowship program.

World.title: Crime Stoppers had 'potentially one of the most harmful data breaches' Canada has seen. What's next?
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Two days after an exclusive CBC investigation revealed the extent of the Crime Stoppers data hack in Canada, experts are now weighing the long-term implications of what could be among the country's most dangerous privacy failures.

"It strikes me as potentially one of the most harmful data breaches we've ever seen in Canada," said Michael Geist, a law professor at the University of Ottawa and the Canada Research Chair in Internet and E-commerce Law.

When it comes to the Canadian law, he says, both Crime Stoppers, the organization that collected the data, and Navigate360, the company it hired to manage it, could be held accountable.

"[How] Canadian privacy law functions is that the organization that collects the personal information is the one that's responsible," said Geist. "And even where they use third parties or subcontractors as part of what takes place, it's on them to ensure that no matter who gains access to the information, it has that appropriate level of protection."

However, enforcing those rules across borders — Navigate360 is U.S.-based — is notoriously difficult, he says, and the domestic penalties are weak.

"These kinds of incidents keep happening. There's a real urgency to addressing Canadian privacy law, which is woefully out of date," he said.

"And at the top of the list has been really weak enforcement."

Expert fears company doesn’t know leak's true scale

At the heart of the breach is Navigate360 and its tip management platform, P3. All Crime Stoppers chapters, including those in Canada and the U.S., relied on P3 to keep their data anonymous.

The information was stolen last March by a hacktivist collective Internet Yiff Machine, who stated they wanted to disprove the company's claim that its platform was "anonymous" and "secure." CBC News analyzed a copy of the hacked data and found that over 1.5 million tips submitted to Canadian Crime Stoppers programs over the last 25 years were exposed, along with tens of thousands of unredacted personal details.

CBC has reached out repeatedly to Navigate360 and shared the highlights of its investigation, but the company has not responded.

Adding to the controversy are accounts provided by the Toronto and Guelph Wellington Crime Stoppers chapters, where Navigate360 appeared to change its narrative about how much data had been stolen and what was affected.

According to a Wednesday statement from the Toronto chapter, Navigate360 initially told the organization that no Canadian data was taken, then said Toronto wasn't impacted, before finally revealing months later that years of Toronto data was compromised. Guelph Wellington shared a similar statement on Thursday.

Cybersecurity expert Ali Dehghantanha, who reviewed samples of the compromised data as part of CBC’s original investigation, said it was alarming that Navigate360's claims to Toronto Crime Stoppers appeared to change.

"They apparently received six different [accounts] in seven months from the vendor," he said, adding that this raises massive red flags about the company's ability to investigate the hack and fix the vulnerabilities that might have allowed it.

Dehghantanha, who has conducted digital forensics investigations for over a decade, said he is also very surprised at how quickly Navigate360 seemed to have returned its system to an operational state following the hack.

WATCH | More about the investigation: Crime Stoppers hack exposes personal information of tens of thousands of Canadians | Duration closed caption 3:40 A massive data breach leaked 25 years worth of unredacted personal information from Crime Stoppers, compromising the identities of thousands of Canadian tipsters. The Toronto branch of Crime Stoppers has asked the public not to send in tips until the issue is resolved.

Toronto Crime Stoppers said it was told about the leak on March 18; a week later on March 25, Navigate360 told the organization that the system was "safe and fully operational."

"It doesn't seem that there was a full investigation there," Dehghantanha said, "that you could do and you could say, 'Oh, only these clients have been impacted.'"

Internal memo advises against calling privacy commissioner

Meanwhile, Geist says tipsters whose information has been leaked may be limited in their options for justice.

"In terms of actual compensation to the affected individuals, current privacy law doesn't really focus on that," he added. "You've got to look to other mechanisms like class actions if what you're looking for is actual compensation."

Beyond that, another avenue could be to launch a privacy commissioner investigation — but Geist warns that could take years, and any recommendations for the future would not be legally binding.

WATCH | Ont. police suspend tip lines: Multiple Ontario cities suspend Crime Stoppers tip lines over massive data hack | Duration closed caption 1:58 Toronto, Halton and Guelph are among the Ontario cities temporarily pausing Crime Stoppers tip programs after a CBC News investigation revealed a massive data breach exposed 1.5 million tips over the past 25 years to possible exploitation by hackers.

He noted that even if Canada's privacy commissioner investigates the matter, it can only issue a "non-binding finding" directing a company to fix bad practices — it cannot force a company to compensate victims.

Still, even with those limited powers, the privacy commissioner may have already been top of mind for the Canadian Crime Stoppers Association (CCSA) in the months following the hack, according to a copy of a June 18 internal memo obtained by CBC.

"We currently do not believe that you are required, nor should you contact the privacy commissioner in your region at this time," instructs CCSA president David Forster, saying his organization has "previously assessed that they [the commissioner] do not have jurisdiction over Crime Stoppers."

Crime Stoppers is best known for its public appeals, often partnering with police, for help with unsolved crimes and to advance investigations — all with the promise of anonymity for tipsters who contact them. (Tyson Koschik/CBC)

CBC has reached out to the CCSA for comment on the contents of the memo.

We have also contacted the Canada and Ontario Privacy Commissioners to ask if they are investigating the data breach, if they have received any citizen complaints, and whether they actually have jurisdiction over Crime Stoppers.

In a public statement on Thursday, Forster offered reassurance to the public: "Navigate360 has advised us that third-party cybersecurity experts investigated the breach, identified vulnerabilities and completed remediation."Those measures strengthen protections for current and future tips, he said.

However, he noted: "They cannot undo the exposure of information already taken, which remains a serious concern."

World.title: The saga is over as Winnipeg Jets trade Connor Hellebuyck to New Jersey

The Connor Hellebuyck era is over in Winnipeg after the Jets traded the all-star goalie on Friday.

The 33-year-old from Michigan is headed to the New Jersey Devils.

World.title: Canadian woman dies in U.S. after fears of detainment prevented her from seeking medical care
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A 61-year-old Canadian woman living in the isolated U.S. town of Point Roberts, Wash., has died after refusing to seek medical care out of fears she would be detained or deported.

Paige Adamson made headlines last month when she was stopped at the Point Roberts border crossing, south of Tsawwassen, and interrogated for hours about whether she had unlawfully voted in a U.S. election.

The U.S. permanent resident was scheduled to appear at a deportation hearing before a federal immigration judge in Seattle on Nov. 4.

Point Roberts community support officer Annelle Norman said Adamson called her on Thursday night asking to borrow a pair of crutches from local nonprofit Circle Of Care.

"I took them over and found her literally debilitated on the sofa, in very, very bad pain," Norman said.

"She told me that she had slipped and fallen on her right side … she was relying on the help of a few friends to come and help her get up and take her to the bathroom."

Norman, who was also a friend and neighbour of Adamson, said she urged the distressed woman to call paramedics or visit the local Point Roberts health-care clinic.

"And she said, 'No, no, I'm afraid if I go, I won't be able to come back. They'll keep me or they'll deport me.'"

Point Roberts community support officer Annelle Norman says she urged Paige Adamson to call paramedics or visit the local health-care clinic. (CBC News)

Point Roberts is a U.S. pene-exclave at the southern tip of the Tsawwassen Peninsula, completely cut off by land from the rest of the country.

U.S. immigration lawyer Len Saunders said Adamson had mentioned not feeling well and needing to see a doctor. Residents of Point Roberts have to cross into Canada in order to get to other parts of Washington state or the U.S. and there was a risk she would be detained by ICE upon return to the U.S.

Adamson was a permanent resident of the U.S. who had been living in Point Roberts for more than 14 years and crossed the Canadian border countless times. (Ben Nelms/CBC)

"She was quite frankly scared about trying to drive up to Canada and come back in," Saunders said.

"There are no doctors where she lives. For all practical purposes, she was in detention," he said.

"I mentioned to her that I'd heard of people in the past maybe taking a boat or taking an airplane. But financially, I don't think she could afford it. She didn't have a lot of money."

Norman said she checked in on Adamson over the weekend, but her friend's condition had not improved.

"The next message that I got was on Monday, telling me to show up at her address," she said.

"She had died sometime in the hours previous."

In a statement, Whatcom County Sheriff public information officer Deb Slater said the death "appeared to be of natural causes."

Louise Trapp, operations manager with the medical examiner, said Adamson's body was in her office's care pending examination by a forensic pathologist.

'Absolute worst case outcome'

Adamson was a permanent resident of the U.S. who had been living in Point Roberts for more than 14 years.

According to Saunders, her status meant she was legally entitled to leave and enter the country while awaiting deportation proceedings, but border officials had the right to detain her if they saw fit.

"Officers have the right to take you into detention and send you on a one-way trip to the Northwest Detention Centre down in Tacoma," he said.

Immigration lawyer Len Saunders says Paige Adamson had been missing appointments with her doctor in Bellingham, Wash., due to fears of being detained or deported trying to cross the border. (Martin Diotte/Radio-Canada)

"I asked her to speak to the Peace Arch port-of-entry. I believe she had called them but was given no guarantees on what would happen … I could understand her concerns."

As a U.S. resident, accessing health care in British Columbia was not an option. CBC News reached out to U.S. Customs and Border Protection for comment but did not hear back before deadline.

Saunders said he couldn't believe it when he was advised of Adamson's death on Sunday.

"This is an absolute worst case outcome. Here's a lady with no prior immigration violations, no criminal convictions. She was about as squeaky clean as you could get," he said.



Adamson is survived by two sons, both residents of B.C.

World.title: Developer wants to build 500 modular homes on roof of struggling Sask. mall
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Louai Alrifai says the future of a struggling mall in central Saskatchewan comes down to a math equation: "700 cars and light trucks weigh around 3,000,000 pounds. Our modules weigh much less."

Alrifai's firm bought the Gateway Mall in Prince Albert, Sask., earlier this year and has announced plans to build 500 modular housing units on its roof, replacing a parking lot.

It's a reflection of a national trend toward building denser housing within city boundaries, according to one expert.

Though there are cases of builders incorporating new homes into existing malls, CBC News could not identify another case of modular housing units going on top of one.

Alrifai says his company focuses on properties others don't want. (Submitted by Louai Alrifai)

"Due to the size of the land, it makes much more sense to go on the roof," said Alrifai, who is president and CEO of Alrifai Real Estates.

He said the one-bedroom homes would each be about 329 square feet and geared toward students, young professionals and health-care workers.

He expects them to be ready in 2027, with a monthly rent of $1,000, including utilities.

Alrifai's company bought the mall building earlier this year. He said he plans to spend $40 million on the housing development and an additional $10 million on the interior of the mall, fixing a leakage issue and encouraging new stores and study spaces.

"I think people in Prince Albert are great, hardworking people and they deserve to improve their downtown," he said.

The company intends to build more parking spaces to replace what's on the roof. Greg Dionne, former mayor of Prince Albert, is an advisor for the firm.

A conceptual rendering of what a unit might look like. The company says each will cover 329 square feet and will rent for $1,000 a month. (Supplied by Alrifai Real Estates)

Alrifai said they're preparing to submit formal plans to the city and have received a positive reception from city staff and officials.

Michael Nelson, acting director of community development for the city, said Prince Albert needs more housing.

"We do have a shortfall on some housing units that we do want to help achieve and we're always open to new ideas and new developments."

Nelson said a series of assessments and reviews will determine if Alrifai's plan is feasible.

"I think anything's possible, it's just all the proper reviews and approvals have to be in place."

Nelson said the company can apply for financial incentives. Alrifai said they're optimistic about receiving support, but the project is about more than money.

"I didn't buy Gateway Mall to collect rent only. I bought it to reposition the whole thing, to actually turn it into a true hub for the downtown of Prince Albert," he said.

Expert sees national trend of denser housing

Scott Bell, a professor of geography and planning at the University of Saskatchewan, said he's never seen anything quite like this proposed project.

"It does seem novel. I have seen small house developments, I've seen redevelopment within city limits of different types. I've not seen one like this where it's using an existing structure and then placing housing units on top of that structure," he said.

Scott Bell is a professor of geography and planning at the University of Saskatchewan. (Submitted by Scott Bell)

Bell said there's been a rise in construction of dense housing within city limits over the past few years, since the federal government increased incentives to encourage it.

He cited the federal Housing Accelerator Fund, which ties funding for cities to how much centrally located and dense housing is built.

"These look like tiny container homes, so melding that type of construction and house type with redevelopment is maybe pushing the next step for urban growth…. not crazy, but it's pushing the limits," Bell said.

World.title: Same scam. 2 countries. Why Canadians don’t get their money back
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Two people described the same financial scam to both the police and their banks over the past year. The only difference was where they lived — one in Canada, the other in the U.K.

And that determined what happened next.

Asif Mohammed lost $7,200 this spring and never got it all back. Meanwhile, Samantha Bradshaw was out £11,000 (nearly $21,000 Cdn) but her financial institution reimbursed the money within days.

That's because British banks are required by law to make most of their customers whole when money is lost to a scam, often returning the sum within days of making a claim. In contrast, Canadian banks have no such legal obligation, leaving scam victims here largely unprotected.

As CBC’s Marketplace found out, it also means British banks are incentivized to crack down on fraudsters in a way Canadian banks are not.

WATCH | Bank scammer confronted by CBC Marketplace: Bank scammer confronted by CBC Marketplace | Duration closed caption 2:01 David Common confronts a bank scammer who lures victims by pretending to be the fraud department at their financial institution.

'I've made a big mistake'

Toronto-based Mohammed was working on a major engineering project when he received a call that appeared to be coming from his bank, Tangerine.

The caller identified herself as a representative from Tangerine’s fraud investigations department and told him there had been multiple attempts to use his debit card at a Best Buy in Edmonton.

Mohammed explained the charges weren't his, and was told his card needed to be collected as evidence. The caller said Mohammed's case had been transferred to Toronto police, who sent a courier to his worksite. He handed over the debit card to this "courier" but says he didn't provide the PIN.

Minutes later, his wife, Salwa Sultana, texted him to say money had disappeared from the account — $1,200 to be exact.

"At that point, I realized that I've made a big mistake," Mohammed said.

The couple reported what happened to the real Tangerine but were told they would be on the hook for the losses.

WATCH | 'Real panic, real crying': U.K. victim recounts being scammed: 'Real panic, real crying': U.K. victim recounts being scammed | Duration closed caption 1:02 Samantha Bradshaw tells Marketplace's David Common about her experience as a victim of a bank impersonation scam.

Samantha Bradshaw received a near-identical call at her home in England’s East Midlands last fall that lasted four hours.

She was also told multiple cards had been compromised. A courier came to pick them up and scammers then used her cards to make purchases.

More worrying for Bradshaw, the scammers knew where she lived. She told Marketplace she called the police and the emergency operator instructed her to lock her doors.

"'Make sure everybody is safe,'" Bradshaw said she was told. "And then it was real panic, real crying, real horrible emotions coming through. My trust was completely gone."

Yet within days, Bradshaw’s bank called to tell her the entire loss was covered, under Britain’s reimbursement rules.

After months of pleading with Tangerine, Asif Mohammed and Salwa Sultana reached a settlement with the bank. While they aren’t able to tell CBC News about the details, it does not cover their entire loss.

Tangerine wouldn't comment on this particular case but said they use "fraud monitoring, security controls, client education… to identify and help prevent unusual account activity."

Multiple major police services across Canada have issued public warnings saying they would never send a courier to collect debit or credit cards.

Does reimbursement slow scams — or supercharge scammers?

Shifting the burden of responsibility from customer to bank is a recognition that financial institutions are better able to identify and stop scams, says Andrei Skorobogatov, a strategic advisor of Britain’s regulations.

Andrei Skorobogatov helped advise on the reimbursement rules in the U.K. and now works with the Global Anti-Scam Alliance. (Nelisha Vellani/CBC)

Skorobogatov, who works with the Global Anti-Scam Alliance, believes all countries have the responsibility to act.

"The public going about their day-to-day business will probably struggle to be able to detect [a scam] in a way that the bank with their highly sophisticated detection mechanisms are in a much better place to do," he said.

Britain’s third-largest bank agrees. Since the introduction of bank liability two years ago, Santander has introduced new measures to flag suspicious transactions and rapidly intervene when customers appear to be sending money to an unknown contact.

The new regulations have "pushed financial institutions," Chris Ainsley, head of fraud risk management at Santander, told Marketplace during a visit to the U.K. headquarters. "That's now a signal for us to take extra action to prevent more fraud and stop more at source."

Global anti-fraud groups track the multibillion-dollar scam industry, which has become extremely lucrative for individual fraudsters. One scammer, who identifies himself with the name "Cameron," told Marketplace he makes up to £5,000 ($9,400 Cdn) from each victim.

CBC Marketplace confronted this bank impersonation scammer about his role in stealing money from victims. (CBC)

He displayed no sympathy for those victims in a video call with Marketplace, in which he used a mask and sunglasses to conceal his face. He believes U.K. reimbursement rules mean that only the banks end up paying for his crimes.

In fact, banks recoup their losses through fees collected from all customers. Victims of these crimes may get their money back but often feel a deep loss of trust and embarrassment.

British banks are taking action to prevent scams. For instance, Santander uses machine learning to identify suspicious transactions, based on hundreds of thousands of past scams. The bank will message or call customers in real time, trying to "break the spell that the fraudsters put them under," Ainsley said.

The intervention on red-flagged transactions can sometimes delay legitimate transactions. But the vast majority of bank transfers in the U.K. still take less than 10 seconds, compared to multiple days in Canada.

If money is transferred to scammers, the British rules dictate that the sending bank and receiving banks are each responsible for half of the reimbursement to the customer who was scammed — except in cases of extreme negligence.

Will Canada follow Britain’s lead?

Marketplace asked Canada’s finance minister directly if he was considering forcing Canadian banks to reimburse scammed customers.

Canada’s Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne says the government is working to better protect Canadians but didn’t commit to reimbursement. (Nelisha Vellani/CBC)

François-Philippe Champagne detailed a number of new efforts, including the introduction of Bill C-29, an act to establish the Financial Crimes Agency earlier this year, but stopped short of committing to liability for financial institutions.

"I would say we need to consult. There's many actors. There's the telecoms, there's the banks, there's other people in that ecosystem."

Champagne says specially trained federal officers have been deployed in an effort to arrest those responsible and prevent fraud in the first place.

"We put boots on the ground," he said. "I have officers who are embedded with the police force — for example, in Surrey, some regions in Ontario. And that has been the most effective thing because… it's about following the money."

World.title: Canadian planemaker Bombardier to spend $270M US expanding in 4 states
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Aerospace manufacturer Bombardier says it plans to invest millions in the U.S. to expand its business south of the border.

The Montreal-based company said Friday it plans to add 800 jobs in Kansas, Texas, Indiana and Connecticut, 500 for which it is actively recruiting.

Bombardier says it's earmarking about $270 million US to build infrastructure in the initial phase of the investment.

The company's president and CEO called the American side of the business a "key pillar" of its growth strategy.

"Based on our constructive conversations with the U.S. administration, we see a bright path forward for our highly skilled aerospace workers as well as a positive environment for Bombardier to continue pursuing direct investments to grow our American footprint," Eric Martel said in a statement.

The announcement comes after U.S. President Donald Trump said on social media post that Bombardier was investing in three of those four states, claiming it would create thousands of jobs. He also credited Sen. Roger Marshal of Kansas and Texas Attorney General Ken ​Paxton for the deal.

WATCH | Trump threatens Bombardier: Trump tells Bombardier it can't sell in the U.S. unless it builds in the U.S. | Duration closed caption 5:12 U.S. President Donald Trump said in a social media post Monday that Montreal-based jet maker Bombardier would no longer be allowed to sell in the United States unless it started manufacturing there, even though the company does have a manufacturing footprint in the country.

Trump had threatened Bombardier in September amid the worsening U.S.-Canada trade war, saying the planemaker wouldn't be able to sell in the States unless it started manufacturing there — despite the company having a factory in Kansas and employing about 3,500 people in the U.S.

The president walked that threat back earlier this week at a rally in Wichita, Kansas, which serves as a home base for Bombardier's defence division.

"I always viewed them as a Canadian company ... but now I find out they have a presence here, and we're not hurting them if they're in Kansas. So we'll take care of those people," Trump said.

The company also recently unveiled its North American Learning Center in Wichita, a facility meant to train newly hired aircraft technicians. A $50 million US investment in that facility is part of the $270 million US announced today, a Bombardier spokesperson confirmed to CBC News in an email.

World.title: How the Brewers and Rays got to baseball's biggest stage with small budgets and small ball
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A new World Series champion will be crowned as two of Major League Baseball's most frugal franchises — the Milwaukee Brewers and the Tampa Bay Rays — battle for supremacy.

Neither franchise has won it all before, meaning it will be a history-making outcome no matter who wins the Fall Classic.

Ahead of the first game in the best-of-seven series on Friday, we're taking a look at how the Brew Crew and the D-Rays got here, the Canadian connections, their World Series records and what it means to see two teams with relatively small payrolls make it this far into the playoffs

Tampa Bay Rays pitcher Freddy Peralta celebrates his team's Game 6 victory over the Cleveland Guardians in the ALCS. (David J. Phillip/The Associated Press)

Comparatively puny payrolls

Milwaukee and Tampa are in the bottom-half of MLB's 30 franchises when it comes to payroll spending.

The Brewers had an Opening Day roster payroll of just over $124 million US — 19th in the majors according to The Associated Press. The Rays' payroll was just $88.7 million US, ranked 26th at that time.

Compare that to Toronto's Opening Day payroll of nearly $269 million US, the fifth-highest in baseball. And yet, the Jays missed the playoffs.

The deep-pocketed Los Angeles Dodgers had a payroll of nearly $317 million US at the season's start. And while they made the playoffs, they got swept — by the Brewers.

None of this is helping the argument of the MLB owners, who are pushing for a salary cap to be established in the league, arguing that baseball's richest teams are too dominant. It's all part of negotiations taking place as b aseball's current five-year deal expires in December.

The Associated Press says this year's World Series marks the first time since 1991 that two teams with payrolls in the bottom half of the majors will compete for the title.

Brewers first baseman Jake Bauers hits a home run in Game 3 of the NLCS against the Los Angeles Dodgers. Bauers led his team with 26 homers during the regular season. (Kiyoshi Mio/Imagn Images/Reuters)

Homer drought

The Brewers were tied for the second-lowest, regular-season home-run total, with just 154 round-trippers. Only the Blue Jays hit fewer home runs (152).

Despite this power outage, Milwaukee put together a 103-59 season — the best in the game.

Tampa's lineup slugged 169 homers prior to the playoffs, which put them at 22nd in the majors. The Rays wrapped their regular season with a 98-64 record.

WATCH | Not the 2026 season Jays fans hoped for: Toronto Blue Jays leave fans with little to cheer about | Duration closed caption 2:15 After coming close to winning the World Series last fall, the Toronto Blue Jays are wrapping up this season with little to cheer about, losing more games than they’ve won and scoring the fewest runs in the league.

The power of 'small ball'

The strategy of small ball — getting runners on base and advancing them by stealing bases or putting the ball in play with sacrifice hits and bunts — was key for both Milwaukee and Tampa as they outplayed rivals in their respective leagues.

The Rays led the majors with 45 sacrifice bunts during the regular season. The Brewers had 37, the fifth-most overall.

The two teams also stole a ton of bases: The Rays swiped 164 bases prior to the playoffs, while Millwaukee claimed 162.

This year's World Series could be the first with a 104-mile-per-hour pitch, thanks to Brewers ace Jacob Misiorowski. The 24-year-old threw a record 1,115 pitches of 100 miles per hour or higher in his first full major league season. (Kayla Wolf/The Associated Press)

Triple-digit heat

The Brewers' ace starting pitcher, Jacob Misiorowski, is the most prolific, hard-throwing pitcher in the game.

He's thrown more than 1,100 pitches at speeds exceeding 100 miles per hour this season.

Misiorowski has already set the record for the fastest pitch thrown in a playoff game (104.8 miles per hour) — at least, since tracking started in 2008. Amazingly, that's not the hardest pitch he's ever thrown.

He's slated to start Game 1 for the Brewers on Friday night.

Milwaukee Brewers pitcher Freddy Peralta and catcher Liam Hicks celebrate after a strikeout in Game 2 of the American League Championship Series against the Cleveland Guardians on Oct. 13. (Julio Aguilar/Getty Images)

Canadian catcher

Toronto-born ballplayer Liam Hicks joined the Rays at the trade deadline.

The 27-year-old catcher is in his second big-league season, joining Tampa in August, after first getting to the big leagues with the nearby Miami Marlins.

So far this post-season, Hicks has six hits, one run, three walks and four RBIs across nine games he's played with the Rays.

Tampa Bay Rays manager Kevin Cash has served as the team's skipper for 12 seasons — including in 2020, when the Rays played in the World Series against the Los Angeles Dodgers. (Kim Klement Neitzel/Imagn Images/Reuters)

The ex-Jays catcher

Rays manager Kevin Cash was a player before he was a manager and started out his major-league career in Toronto.

Cash appeared in 101 games for the Jays from 2002-2004. He later played for the Rays, the Boston Red Sox, the New York Yankees and the Houston Astros.

He's managed the Rays for 12 seasons, including in 2020 when Tampa lost the World Series to the Los Angeles Dodgers.

A long wait for Brewers fans

Milwaukee last made it to the World Series in 1982 — back when Ronald Reagan was in the White House, and years before any of the current Brewers players were born.

The Brewers lost in seven games to the St. Louis Cardinals.

Hall of Famer Robin Yount was part of the Milwaukee team that lost to St. Louis, and he recently said he'll "never get over it until the Brewers win one."

On Tampa's side, the Rays have been to the World Series twice, losing both times: First in 2008 and again in 2020.

Brewer Robin Yount plays in Game 4 of the 1982 World Series against the St. Louis Cardinals, which the Brewers went on to lose. (The Associated Press)

Where to watch

Canadian baseball fans can catch the World Series on Sportsnet.

Most games will air on the main Sportsnet channel — except for Games 2 and Game 7 (if necessary), which will run on Sportsnet One.

All games will also stream on Sportsnet+.

World.title: Carney defends doing business with countries that don’t share Canada’s values
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Prime Minister Mark Carney defended his government's approach to balancing human rights and trade on Friday, saying very few countries in the world can meet Canada's standards.

He made the remarks near the end of his trip to Turkey, where he signed a strategic partnership with the government of President Recep Erdogan, which has faced sustained criticism from human rights groups.

The complaints intensified this month when the Turkish government executed several high-profile operations to systematically silence opposition voices, suppress independent journalism, and restrict marginalized groups.

In the past Carney has said Canada is pursuing values-based realism in its approach, recognizing that not every partner will share all Canadian values.

WATCH | Carney asked about Turkey's human rights record: Carney asked about Turkey's record on LGBTQ, human rights: 'Engagement is not approval' | Duration closed caption 4:32 Prime Minister Mark Carney, speaking from Turkey during a visit to announce increased economic and defence ties, said he has not met with rights' groups but did raise the issue during his visit, saying there are 'very few countries' that share 'the standards of Canada.'

"Engagement in those partnerships does not mean approval," Carney said Friday.

"There are very few countries in this world that have the standards of Canada."

A statement from the Prime Minister's Office said Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand raised the issue of human rights with her counterpart during meetings on Thursday.

Carney was asked by journalists on Friday whether he personally raised concerns with Erdogan during their separate meeting. The prime minister refused to be pinned down.

WATCH | Turkey is an 'exceptional partner,' PM says: Carney hails new trade, defence pact with 'exceptional partner' Turkey | Duration closed caption 2:07 Prime Minister Mark Carney announced a new strategic trade and defence partnership between Canada and Turkey, as Ottawa continues its drive to tighten relations with other middle powers and fellow NATO members.

"My approach on these issues is I have direct conversations with leaders," Carney said. "I find those conversations are more effective when they're direct and open and not then reported out in detail, but we have raised these issues."

Concern about the authoritarian reflexes of the Turkish government have partly overshadowed Carney's initiative to deepen trade ties.

The prime minister is looking to make Canada less dependent on the United States market and to diversify its trading markets. Much of the effort has thus far gone into deepening ties with Europe and nations in the Indo-Pacific, but it has also included other states with questionable human rights records, including recently Saudi Arabia.

'Disappointed' by U.S. claims

Carney is holding a series of meetings with business leaders in Istanbul after the political talks in Ankara on Thursday.

One of the deals being pursued involves the possible sale of Canadian nuclear technology to Turkey as the Middle Eastern nation attempts to reach its climate goals.

Carney told reporters, following the signing of the strategic partnership, there were ‌now "good chances" for Canadian engineering firm AtkinsRealis to be picked as a partner to build the two power plants ⁠Turkey is planning.

Also Friday, Carney pushed back more forcefully against allegations of Canadian interference in the U.S. midterm elections.

The U.S. Embassy in Ottawa released a fact sheet on Thursday, officially accusing Canadian leaders of election meddling ahead of the Nov. 3 vote.

"There is no merit to these claims, so I'll call it out that way," Carney said. "I'm disappointed that their envoy sees that as his role to make these suggestions."

The prime minister went on to say Canada has a very deep diplomatic presence in the United States and lots of interaction with American companies, citizens and individuals.

"As a country Canada is very, very careful to not be seen to interfere in the democratic process," he said.
