World.title: France bolster security for protests as businesses fear renewed unrest
World.content:
Some 70,000 law enforcement officers are set be deployed across France on Saturday, while the Louvre and several other major Paris museums will be closed as authorities seek to prevent renewed violence during protests.

 

Last weekend, peaceful demonstrations were overshadowed by violence and unrest which erupted across the country. Masked individuals looted shops and intimidated their owners, stormed public buildings, smashed shop windows, and clashed with police forces.

Demonstrators plan to take to the streets on Saturday to denounce the cost of living crisis, while students are still protesting against what they view as inadequate school conditions. Students, members of the CGT labor union and activists from the “ yellow vest ” movement are set to join.

While some protests have been banned for security reasons in several cities, including Lyon, Nice and Montpellier, marches are expected in many other places including in Paris and Marseille. Authorities have also diverted some protest routes away from shopping streets and public buildings to limit damage.

Landmark museums closed This Saturday

French Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said some 70,000 police officers and gendarmes would be deployed, along with helicopters, armoured vehicles and water cannons. In addition, elite police units will help secure public buildings like city halls in a “highly mobile” security operation, he said.

“There have been numerous calls from radical far-left groups on social media to commit acts of violence and vandalism. There have also been renewed calls for looting, with those messages clearly being spread by rioters," Nuñez said at a news conference.

“We will be absolutely uncompromising" with those involved in violence, he added, warning that police will have a “very firm approach to making arrests, and there will be legal consequences.”

Landmark Paris sites including the Louvre, the Musée d'Orsay, the Picasso museum, along with the Grand Palais will close their doors on Saturday.

Art Basel, one of the world's most prestigious contemporary art fairs, opened to the public Friday — but only for the day, with the threat of unrest prompting organisers to cancel the weekend program.

"This decision has not been taken lightly, and the safety of everyone involved in the fair remains our utmost priority," organisers said in a statement Thursday.

Businesses on edge ahead of protests

The manager of a supermarket in central Paris, which was looted last weekend told Euronews on condition of anonymity that his entire team remained on edge ahead of Saturday's protests, despite bolstered security measures.

He said that his shop would remain open during the morning and that he would "assess the situation" later in the day.

"We have a metal shutter and we've added some plywood, but we know that these metal shutters took about a minute and a half for protestors to break through. The same goes for our electronic door. So, unless we implement security like banks have, there's really no way to stop them. Last weekend they arrived in huge groups, used bricks, it was incredibly violent."

When teenagers violently looted his supermarket last Saturday, overwhelmed police forces were unable to intervene. The next day, when the looting resumed, law enforcement made it to the scene, pushing back gangs of violent teenagers.

Many of the staff remain traumatised, "we've worked so hard to ensure we managed to clean and restock. But, frankly, I haven't had a proper rest in about 13 days. Everyone on our team

"Frankly, I haven't had a proper rest in about 13 days. We're all under a lot of pressure. Everyone on our team is feeling it. There's a palpable tension, and we're trying to manage it, but to keep everyone calm and prevent any major incidents from occurring. Unfortunately, there's a risk that something bad will happen, and we need to prevent that from happening."

Anti far-right protest planned

A demonstration in the city of Orléans, located south of Paris, will also take place on Saturday.

About 50 organisations have called for a protest against the far right on the sidelines of the two-day congress of Marine Le Pen’s nationalist, anti-immigration party ahead of next spring’s presidential election. Organisers include labor unions, left-wing political parties, student organisations and anti-racism groups.

Hugues Moutouh, the prefect of the Loiret region, said that 20,000 to 30,000 demonstrators from across the country were expected.

Le Pen, whom opinion polls place as the front-runner in next year’s election, accused left-wing organisations and political parties of trying to “disrupt a political party’s democratic congress,” on public news broadcaster FranceInfo.

Still, she said she had “no concerns” about security because the government had “recognised the need for measures allowing the congress to proceed safely.”

World.title: UN chief race enters decisive phase as new contender arrives
World.content:
As the race to elect the next UN Secretary-General enters its final phase, former Costa Rican Vice President Rebeca Grynspan retains a challenging lead, but a new contender is emerging, as UAE Minister of State Lana Nusseibeh announced her candidacy this week.

 

The growing excitement around the race is also fueled by the prospect of a female UN secretary-general, something that has never happened in the UN's more than 80-year history.

As part of a complex election process, an informal straw poll of officials in the deciding United Nations Security Council last week gave Grynspan a narrow lead over her closest competitors: Guyana’s former Foreign Minister Carolyn Rodrigues-Birkett and Argentina’s International Atomic Energy Agency Director-General Rafael Grossi.

But after receiving two opposing votes the race has been relaunched allowing new candidates to participate.

The winner needs at least nine votes from the 15-member UN Security Council without opposition from any of the five permanent members — the US, the UK, France, China and Russia — and they have until the end of December to choose the successor to current UN chief Antonio Gutteres, before the UN General Assembly confirms the appointment.

Campaigning alongside Grynspan, Grossi and Rodrigues-Birkett are former Ecuadorian Foreign Minister Maria Fernanda Espinosa, Argentina's Rafael Grossi, former Senegalese President Macky Sall, former UN Under-Secretary-General Olara Otunnu of Uganda, and Ecuadorian diplomat Ivonne A-Baki.

UAE’s Nusseibeh announced as fresh contender

Senior UAE diplomat and UAE Miniaster of State Lana Nusseibeh energised the race when her nomination was announced this week, known for her versatility in “quiet diplomacy” in the campaign for peace and for creating space for wider political settlements.

Launching her candidacy, Nusseibeh said, “I have spent much of my professional life working in and around the United Nations, and I have seen first-hand what determined diplomacy can achieve - countries with profound differences finding common ground, and agreement where people said agreement was impossible.”

In her vision statement, she puts peace and security at the core while also promising to deliver across the board on development and human rights, as well as reform the organisation around focus and results.

"I am standing to be secretary-general because I believe this is a moment to act with greater urgency: to act earlier, bring people together across difference, and drive the work forward until it produces concrete results," she said.

“I wish to offer myself to this office as I would serve it: speaking frankly with every government and answering to none.”

A highly regarded diplomat who grew up between Abu Dhabi and the UK in a family of well-known political figures, Nusseibeh previously served as the UAE ambassador to the UN and is credited with elevating the UAE's profile during that time.

Nusseibeh, 48, who led the UAE’s successful bid for a Security Council seat, said that several countries approached her during the last UN General Assembly and urged her to stand.

“It's recognised today that we need someone who offers generational change for the organisation,” she said.

During the country’s 2022 to 2023 term, Nusseibeh secured the adoption of Resolution 2720, which opened the way for humanitarian aid deliveries into Gaza. A Hebrew speaker, she said she secured support for the resolution by arranging visits from Council members to the Rafah border crossing.

If she succeeds, Nusseibeh would become the first woman to lead the United Nations since its establishment in 1945, the first of Palestinian descent, and the second Secretary-General from the Arabic-speaking world after Egypt's Boutros Boutros-Ghali.

“I think ⁠it would be ​great if the next secretary-general is a woman, but I am not running because I am a woman, I am running because I am stubbornly optimistic about the future of the United Nations and I believe we need someone who is relentless in the pursuit of diplomacy ​to open doors,” Nusseibeh said on Wednesday.

Grynspan holds a challenging lead

Costa Rica's former Vice President Rebeca Grynspan, 70, was born to Jewish parents who fled Poland before World War II, and she has built a Jewish family ever since. She lost her grandparents in the Holocaust after they decided to remain in Poland.

In a May interview with Euronews, Grynspan said, “I know exactly what wars take away from you and what peace allows you to do.”

“I am a generation that have lived in peace. I have never experienced war directly. But millions of people in the world today live in war zones, in conflict. And that is why I am running, because I know the difference, what peace and opportunity can do for you and your family,” she told Euronews.

Currently Secretary-General of the UN Trade and Development (UNCTAD), Grynspan said she agreed with US President Donald Trump’s “constructive” criticism that “the UN has great potential, but it's not living up to that potential,” and that a reformed UN can make a difference.

Grynspan told Euronews how she believes that in our multipolar world “the choice is if we will have multipolarity with multilateralism that bears the promise of prosperity and cooperation, or if we will have multipolarity without multilateralism that will lead us to fragmentation into a world that will be more unstable, more prone to conflict, and less prosper.”

“So we need to create again these spaces. For the convergence of divergent interests,” she added.

On the other hand, she also hailed the “amazing things that are happening in the world: you look at technology and you look at the digital world, the artificial intelligence, what is happening in medicine and in science.”

“You see those breakthroughs that you can bring to the people on the ground, to the millions of people that have right now no opportunity, that live in poverty, in absolute destitution or in hunger.“

“And you know that the world is developing really the capacity, the possibility for everybody to have a dignified life. That will depend on us. It will depend on our choices,” Grynspan explained in an interview for Euronews.

She said that the UN election race was “not like a business-as-usual type of election.”

“Conflicts in the world are going up. Trust between the countries, but also in the multilateral system, is going down. And time is running out," Grynspan told Euronews as she presented the vision of her candidacy to become the new UN secretary-general.

"So this is a moment in which we have to raise to the challenge to bring cooperation, solidarity, the principles of the UN Charter again into the center of the agenda,” she concluded.

World.title: EU trade Chief seeks to rebalance EU-China trade as Brussels weighs tougher measures
World.content:
EU Trade Commissioner Maroš Šefčovič said on Friday that the EU was walking a tightrope in negotiations with Beijing, weighing conventional trade measures against broader political considerations.

 

After several months of negotiations, Brussels and Beijing reached a deal on 9 October to curb imports of hybrid cars from China. However, the agreement is unlikely to significantly narrow the EU’s record trade deficit with China, which has reached €1 billion a day, a gap the European Commission is seeking to reduce.

“There are whole sectors under threat; each head of states and government is concerned that there might be potential heavy losses of the jobs,” Šefčovič said on Friday, after a meeting of the 27 trade ministers in Ireland.

He added: “We have to proceed not only with the traditional trade techniques, but also with a very political approach, how to balance the trade between between China and the European Union.”

A new round of discussions is taking place at a technical level with Beijing until the end of the year, with political negotiation scheduled for January and March 2027.

But given the urgency, EU leaders gave the European Commission a political mandate last week to work on a “kill switch” tool that would allow Europeans to cut off China's access to their market to counter economic distortions.

Under the October deal, the EU will introduce country-specific quotas allowing 350,000 Chinese hybrid cars onto the European market annually over four years, with a fixed annual adjustment rate of 6%.

Striking a deal on new sectors

The Commission aims to extend the agreement to other sectors, but EU officials warn that progress will also depend on Beijing’s response to the EU executive’s efforts to strengthen its trade defence tools.

The Commission is set to present a new instrument on 9 October aimed at encouraging EU companies to diversify their suppliers of strategic products to reduce their dependence on China.

It also hopes to present a proposal for the so-called “kill switch” that same week and ahead of the December summit of EU leaders. Pushed by France and Germany earlier this month, it would allow the Commission to adopt radical measures against Beijing in the event of economic pressure on the EU market.

Another unilateral EU trade defence measure targeting Chinese chemicals and industrial machinery could also come in December, with the risk of prompting Chinese countermeasures.

According to the latest Chinese customs data, China's exports to the EU have continued to surge, rising by 25% over the past year.

World.title: Latest news bulletin | October 23rd, 2026 – Evening
World.content: Catch up with the most important stories from around Europe and beyond in this Euronews news bulletin. In just a few minutes, our newsroom brings you the latest news and breaking news across world affairs, business, politics, culture, entertainment and travel, with the context you need to make sense of a fast-moving day. Reported with the independence and the European perspective that define Euronews, this regular round-up gives you a clear and reliable overview of the stories shaping our world right now, wherever you are watching from.

World.title: Studio DRIFT makes the invisible force of wind visible in stunning new London installation
World.content:
Studio DRIFT, an Amsterdam-based artist duo founded by Ralph Nauta and Lonneke Gordijn, has unveiled Aeolus, a large-scale installation at London’s Ladbroke Hall that uses hundreds of glass rods and hidden lights to make the invisible movement of wind visible.

 

We spoke to the co-founders about how the work captures a moment of wind in motion, the relationship between nature and technology, and the importance of reconnecting with the natural world through physical experiences of art.

The studio is also preparing to open an 8,000-square-metre museum in Amsterdam in early 2027.

World.title: EU vies to expand role in Ukraine-Russia peace talks to influence US thinking
World.content:
The European Union is seeking a greater role in peace talks to end Russia’s war on Ukraine, potentially including direct contact with Moscow.

 

The United States wants to resume trilateral talks at the technical level in November, after its midterm elections. Ukraine says it welcomes any format at any time, while Russia has said it is “ready in principle”.

The peace process stalled in February after the US launched its war on Iran, shifting much of its diplomatic focus to the Middle East.

Brussels sees a possible resumption of talks as an opportunity to move from a trilateral to a multilateral format, bringing European representatives to the table and giving the EU a chance to influence Washington's thinking, which has recently shifted sharply in Moscow’s favour, setting off alarm bells.

Europeans, however, have a track record of being blindsided, dismissed and even ignored by their American counterparts, so there is no guarantee of success.

“Now, there is an expectation that there will be a multilateral-level discussion with representatives at senior official level, and the EU will be present at these talks,” European Commission deputy chief spokesperson Arianna Podestà said on Friday.

“We have always worked to have Ukraine in a position of strength, and we have always worked for a just and lasting peace for Ukraine. We’re doing so on every occasion.”

Podestà said the EU should be represented jointly by the European Commission, the bloc’s executive arm, and the European Council, which represents member states.

Asked whether this could involve European officials meeting Russian representatives face to face, she left the door open.

“At this stage, I wouldn’t have further details to provide. The expectation is that there would be a joint Commission-Council representation that would attend the meetings,” she said. “Beyond that, I don’t have other elements to share.”

Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov did not immediately oppose European participation, as Moscow has done in the past, but stressed that the next round of talks under preparation would remain trilateral.

“Nothing can be ruled out a priori,” Peskov said.

“But these talks we are discussing, which are scheduled for the first half of November in Abu Dhabi, will take place in a trilateral format.”

A seat for two?

It remains unclear whether both EU institutions will have a place at the table.

The last rounds of talks involving Ukraine, Europe and the US, first in Miami and later in Oslo, included only Bjoern Seibert, Commission President Ursula von der Leyen’s powerful chief of cabinet.

Pedro Lourtie, chief of cabinet to European Council President António Costa, was not invited.

National security advisers from Germany, France and the UK — the so-called E3 — and NATO attended the Miami talks. In Oslo, Italy took France’s place.

Discussions focused on security guarantees for Ukraine, sanctions against Russia and post-war recovery. After the Oslo talks, US special envoy Steve Witkoff met Russian President Vladimir Putin in Saint Petersburg for nearly three hours.

The Kremlin later dismissed Witkoff’s proposals as offering “little of real value” towards ending the war, while signalling its readiness to resume technical-level talks.

EU officials and diplomats say Moscow has yet to show signs of abandoning its maximalist demands or engaging meaningfully in the peace process. But with the stakes so high, they argue, Europe cannot afford to sit on the sidelines.

US President Donald Trump’s decision to strike a diesel supply deal with Putin and ease long-standing sanctions on Russia has alarmed European capitals, reinforcing their view that the EU’s presence at the table is essential as a counterweight to Washington.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, whom Trump has repeatedly criticised, has urged European leaders to establish their own diplomatic channel with Moscow.

Earlier this year, Costa quietly opened a line of communication with Russia, but the initiative failed to yield results and was put on hold.

The idea of appointing a special envoy was discussed again by EU leaders at last week’s summit. No consensus candidate emerged, but Finnish President Alexander Stubb has returned to the conversation after co-hosting the latest round of talks in Oslo.

Moscow later said it could accept Stubb as an intermediary, provided he did not “parrot” the European position — a condition unlikely to sit well with the Finnish president, a staunch supporter of Ukraine.

World.title: Kenya: huge piles of rubble after high-rise building collapses
World.content:
A multi-storey building under construction collapsed in Nairobi’s Eastleigh district on Friday 23 October, leaving a vast heap of concrete rubble and twisted debris. The Kenya Red Cross said the structure came down at about 1:40 pm local time along Yusuf Haji Avenue and dispatched emergency response teams to assist search-and-rescue efforts.

 

Footage from the Kenyan capital showed the scale of the destruction, with large sections of the unfinished structure reduced to piles of broken concrete. An excavator was deployed among the wreckage while Red Cross personnel worked at the site, urging the public to stay clear so rescuers could operate safely.

Several people were feared trapped beneath the rubble, although authorities had not yet confirmed casualties, injuries, or the number of missing persons. The Nairobi County governor’s office noted reports of trapped individuals, while Reuters reported that the ground floor of the building had been occupied.

There were conflicting accounts over the building’s height, ranging between 10 and 18 storeys. No official height or cause of the collapse have been confirmed.

The collapse has once again raised questions about construction standards in Kenya, where similar disasters have repeatedly claimed lives amid concerns over inadequate safety checks and enforcement.

World.title: CICA members look to turn regional dialogue into action
World.content:
For more than three decades, the Conference on Interaction and Confidence-Building Measures in Asia (CICA) has provided a platform for dialogue among countries with different political and economic priorities. Its 28 members are now looking at ways to strengthen cooperation on regional security, economic development and emerging challenges.

 

Under Azerbaijan's chairmanship, which began in 2024, discussions have focused on strengthening the organisation's institutional framework and making cooperation more practical. Migration, climate change and artificial intelligence were among the issues raised, alongside finance, education and business. As CICA enters a new phase, attention is turning to how member states can translate discussions into lasting cooperation.

World.title: Jordan: Karak church shooting leaves 7 dead, dozens injured
World.content:
A shooting at a Greek Orthodox church in southern Jordan happened during a funeral, according to local authorities. Two unidentified men opened fire on the procession.

A shooting at a church in the southern Jordanian governorate of Karak left seven people dead and another 34 wounded on Friday, Jordan's public security director Obaidallah Maaytah said.

What do we know so far?

The shooting occurred at the Hammoud Church. The shooting reportedly occurred during a funeral.

The attackers' identities and motives remain unclear. Two men opened fire on the funeral procession.

A witness told Jordanian state media there were 150 to 200 people present at the church at the time of the shooting. Videos circulating online showed wounded people on the floor of the church covered in blood, but this footage cannot be verified by DW.

Jordan's Interior Minister Mazen Al-Faraya said a group of "extremists" carried out the massacre. According to Jordanian outlet Roya News, Al-Faraya said authorities already possess the names of suspects behind the attacks but would not publicly disclose their identities as of now.

Jordanian government spokesperson Mohammad al-Momani said security forces have launched a probe into the attack.

Jordan King Abdullah II: 'We will strike with an iron fist'

Jordan King Abdullah II said "the terrorist attack against Karak will be met with the harshest retaliation."

"Those who delude themselves into thinking that they can divide Jordanians with their bullets have no chance in the face of our unity," Abdullah II said, adding, "We will strike with an iron fist against those who dare to threaten our nation."

Lebanese President Joseph Aoun, a Christian, also condemned the "heinous terrorist attack" in Jordan and expressed condolences to the victims.

US Ambassador to the UN Mike Waltz said the news regarding the attack is "devastating."

"Praying for the victims, their families and all those affected by this depraved and brutal attack on a house of worship," Waltz said. "Attacks on Christians continue to escalate worldwide and must be stopped."

Gun attacks like the one on the church in Karak are rare in Jordan.

Although Jordan is largely a Muslim-majority country of around 11.5 million people, there is a small Christian minority of a couple hundred thousand. The Karak region, about 180 kilometers (110 miles) south of Amman, has a significant Christian population.

World.title: Afghan women could lose one of their last paths to a higher education
World.content:
The US has defunded one of the last universities giving Afghan women the chance to receive an education after the Taliban takeover in 2021. DW spoke with a student who says she's lost hope of ever earning a degree.

"Laila" awoke in the middle of the night for a glass of water, checked her phone almost by accident, and saw an email that made her stomach drop. The US would stop funding the American University of Afghanistan (AUAF), one of the last places women can still study in the country.

Laila said she sat on her bed, staring, her thoughts racing through the past five years and everything she had endured just to get an education.

It had not been easy to find a way to study in Afghanistan after the Taliban outlawed women's education.

The American University campus was already taken over by the Taliban, but she could study secretly through the university's online program. But now that the university is losing its financing, she told DW she and her classmates fear it will shut down entirely. Her name has been changed for safety reasons.

In Afghanistan, girls study in secret to skirt Taliban ban To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

A hidden education for women in Afghanistan

Laila is in her mid-twenties. She studies political science and international studies and is one of around 1,000 enrolled students at the university, three-quarters of them women.

When the Taliban returned to power in August 2021, Laila was studying at another university in Kabul, with just two final exams remaining to finish her semester. Then, in December 2022, the Taliban announced the ban. Laila's degree was left unfinished.

Laila secured a scholarship to AUAF and started over. "Not every girl got that opportunity," she said.

Laila has told few people outside of her family about her online studies. On most days, she stays home for remote lectures, alongside classmates who use aliases and keep their cameras off for security. "I just know their voices," she said.

Laila speaks English with an American accent. She learned it as a child, watching cartoons. In her early twenties, she was learning even more about the world outside Afghanistan and studying foreign governments.

Then on August 14, 2021, Laila's life changed. She and a friend sat in a restaurant in Kabul. They had just finished an exam and wanted to celebrate passing the test by ordering coffee and cake. Suddenly, a man came in, stopped at the entrance, and shouted "Allahu Akbar." He yelled that the mujahideen would always be victorious.

That was the day the Taliban retook power in Afghanistan, they soon forced women out of public life, banning them from many jobs and from attending school and university.

Exiled Afghanistan envoy still advocating for women's rights To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Laila said she recalls losing feeling in her hands or feet. She pulled money from her purse and slammed it on the table without checking the amount. "We all thought maybe this would be the last day that we are alive," she said.

Since then, some of Laila's peers have received threatening calls and messages. Now, whenever she leaves home, she worries that Taliban authorities might search her phone.

"What if they see my emails from my work, from my university?" she said. "It's always in the back of my head that maybe tomorrow it's my turn. Maybe they will detain me."

Even her home isn't safe. Laila said Taliban authorities have entered on several occasions to search their belongings.

Yet, she has continued studying. For all its limitations and risks, the online program offered a chance to graduate.

A place for Afghanistan's 'future leaders'

With the US pulling out as the university's primary funder, Laila said she doubts whether she has the strength to start over.

The American University of Afghanistan was always intended, largely, for women. Before the campus opened in 2006, former US first lady Laura Bush announced that the US had committed millions to support it.

Appearing in Kabul, Bush said the new university would teach "future leaders," particularly women. Women like Laila, who was four years old at the time.

"These are more than just development projects," Bush said at the time. "They also signify the bond between the American and Afghan people. They are symbols of our shared hopes and dreams."

Patrick Fine was Afghanistan mission director at USAID, the now-defunct American development agency. Fine told DW that many at USAID considered the university idea risky. Critics thought training elites was a waste of money.

But the Bush administration saw an opportunity to stabilize a budding democracy, Fine said.

By 2003, the Taliban had been driven from power. US President George W. Bush wanted to foster goodwill for the US-backed interim government that had replaced the Taliban. The university served that goal, and also offered other "facets of advantage" in educating women, training future politicians, and supporting the Afghan economy.

"It really impacted the lives of thousands of Afghan youth," Fine said, referencing alumni. "The organization has managed to achieve that against incredible odds."

How 5 years of Taliban rule have changed Afghanistan To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Washington pulls the plug

The university continued with US support. But in Washington, that support started to come under question.

The US government suspected the university of mishandling money. In 2016, US inspectors opened an investigation into its finances. By 2018, investigators said they could not tell exactly how it was spending US aid money, because its accounting was so poor.

John Sopko, a former US federal inspector, oversaw that investigation. When DW contacted him for this story, he replied, "I was surprised they were still funding AUAF."

This year, after the funding was pulled, the US State Department Press Office told DW in an email that the move was made given the university's "history of repeated lack of accountability for millions of American taxpayer dollars."

Fine, the former USAID director, rejected the State Department's fraud explanation.

"Those are just smear tactics," he said. He conceded that past audits found the university struggling to keep up with USAID's extensive rules, "but they didn't find major fraud," he said.

"It is still a useful investment, a worthy investment," Fine said, "and the reason for that is that it's one of the few organizations left that is reaching Afghan women."

The US isn't the university's only funder, but it has long covered most of its costs: nearly 90% as of 2018, according to a US report.

The US State Department told DW that the university is "free to identify other funders and partners, so the end of their receipt of American taxpayer money does not necessarily equate to an end to their operations."

But without the $25 million grant the State Department recently refused, the university's future is in doubt.

What is next for women students in Afghanistan?

"I have lost all my motivation and hope," Laila said, adding that each time she prepares for a lecture, she wonders whether there will be another.

Since she learned about the funding cut, she said she's barely left her room. Her curtains are usually closed, and she's lost her appetite. "Maybe I'm so disappointed that I can't even cry about it," she said.

She said she was supposed to have graduated years ago. She was supposed to be making the world a better place. She was supposed to be studying for a master's degree abroad. Now, she's thinking, maybe she'll find a way in five or ten years.

World.title: Romania blames Russia for ship attack in the Black Sea
World.content:
Russian strikes against ships attempting to export Ukrainian grain and cargo through the western Black Sea have sharply increased this month.

Romanian President Nicusor Dan blamed Russia for an attack on a merchant vessel in the Black Sea on Friday morning.

A drone strike sank the merchant ship, with 13 Ukrainian and Azeri crew members on board, near Romanian territorial waters.

The attack killed at least 1 sailor, and three others were still missing, according to Dan.

Nine of the 13 crew members have been rescued.

Attack on merchant shipping on the rise in the Black Sea: What to know

The drone strike on the ship, called Khoryv, is believed to be the fourth merchant vessel to have been attacked off the coast of Romania this month.

Two weeks ago, two merchant vessels were also set ablaze in the western Black Sea, which is a vital shipping corridor heavily used by Ukraine.

One of those ships was inside Romanian territorial waters. Romania raised concerns about Russian provocation in waters at the edge of or controlled by NATO members.

Bulgaria, also a NATO member like Romania, has raised similar concerns.

Bulgaria has blamed Russia for having edged too close to its exclusive economic zone in the Black Sea after merchant ships were hit by drones near the country's coastline earlier this month too.

Both Romania and Bulgaria have called on NATO to do more to protect commercial shipping in the Black Sea.

NATO said earlier this week that it was sending more maritime patrol aircraft and radar systems to the Black Sea without having blamed any country for the attacks there.

About 23 sailors had been reported dead or missing in incidents in the Black Sea in the 10 days leading up to October 15, according to Reuters.

That tally is higher now.

Ursula von der Leyen, the president of the European Commission, condemned the increasing attacks on vessels in the Black Sea too, earlier this month calling it "unacceptable" that "the Black Sea has become another front of escalation of the Russian war in Ukraine."

World.title: Ukraine tries to shut Moscow's airports with drone strikes on Russia
World.content:
Repeated Ukrainian drone attacks are increasingly disrupting operations at Moscow's airports. The pounding is part of Ukraine's plan to shut down Russia's airpace.

For months, drone strikes by Ukraine have forced the suspension of flights to and from airports in Russia. Moscow's Domodedovo, Sheremetyevo, Zhukovsky and Vnukovo airports have had to shut down operations almost daily in October, according to reports from the independent investigative media outlet Agentstvo. On some days, the airports were reportedly closed for up to nine hours.

In early September, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy announced that Ukraine would seek to cut off the airspace around Moscow and other destinations in Russia. "Today, we would like to warn every airline that uses Russian airspace, every insurer, and everyone who continues to use major Russian airports: Russian airspace will become completely unsafe," Zelenskyy said.

The following day, Ukraine sent a corresponding warning to the International Civil Aviation Organization.

Ukraine's airspace has been closed since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022.

Poland's ex-president: Putin's war in Ukraine was a miscalculation To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Can Ukraine succeed?

Russia's aviation authority, Rosaviatsiya, has issued an emergency safety "carpet" protocol that is designed to immediately shut down the airspace over a specific region or around affected airports if an aircraft violates Russian airspace, weapons are used, or unidentified objects appear in the skies. Once the protocol is announced, drastic restrictions apply to all air traffic.

"If there is a military threat, a specific section of airspace is closed off, and this carpet is declared," Oleksandr Laneckij, the chief executive officer of the Friendly Avia Support consultancy, told DW. "Essentially, every drone poses a military threat."

Laneckij noted that Yemen's Houthis have managed to significantly disrupt Saudi airspace. "I think Ukraine's military capabilities far exceed those of the Houthis," Laneckij said.

Sheremetyevo International Airport is the busiest in Moscow Image: Valery Sharifulin/TASS/dpa/picture alliance

The military analyst Jan Matvejev also said Ukraine would have little trouble severely disrupting Moscow-area air traffic. Though Ukraine has not yet managed to completely shut down Russian airspace as Zelenskyy plans, Matvejev said, its armed forces "remain committed to this idea."

"To close off the airspace and trigger the 'carpet' plan, all you need are simple drones that don't have to be equipped with a warhead or even have a long range," Matvejev said. Ukraine's arms industry can produce hundreds of combat-ready long-range drones in a day, he added. That is why he believes Ukraine could have the necessary resources to shut down Moscow's airports.

Indeed, Ukraine's efforts to shut down Russian airspace are "just getting started," Simon Shuster wrote in October in the US magazine The Atlantic, citing well-informed sources.

Can Russia stop Ukraine's drones?

Matvejev said Russia's air-defense systems were not entirely effective in efforts to prevent Ukrainian drones from penetrating Moscow's airspace. "If it were possible to shoot them down, they would have done so by now," he said. He added that Russia would have deployed additional air-defense troops if they were available.

Laneckij said Russia might lower the threshold for declaring the carpet protocol, which could increase the risk of deadly incidents such as the 2024 Christmas day crash of an Azerbaijan Airlines flight. Investigators say the flight was struck by a Russian air-defense missile that was being used to defend against drones, killing 38 people.

Matvejev seconded the fear that Russia's defenses could again mistakenly target civilian aircraft instead of military objects. He said little had changed about Russia's air-defense protocol since the Azeri flight was shot in 2024.

In an operation against a low-flying drone, the target is visually identified and fired upon with a machine gun. In such a scenario, the danger to aircraft is extremely low, unless they happen to be flying in the immediate vicinity.

The risk to civil aviation increases significantly when anti-aircraft missiles are deployed, Matvejev said. A missile could have defects that are practically unavoidable in mass production and could veer toward an aircraft flying nearby. Matvejev said such defense measures could not guarantee the safety of civilian aircraft during operations.

The site of the Azerbaijan Airlines plane shot down by a Russian missile Image: Meiramgul Kussainova/Anadolu/picture alliance

He said drones did not have to carry explosives to be disruptive. A collision between an airplane and a basic drone can have serious consequences — and, he said, a drone sent from Ukraine all the way to Moscow must be relatively large, "weighting dozens of kilograms."

In the summer of 2023, Ukrainian armed forces attacked the airport in the Russian city of Pskov, where both military and civilian aircraft were parked. Earlier this month, drone debris fell on the Sochi airport, on Russia's Black Sea coast.

Russia also attacks Ukraine's airports. In September, Zelenskyy said Kyiv's airport had been struck, as well as the Boryspil airport near the capital.

How will international airlines react?

Laneckij said three factors would determine whether international airlines suspend their flights to Russia: the military threat, the degree of demand and the insurance cost.

He said issues could emerge around insurance. When insurers rate the security risk of flying to Russia as very high, they could significantly raise their rates for aircraft headed there. This would cause ticket prices to skyrocket.

Competition within Russia's aviation market has already declined because many airlines are no longer in business, Laneckij said. This has increased demand for tickets from the remaining foreign airlines.

"Whether they stay or not depends on the price they have to pay for the danger faced," he said.

This article was translated from German.

World.title: Many feared trapped under collapsed building in Nairobi
World.content:
People are feared to be trapped after a large, unfinished building in Nairobi collapsed during construction. Rescue operations have proven complicated as police fired tear gas to disperse looters.

A multi-story building that was still under construction collapsed in the Kenyan capital of Nairobi on Friday, resulting in casualties and looting at the site, according to local media.

The Nairobi County governor's ​office confirmed the collapse, adding in a ​statement that people may be trapped beneath rubble.

Videos spreading online showed a dramatic crash and huge clouds of dust as the building came down in a busy business-residential mixed-use district.

The Red Cross sent teams to the site, posting on social media: "At around 1340 hours, a multi-story building under construction collapsed on 9th Street in Eastleigh, Nairobi."

There were conflicting reports on the size of the unfinished building. Nairobi Police Chief Issa Mohamud said the building had more than 10 floors under construction, while other accounts range from 12 to 18 stories.

Governor Johnson Sakaja's ​office said only the building's ground floor ​was occupied.

"There were some businesses in the basement, and workers who were busy building," local resident Abdi Aziz, 25, told the AFP news agency. "But since it was Friday prayers, a lot of them were at the mosque."

Rescue work underway at Nairobi building collapse site

A video published by Reuters news agency showed people gathered at the scene as ⁠an excavator moved rubble.

But rescue operations were proving complicated. Police officers sought to clear the area and provide access to emergency response teams but had to fire tear gas at people who had begun looting neighboring shops.

Eastleigh is a densely packed residential and market area, known as a hub for the Somali community.

It was not ​clear what caused the building to collapse. Nairobi is undergoing an extremely rapid construction boom, with high-rise buildings shooting up all over the city as Kenya's population expands.



Rescue work was underway in Nairobi, with some people feared trapped Image: Brian Inganga/AP Photo/picture alliance

Kenya: How common are building collapses?

Building collapses are a recurring problem in Nairobi.

County officials responsible for issuing building permits have been accused of failing to conduct adequate inspections to ensure developers comply with construction standards and safety guidelines.

There were 86 building collapses between 2009 and 2019, killing an estimated 200 people, according to a report by the Kenya Institute for Public Policy Research and Analysis.

Meanwhile, a separate audit of almost 15,000 buildings by the National Building Inspectorate found that 4.8% were very dangerous while 72.3% were classified as unsafe.
