World.title: Prague Airport Adds 20 Destinations to Winter Flight Schedule
World.content:
Prague Airport will offer direct flights to 145 destinations this winter, including 20 new destinations, as its winter flight schedule takes effect on Sunday, October 25.

The 2026/2027 winter schedule will run until March 27, 2027, with 69 airlines operating flights from Václav Havel Airport Prague.

Among the new destinations are Lille, Palermo, Turin, Venice and Bergen. Travellers will also have new options for reaching ski destinations, including Bolzano in Italy and Poprad in Slovakia.



The winter schedule also introduces new long-haul connections to Almaty in Kazakhstan and Hanoi in Vietnam, operated by Vietjet.

Charter flights will add further options, including Phuket in Thailand, La Romana in the Dominican Republic and Sihanoukville in Cambodia.

EasyJet will launch a new route to Marrakesh, Morocco, while Smartwings will introduce scheduled flights to Lisbon, Portugal.

Several routes previously operated mainly during the summer will continue into the winter season. These include easyJet flights to Newcastle in the UK and Wizz Air services to Vilnius in Lithuania.

More Flights to Popular Destinations

Several existing routes will see increased frequencies during the winter months.

Air Serbia will increase its Prague–Belgrade service from nine to 11 flights per week, while Pegasus Airlines will raise the number of weekly flights to Istanbul’s Sabiha Gökçen Airport from 14 to 17.

TAP Air Portugal will increase flights to Lisbon from seven to eight per week. Korean Air will also add a weekly service to Seoul, bringing the total to four flights per week.

Jazeera Airways will operate flights to Kuwait during the winter season for the first time.

New airlines operating passenger services from Prague this winter include Vietjet, SkyAlps, Fly2Galicia, Jazeera Airways and STARLUX Airlines. TUI Airways and Enter Air will also operate charter flights.

More Routes Planned for Summer 2027

Prague Airport has also confirmed new routes for the 2027 summer season. Delta Air Lines will launch flights to New York in mid-April, while SkyUp Airlines will introduce a new connection to Chișinău, the capital of Moldova.

World.title: Prague Reopens Bobsleigh Track With a New Alpine Coaster
World.content:
Prague’s Prosek bobsleigh track has reopened after a CZK 100 million renovation, introducing a second alpine coaster and doubling the attraction’s capacity.

Located on Mahalka Hill in the Prosek district, the facility has operated for 22 years. It reopened on Wednesday, October 21, with two tracks supplied by German manufacturer Wiegand.



The original track, measuring 700 metres, features a stainless-steel trough in which wheeled carts travel along a concave surface. The new 650-metre track uses the Alpine Coaster 2.0 system, with carts running on a monorail.

Both tracks allow riders to reach speeds of up to 45 kilometres per hour. Passengers can regulate their speed using a manual handbrake.

The newer coaster also incorporates an automated safety system. Around 2,000 magnetic sensors positioned along the track monitor the location and speed of individual carts. If necessary, induction brakes are activated automatically to prevent collisions or carts leaving the track.

Unlike the original ride, the Alpine Coaster 2.0 requires passengers to wear seatbelts.

The renovation has also brought improvements to the surrounding facilities, including a new café and an observation deck. A children’s playground and a rooftop relaxation area are still under construction, with completion planned for spring 2027.

Prices and Opening Hours

The attraction is located at Prosecká 906/34b in Prague 9. Tickets can be used on either track, with visitors choosing which one to ride when they arrive.

Ticket prices

– One ride – CZK 99

– Five rides – CZK 400

– Ten rides – CZK 700

– Twenty rides – CZK 1,300

– Thirty rides – CZK 1,800

Tickets for one, five and ten rides are valid for three months from the date of purchase. Twenty- and thirty-ride passes are valid for one year.

Opening hours

– Monday to Thursday – 10 am to 10 pm

– Friday and Saturday – 10 am to 11 pm

– Sunday – 10 am to 8 pm

World.title: GALLERY: The Czech Republic’s Largest LEGO Store Opens in Prague
World.content:
The Czech Republic’s largest official LEGO Store opened on Thursday, October 22, on Na Příkopě.

The two-storey store covers 496 square metres and combines retail space with interactive attractions, creative activities and displays inspired by the Czech capital.

Among the features greeting visitors at the entrance are the words “Ahoj Praha” (Hello Prague), a model of a No. 23 tram, and figures depicting a lion, Emperor Charles IV and a traditional Prague lamplighter.



The ground floor houses shelves of LEGO sets alongside glass display cases showcasing models and figures. The displays were developed with the involvement of staff at the LEGO factory in Kladno, whose work is also reflected in the store’s custom-built models.

The first floor features a Christmas-themed play area where visitors can build their own decorations from LEGO bricks and hang them on a specially prepared Christmas tree. The activity is open to children and adults alike.

A separate wall made entirely of LEGO bricks gives visitors the freedom to create their own pictures without following instructions or predefined designs.

Visitors who take the stairs to the second floor will find another part of the store’s design. The staircase and surrounding walls feature murals inspired by Prague, including a city panorama and Prague Castle.

The second floor contains further interactive attractions and creative spaces. Its centrepiece is a three-metre-tall replica of Prague’s Astronomical Clock.

World.title: Prague’s Indian Community to Celebrate Navratri With Music and Dance
World.content:
The Indian community in Prague will gather for an evening of traditional music, dancing and food on Saturday, October 24, as Navratri 2026 returns to Top Hotel Prague.

Organized by Bharatiya Gujarati Samaj, the event will celebrate the cultural traditions of Gujarat, a state in western India known for its distinctive music, colourful clothing and energetic folk dances.

The programme will start at 5 pm and is open to people interested in Indian culture and traditions.



The celebration will feature Garba and Dandiya Raas, two traditional dances closely associated with Navratri festivities in Gujarat.

Visitors will also have an opportunity to enjoy Indian food, see traditional clothing and learn more about Gujarati culture.

Garba will be one of the main attractions of the event. The traditional Gujarati folk dance is performed in circles, with participants moving rhythmically to music and following a series of coordinated steps. The dance is closely associated with Navratri, a Hindu festival celebrated over nine nights in honour of the goddess Durga and the feminine divine.

Dandiya Raas is another traditional dance associated with the festival. Participants dance in pairs or groups while striking decorated wooden sticks together in time with the music. The movements, rhythms and colourful outfits make it one of the most recognisable features of Gujarati Navratri celebrations.

Beyond the dancing, the event will offer visitors an opportunity to explore different aspects of Gujarati culture, including traditional clothing and Indian food.

Traditional clothing is also an important part of the festivities. Women often wear colourful chaniya cholis, while men may dress in traditional kediyu outfits. Embroidery, decorative patterns and bright colours are common features of clothing worn for Garba and Dandiya Raas.

Tickets and further information are available on the Bharatiya Gujarati Samaj website.

World.title: Czech Constitutional Court Rules Sex Workers Must Pay Taxes
World.content:
The Czech Constitutional Court has ruled that income from voluntary sex work is subject to taxation, placing it on the same footing as earnings from other self-employed professions.

The decision clarifies that collecting taxes from sex workers does not amount to state approval of the activity.

The case concerned a woman who was ordered to pay more than CZK 900,000 in back taxes for income earned from paid sexual services in 2013 and 2014.



She challenged the assessment in court, but lower courts upheld the decision of the Czech Financial Administration. She subsequently appealed to the Constitutional Court, Novinky reported.

The woman argued that taxing prostitution effectively turned the state into a pimp, pointing to the distinction in Czech law between providing sexual services voluntarily for payment and acting as an intermediary in such activities.

While the former is not a criminal offense, procuring or facilitating prostitution in certain circumstances can be punishable under the Criminal Code.

The Constitutional Court rejected her argument, ruling that taxation serves a different purpose. According to the judges, the state is not profiting from another person’s labor but ensuring that taxpayers contribute fairly to public finances.

The court added that taxation should not be interpreted as moral approval of sex work or as official state recognition of the activity.

Under the ruling, income from prostitution falls into the category of earnings from independent professions.

The same broad category includes income earned by entertainers, coaches, athletes and models, as well as people who publish sexually explicit material on subscription platforms such as OnlyFans.

The court warned that exempting income from sex work would undermine the fair distribution of the tax burden and discriminate against other taxpayers.

The ruling does not legalize every activity associated with prostitution. Instead, it establishes that income earned through voluntary sex work must be declared and taxed under the same general principles that apply to other forms of self-employment.

World.title: Prague’s First Film Screening Took Place 130 Years Ago
World.content:
Prague’s first public film screening took place on October 18, 1896, at the Hotel U Černého koně on Na Příkopě Street.

Organized by the French branch of Thomas Edison’s company, the presentation introduced audiences to moving pictures, a technology that would soon transform entertainment across Bohemia.

The screening marked another milestone in a period of rapid technological change that had begun five years earlier.

In 1891, Prague hosted the Jubilee Provincial Exhibition, celebrating a century of industrial progress. The event helped reshape the city, leaving behind landmarks including the Industrial Palace, Petřín Lookout Tower and mirror maze.



The Hotel That Brought New Technology to Prague

The Hotel U Černého koně, or At the Black Horse, was among Prague’s most luxurious establishments in the late 19th century. Its owners, brothers Jindřich and Karel Cífka, were quick to recognize the commercial potential of new inventions.

Later in 1896, the hotel introduced another technological novelty, the X-ray machine. The device had been developed by German physicist Wilhelm Conrad Röntgen, who announced his discovery in December 1895.

Initially presented as an attraction, the machine soon acquired medical significance. In January 1897, physician Rudolf Jedlička used it to examine a patient suspected of having swallowed a foreign object. The image revealed a nail lodged in the man’s stomach.

Edison and the Lumière Brothers Compete for Audiences

The first film screening was organized by Adolf Oppenheimer, an optician and mechanic who operated a cinematograph supplied by Edison’s French company.

According to a contemporary invitation reproduced by Czech Radio, screenings took place daily, beginning at 4 p.m. and continuing hourly until 8 p.m. Additional shows were held on Sundays and public holidays. Admission cost 40 kreutzers, with discounts for schools.

Competition arrived almost immediately. Just five days after the Edison presentation, the Lumière brothers’ cinematograph was shown at the Hotel U Saského dvora on Hybernská Street.

Both companies promoted their technology as the genuine article. Their s emphasized the quality of their moving pictures and their international reputations, reflecting the intense competition surrounding the new medium.

Czech filmmakers soon began producing their own material. In June 1898, Národní listy reported on a cinematograph pavilion at the Prague Exhibition Grounds where two young architects presented original films, including scenes from everyday life in Prague.

Viktor Ponrepo Opens a Permanent Cinema

For several years, traveling cinematographs brought films to audiences around the country. A permanent venue eventually followed.

In September 1907, Dismas Šlambor, better known as Viktor Ponrepo, opened what is widely regarded as the first permanent cinema in the Czech lands. It was located in the U Modré štiky building on Karlova Street.

Originally a magician and illusionist, Ponrepo had become interested in image-recording technology after encountering Edison’s phonograph at the 1891 exhibition. He later toured the country with a traveling cinema before establishing his Prague venue.

Ponrepo became famous for greeting audiences with a bow before every screening. He eventually filmed the gesture and projected it before his shows, turning it into his personal signature.

By then, moving pictures had evolved from a technological curiosity into a new form of mass entertainment, with Prague among the cities embracing the change.

World.title: Meet Paulo Dias, the Expat Behind Prague’s Pintz Beer App
World.content:
Finding a good beer in Prague is rarely a difficult task. Finding the right pub, knowing what a pint costs and deciding where to go next is a different question.

For Paulo Dias, that challenge became the idea behind Pintz, a web app built to help people navigate Prague’s rich beer scene.

Originally from Portugal, Paulo has spent almost 15 years living abroad, moving between Slovakia and the UK before eventually taking a job in the Czech Republic.



He first arrived in the Czech Republic in 2021, spending several months in Opava before moving to Prague in February 2022. Even after the move, he was cautious about settling in. “When I moved to Prague, I wasn’t buying many things for my apartment, because if I moved again, I’d have to pack everything,” Paulo recalls.

That changed once his new job became more stable. By the end of the year, he was already thinking about staying.

I think the quality of life in Prague is quite amazing. It’s one of the best, if not the best, of the cities I know. I feel good here, I feel at home. That’s why I decided to stay.”

Prague’s pub culture

Prague’s pub culture became one of the ways Paulo built a social life after moving to the city. He started with local pubs in Žižkov.

“I started to make friends there, and then I thought it was a good opportunity for me to become more social.”

What struck him was how different the culture was from Portugal. He describes drinking there as more centered around wine, home gatherings, watching football with friends or celebrating birthdays, rather than regularly meeting at pubs during the week.

“I know people who meet every Monday. It’s impossible in Portugal, this mindset. People just stay at home or go for a coffee after dinner. There’s no culture like going to a pub.”

In Prague, meeting for a beer could instead become part of an ordinary weekday. That was something Paulo gradually came to appreciate about his new home.

“I don’t need to wait for the weekend to have my social life active.”

From sneaker prices to Pintz

The idea for Pintz grew out of a sneaker-price platform “The Real Sneaker Index” Paulo had been working on in his spare time. The two projects are quite different, but the first gave him a way of thinking about how prices could be collected and compared.

The connection to beer came almost as an afterthought. Paulo was already spending time in Prague’s pubs, and the idea eventually brought his side project closer to something he was experiencing himself.

“I was thinking, maybe I could apply the same idea to something more connected to everyday life. And then I thought, why not use it to track beer prices?”

What started as a price tracker gradually expanded into a way of exploring pubs. Users can now add information about individual places, from terraces and beer gardens to the beers they serve, while ratings give people a way to share their own experiences. “It’s not only about finding the cheapest beer. It started that way, but it’s really about quality.”

Pintz is now present in the US, Mexico, Atlantic Islands and across many countries in Europe.

Building it alone with AI

Paulo has been building Pintz alongside his Lead AI Platforms job, developing the platform himself with the help of AI. He works on it in the evenings, at weekends and whenever he can find the time.

“I’m not a coder, I’m not a developer, but I know what I want to do.”

AI has allowed him to take those ideas further without having to build every part of the platform from scratch himself. He sets up processes, monitors how they work and keeps adding and improving features as the project develops.

The speed at which he can turn an idea into something functional has been one of the biggest surprises for him.

“What impressed me the most is the capability of building anything with AI, especially digital products.”

What’s next for Pintz?

For now, his focus is on getting more people to use Pintz and bringing more pubs, breweries and beer brands onto the platform. He is also looking at sponsorships and other ways of turning the project into a sustainable business.

At the same time, he is conscious of how easily monetisation could get in the way of the experience he is trying to create. He does not want users to feel like they are constantly being sold something while using the app.

“I don’t want this to become an advertising app that people are annoyed to use.”

World.title: Prague Light Park at Žluté Lázně Takes Visitors Back to the 14th Century
World.content:
Prague’s Žluté lázně has opened a new edition of the Story of Lights, a seasonal light park inspired by the city’s medieval history.

Running from October 16, 2026, to January 31, 2027, the event features illuminated sculptures, interactive installations and, from November, evening boat trips on the Vltava River.



The park takes visitors back to 14th-century Prague during the reign of Charles IV, the Bohemian king and Holy Roman Emperor whose rule helped shape the city’s development.

Thousands of LED lights illuminate the grounds after dark, forming a route through displays inspired by the architecture, symbols and history of medieval Prague.

Among the installations are illuminated representations of Charles Bridge, Gothic towers, church arches, royal crowns and coronation regalia. The displays reinterpret historical motifs using modern lighting technology.

Some installations are interactive, with the organizers targeting families with children as well as adults looking for an evening activity outdoors.

The historical theme focuses on a period when Prague underwent major urban development.

Charles IV initiated the construction of Charles Bridge, founded the New Town in 1348 and helped establish Prague as an important political, cultural and religious centre in medieval Europe.

From November 6, visitors will also be able to combine their visit with an illuminated boat trip along the Vltava. The evening cruises are scheduled for Fridays, Saturdays, Sundays and public holidays.

World.title: EU flight compensation rules: What changes from today, 23 October, and what must wait until 2027?
World.content:
New EU flight compensation rules promise faster refunds, simpler claims and stronger passenger protection across Europe. However, despite the attention surrounding the latest reforms, travellers should be aware of an important distinction: the newly approved reimbursement measures will not apply until 23 October 2027.

The European Parliament approved legislation strengthening passenger rights on 20 October 2026, with 652 votes in favour, two against and eight abstentions.

According to AIRportal.hu, the changes will introduce standardised refund and compensation procedures, clarify the responsibilities of online booking platforms and improve assistance for passengers with disabilities.

The legislation is part of a broader European effort to make passenger rights easier to enforce across different forms of transport.

EU flight compensation rules: What is changing?

One of the most important developments is the introduction of standardised EU forms for reimbursement and compensation claims.

Instead of navigating different procedures for individual airlines or transport companies, passengers will be able to use common European forms available in all official EU languages.

The European Commission will make these forms accessible online, while transport operators will also be able to provide equivalent alternatives.

According to the European Commission, the legislation is intended to make passenger rights more transparent and improve their enforcement.

The changes will cover several transport sectors, although some requirements differ depending on the mode of transport.

If you missed it: Flight diversion plans need a passenger plan too

Flight refunds within 14 days

The reforms also address a common difficulty faced by air passengers: recovering money for tickets purchased through travel agencies or online booking platforms.

Under the new arrangements, passengers will generally be entitled to a full refund within 14 days when reimbursement is handled through an intermediary.

The process will involve two stages:

First seven days: The airline transfers the refund to the intermediary.

The airline transfers the refund to the intermediary. Following seven days: The intermediary returns the money to the passenger.

The reimbursement will generally include the original airfare and applicable intermediary fees, although limited exceptions may apply.

Booking platforms will also have to explain the relevant refund arrangements before a passenger completes a purchase.

The new rules are designed to prevent situations in which passengers struggle to determine whether the airline or booking platform is responsible for returning their money.

What compensation can passengers claim for delayed or cancelled flights?

It is important to distinguish between ticket refunds and financial compensation.

A refund allows passengers to recover the price of an unused ticket in qualifying circumstances. Compensation is an additional payment that may be available when flights are significantly delayed, cancelled at short notice or passengers are denied boarding.

Under the EU’s existing compensation framework, eligible passengers may receive:

€250 for flights of up to 1,500 kilometres.

for flights of up to 1,500 kilometres. €400 for longer flights within the EU and certain flights between 1,500 and 3,500 kilometres.

for longer flights within the EU and certain flights between 1,500 and 3,500 kilometres. €600 for other flights exceeding 3,500 kilometres.

These amounts have been maintained under the revised air passenger rights framework, as confirmed by the European Parliament’s legislative documentation.

However, airlines are not automatically required to pay compensation for every disruption. Extraordinary circumstances, including certain severe weather events, can affect eligibility.

Stronger protection for passengers with disabilities

The legislation introduces additional safeguards for passengers with disabilities or reduced mobility.

When an airline requires a passenger to travel with an accompanying person for safety reasons, the companion will be entitled to travel free of charge.

The aim is to bring air travel protections more closely into line with arrangements already available in other European transport sectors.

National enforcement authorities will also receive stronger powers to investigate potential violations of passenger rights, including launching checks without waiting for individual complaints.

The Council of the European Union has described these measures as part of efforts to strengthen the enforcement of passenger rights throughout the EU.

What do the changes mean for travellers flying from Hungary?

The reforms will also be relevant to travellers using Budapest’s Ferenc Liszt International Airport and other Hungarian airports.

For international visitors, EU air passenger rights generally apply to flights departing from airports within the European Union, regardless of the passenger’s nationality.

They also cover flights arriving in the EU from non-EU countries when operated by qualifying European airlines.

For example, a British, American or Canadian tourist departing from Budapest may benefit from EU passenger protection even if they do not hold EU citizenship.

Passengers booking flights through third-party travel websites should particularly benefit from clearer responsibilities and more predictable reimbursement procedures once the new legislation becomes applicable.

When will the new rules actually apply?

Although the broader EU air passenger rights reform has already progressed through the legislative process, the latest measures concerning enforcement and refunds are not applicable on 23 October 2026.

The enforcement legislation still requires formal approval by the Council of the European Union before publication in the EU’s Official Journal.

The new provisions are scheduled to apply from 23 October 2027, alongside the revised air passenger rights framework.

Until then, travellers affected by cancellations, long delays or denied boarding should continue to rely on the applicable EU passenger rights rules.

For passengers flying to and from Hungary, the reforms should eventually mean clearer information, simpler procedures and stronger safeguards when seeking refunds or compensation. The key point for travellers today is that existing rights remain enforceable, while the latest improvements are still awaiting implementation.

World.title: Hungarian Revolution of 1956: Why does its legacy still divide Hungary?
World.content:
The Hungarian Revolution of 1956 is one of the country’s most important historical events. Yet 70 years later, its legacy remains a subject of political debate. As Hungary commemorates the anniversary on 23 October, a new analysis by Hungary Insider examines why a revolution fought for freedom has become such a contested symbol in modern Hungarian politics.

Almost every major political movement in Hungary recognises the historical significance of the 1956 uprising against Soviet domination and Communist dictatorship. However, the lessons drawn from those events often differ considerably.

For some, the revolution represents national sovereignty and resistance to foreign interference. Others place greater emphasis on democratic freedoms, political pluralism and the struggle against authoritarian rule.

These interpretations are not necessarily contradictory. Indeed, both national independence and individual liberty were central demands of the revolutionaries.

Who owns the legacy of the Hungarian Revolution of 1956?

In its latest analysis, Hungary Insider explores how the memory of 1956 continues to influence Hungary’s contemporary political debates.

The article examines why different political movements seek to identify themselves with the revolution and whether any political camp can legitimately claim to be its sole heir.

It also recalls an often-overlooked aspect of the uprising: the revolutionaries came from different political and social backgrounds, and their visions for Hungary’s future were not identical.

A shared history in a politically divided country

The 70th anniversary also raises questions about the relationship between national remembrance and contemporary politics.

Can Hungarians commemorate the same historical events while drawing different political conclusions? And can the revolution remain a symbol of national unity without erasing the diversity of those who participated in it?

The analysis considers these questions while explaining why the events of 1956 remain relevant to understanding Hungary today.

Read the full analysis on Hungary Insider:

1956 belongs to every Hungarian – so why is its legacy so divisive? →

Read here more about The Hungarian Revolution of 1956

World.title: Hungarians commemorate 1956 in South Australian Parliament
World.content:
A solemn commemoration was held in Adelaide to mark the 70th anniversary of the 1956 Hungarian Revolution and War of Independence. Event at the South Australian Parliament:

A special and moving event took place on 21 October 2026 at the South Australian Parliament House in Adelaide, where representatives of the local Hungarian community and invited guests from South Australian public life gathered to mark the 70th anniversary of the 1956 Hungarian Revolution and War of Independence.

The commemoration was held at the invitation of Joe Szakács, South Australia’s Minister for Infrastructure and Transport, and Peter Malinauskas, Premier of South Australia. Numerous representatives of the Hungarian community attended, including community leaders, local businesspeople, heads of educational institutions and representatives of Hungarian organisations. Attendees also included Attila Szabó, Honorary Hungarian Consul, and Péter Martonosi, Hungary’s Chargé d’Affaires, who travelled from Canberra and also delivered a commemorative address.

Personal Memories and Our Shared History

At the beginning of the ceremony, Joe Szakács welcomed those present. In his speech, he also recalled his personal family history: his father, Joseph Szakacs, took part in the 1956 Hungarian Revolution, then fled Hungary after the uprising was crushed and later found a new home in Australia.

His father’s story is a powerful example of the fate that shaped the lives of so many Hungarian families. Following the 1956 Revolution, thousands of Hungarians were forced to leave their homeland, leaving behind their families, homes and former lives in order to build a secure future for themselves in a new country.

Joe Szakács’s personal connection brought the events of 1956 particularly close to those present. The legacy of the revolution is not merely a defining chapter in Hungarian history, but also the story of families, generations and communities whose impact can still be felt in distant parts of the world, including Australia.

Peter Malinauskas, Premier of South Australia, then delivered a commemorative address. His personal reflections and moving recollections made the commemoration especially memorable. His speech provided a fitting opportunity for those present to pay tribute together to the heroes of the 1956 Revolution, those who fought for freedom, and all those whose lives were forever changed by the events of that time.

Attila Szabó, Honorary Hungarian Consul, also welcomed the guests, followed by Péter Martonosi, Hungary’s Chargé d’Affaires from Canberra, who shared his commemorative thoughts.

The cultural programme was enriched by a performance from Adelaide’s Kaláris Folk Dance Group, which brought the traditions and cultural heritage of Hungarian folk dance to the audience.

If you missed it: Adelaide Bridge shines in Hungarian colours for 20 August – photos, video

Hungarian Flavours and Informal Gatherings at

Following the official programme, participants had the opportunity to engage in informal conversations, greet old acquaintances and establish new connections. The gathering was complemented by Hungarian hospitality: the tables featured, among other dishes, mini lángos, stuffed cabbage, Hungarian sausage and a goulash version of the distinctive Australian meat pie.

The traditional Hungarian flavours created a special atmosphere and also reminded those present that shared meals, the preservation of traditions and time spent together all play an important role in maintaining national identity.

At the end of the event, Joe Szakács also gave interested guests an informal tour of the chamber of the South Australian House of Assembly. Visitors were therefore able not only to take part in a historically significant commemoration, but also to gain an insight into one of the important settings of parliamentary work in South Australia.

A Living Legacy After Seventy Years

The Adelaide commemoration was more than a simple anniversary event. Within the walls of Parliament, those who are personally connected to the legacy of 1956, or who relate to it through their family histories, were able to remember together with South Australian public figures who consider it important to recognise the history and traditions of the Hungarian community.

It was particularly meaningful for local Hungarians that the leadership of South Australia showed such consideration towards the community and provided a dignified venue in Parliament House for the celebration marking the 70th anniversary.

The event once again demonstrated that the memory of the 1956 Revolution and War of Independence knows no national borders. The message of freedom, courage and devotion to one’s homeland continues, seven decades later, to connect Hungarians living in different parts of the world.

For the participants, one of the most important experiences of the day was being together, remembering collectively and experiencing a sense of belonging. It was heartening to come together as Hungarian.

World.title: Hungary’s 23 October national holiday begins with flag-raising ceremony at Parliament – VIDEO
World.content:
Hungary’s 23 October national holiday began with a traditional military flag-raising ceremony outside the Hungarian Parliament in Budapest on Friday morning, marking the 70th anniversary of the 1956 Revolution and War of Independence. President András Baka, Prime Minister Péter Magyar and Speaker of the National Assembly Ágnes Forsthoffer attended the solemn event on Kossuth Lajos Square.

The Hungarian national flag was raised to the sound of the national anthem by an honour guard of the Hungarian Defence Forces, continuing a longstanding tradition that marks the beginning of the country’s official 23 October commemorations.

The ceremony featured the Central Military Band, the National Ceremonial Cavalry Unit, the 32nd Guard Regiment of the Hungarian Defence Forces’ Budapest Garrison Brigade and the Count Ferenc Nádasdy Hussar Squadron.

Representatives of the government, state institutions, military organisations and the diplomatic corps were present, alongside invited guests. Members of the public also gathered on Kossuth Square to watch the ceremony.

Hungary’s 23 October national holiday: Why is the flag raised every year?

The flag-raising ceremony outside Parliament is one of the central traditions of Hungary’s national commemorations.

Held annually on 23 October, the event symbolically honours those who participated in the 1956 uprising against Soviet domination and Communist dictatorship.

Kossuth Lajos Square has particular historical significance. On 23 October 1956, enormous crowds gathered outside Parliament, where reformist politician Imre Nagy addressed demonstrators demanding political change.

According to the Hungarian government’s historical overview of the national holiday, official commemorations traditionally continue after the flag-raising ceremony at several locations associated with the revolution.

These include the Budapest University of Technology and Economics, Bem József Square and other sites where decisive events unfolded in 1956.

For visitors to Budapest, the annual ceremony offers an opportunity to witness one of Hungary’s most important state traditions in the historic centre of the capital.

What happened during the Hungarian Revolution of 1956?

The revolution began on 23 October 1956 with peaceful demonstrations led by university students in Budapest.

Protesters demanded political reforms, greater national independence, freedom of expression and the withdrawal of Soviet troops stationed in Hungary.

The demonstrations rapidly developed into an armed uprising against the Communist dictatorship associated with Mátyás Rákosi and Soviet control.

One of the most recognisable symbols of the revolution was the Hungarian flag with a hole in its centre. Protesters removed the Communist-era emblem from the national tricolour, creating an enduring symbol of resistance.

Although the uprising initially achieved important political changes, Soviet forces launched a large-scale military intervention on 4 November 1956.

The revolution was eventually crushed, followed by imprisonment, executions and widespread political reprisals. Hundreds of thousands of Hungarians fled the country.

The events nevertheless became a defining chapter in Hungary’s modern history and its struggle for national sovereignty.

More than a flag-raising ceremony: How Hungary commemorates 23 October

While the morning flag-raising is one of the most recognisable official events, Hungary’s 23 October national holiday is traditionally marked by commemorations throughout the country.

Every year, wreath-laying ceremonies, memorial speeches, exhibitions and cultural programmes remember the participants and victims of the revolution.

In Budapest, important memorial locations include Bem József Square, the Hungarian Radio building, Corvin Passage and the 1956 memorial sites near the Parliament. As we wrote earlier, PM Magyar said in 1956, demonstrators became free Hungarian citizens.

This year’s 70th-anniversary programme also includes exhibitions, performances and commemorative activities near Parliament, including events around Vértanúk Square and Alkotmány Street.

Prime Minister Péter Magyar is also scheduled to address the public on Kossuth Lajos Square later on Friday. Details: Hungary to build a dedicated 1956 revolution museum, Magyar announces

The commemorations began before the national holiday itself, with memorial events and a torchlight procession taking place in Budapest on Thursday.

October 23 – PM pays tribute to 1956 heroes in New Public Cemetery

The prime minister paid his respects to the heroes of the 1956 revolution and freedom fight at plot 301 of the New Public Cemetery on Friday morning.

Peter Magyar, accompanied by Balint Ruff, the head of the Prime Minister’s Office, laid flowers at the graves of Prime Minister Imre Nagy and other martyrs and victims of the revolution.

At the commemoration, the Magyar said Hungarians today remembered “one of our country’s most important historical events, the 70th anniversary of the 1956 revolution, and the thousands of victims and heroes of the freedom fight“.

“Today is a deeply moving and very important day, the whole world is celebrating with us,” Magyar said, encouraging everyone to take part in the commemorative events.

He also noted that more than 200,000 people left the country in 1956 and that descendants of many revolutionaries now live all over the world.

Today, commemorations are taking place in Hungary and across the Carpathian Basin, with a wide array of programmes.

Why is 23 October a public holiday in Hungary?

The date has two major historical meanings for Hungary.

Beyond marking the outbreak of the 1956 Revolution, it also commemorates the proclamation of the Hungarian Republic on 23 October 1989, during the country’s transition from Communist rule to democracy.

Parliament declared 23 October a national holiday in 1990. Its status was subsequently reaffirmed in legislation adopted in 1991 and in Hungary’s Fundamental Law.

Today, 23 October is a public holiday, meaning that many businesses, schools and public offices are closed.

Seventy years after the uprising, the annual flag-raising ceremony remains a powerful reminder of the events that shaped modern Hungary. Alongside the official ceremonies, the anniversary provides an opportunity for new generations and international visitors to learn about the country’s struggle for freedom and independence.

World.title: Fitch: Hungary’s 2027 budget supports euro adoption
World.content:
Fitch Ratings said the Hungarian government’s 2027 budget draft “shows commitment to consolidation” and euro adoption in a note on Thursday.

“Hungary’s draft 2027 budget and medium-term deficit targets are consistent with the government’s objective of meeting euro-adoption criteria by 2030,” Fitch said.

The rating agency added that its assessment of the government’s capacity to deliver frontloaded fiscal consolidation, given the significant fiscal deterioration in 2026, would be “central” to its sovereign rating analysis.

Fitch rates Hungary BBB with a negative outlook.

Fitch noted that the 2027 budget draft, presented by the government earlier in the week, targets a reduction in the general government deficit to 4.9pc of GDP from an estimated 7.5pc in 2026. It indcludes expenditure cuts equivalent to 1.5pc of GDP, the expiry of temporary and one-off pre-election measures worth 1.4pc of GDP, and lower interest payments of up to 0.2pc of GDP, reflecting falling costs on inflation-linked bonds and lower bond yields amid improved market sentminent, it said. Additional revenue measures of about 1pc of GDP are also planned, it added.

If you missed it: Hungary’s economy could boom: Experts predict euro falling to HUF 350

The proposed spending cuts focus on concession contracts, economic development subsidies, government communications, public media, and state investment and operating costs, including a planned reduction of at least 10pc in operating expenditures of ministries and state-owned companies.

The government expects tax increases to raise 0.25pc of GDP through higher corporate and innovation taxation, 0.2pc from a wealth tax, 0.1pc from a levy on energy companies, and smaller increases in mining royalties, a tax on corporate fleets and an advertising tax.

“Sustained lower interest costs could support consolidation if favourable financing conditions persist, but savings from expenditure reviews and public-sector efficiency measures remain uncertain,” Fitch said.

Fitch projects the general government deficit will narrow to 5.4pc of GDP in 2027 from 7.3pc in 2026, and fall below 3pc by 2030. It expects state debt, relative to GDP, to peak at 77.7pc in 2027-2028.

World.title: Hungarian FM Orbán says her trips cost just a tenth of former FM Szijjártó’s
World.content:
Foreign Minister Anita Orbán says her ministry has cut travel costs dramatically, with 23 trips costing less than HUF 63 million between May and October, compared with more than HUF 960 million under her predecessor. Fidesz has hit back, arguing that Péter Szijjártó delivered billions in investment and thousands of jobs.

Hungary’s Foreign Minister Anita Orbán says official trips under her leadership have cost barely a tenth of what they did under her predecessor, Péter Szijjártó, as the ministry seeks to reduce spending and improve efficiency.

In a Facebook post, Orbán said the ministry had reviewed its central administrative expenditure as part of preparations for the 2027 budget. She also announced savings in public diplomacy and development programmes, insisting that these cuts had not required the cancellation of any programmes.

Travel costs fall from HUF 960 million to less than HUF 63 million

According to Orbán, the previous foreign ministry spent more than HUF 960 million on 37 trips between May and October 2025. During the same period in 2026, the ministry under her leadership made 23 trips at a total cost of less than HUF 63 million.

This means the average cost per trip fell from more than HUF 25.9 million under Szijjártó to less than HUF 2.7 million under Orbán.

“In other words, one trip cost barely more than a tenth of what it did last year during the same period,” the foreign minister wrote.

Orbán attributed the savings partly to a decision to stop using individually chartered aviation services for temporary overseas assignments involving ministerial delegations. She said this change alone would save close to HUF 1.2 billion in operating expenditure.

The ministry has also terminated or streamlined several contracts following a review of its running costs.

Ministry claims 30% savings without cancelling programmes

Travel costs are not the only area where the ministry says it has made savings. Orbán said public diplomacy programmes and the development portfolio had achieved overall savings of 30% without cancelling a single programme.

She stressed that the reductions resulted from professional reviews and rationalisation rather than cuts to the programmes themselves.

“The Ministry of Foreign Affairs’ key objective is to establish an organisation that operates more efficiently and manages public funds responsibly,” she wrote.

The figures come amid scrutiny of the cost of official travel under the previous foreign minister. According to figures previously published by Telex, Szijjártó’s hired-aircraft trips alone cost Hungarian taxpayers more than HUF 2 billion in 2025.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official Telegram channel!

Fidesz counters with investment and job figures

Fidesz, the former governing party now in opposition, quickly responded to Orbán’s announcement, arguing that the cost of a foreign minister’s travel should not be the only measure of their performance.

The party said Szijjártó had announced, launched or handed over investments worth HUF 1,635 billion during the corresponding period, which it linked to the creation of 22,552 new jobs across Hungary.

“Péter Szijjártó served his country with thousands of billions flowing into the Hungarian economy and tens of thousands of jobs. Anita Orbán does so by costing less,” the party said in a statement, ending with a sarcastic “Well, that’s something too – congratulations!”

Fidesz also summarised its comparison with the slogan “Péter Szijjártó–Anita Orbán: 22,552–0”, referring to the number of jobs it attributed to the two ministers.

World.title: PM Magyar: In 1956, demonstrators became free Hungarian citizens
World.content:
Prime Minister Péter Magyar paid tribute to the demonstrators of 1956 and their yearning for freedom in an address at a ceremonial wreath-laying on Bem Square in Budapest on Thursday, held to mark the 70th anniversary of the Revolution and Freedom Fight. Magyar also announced the establishment of a museum commemorating the heroes and victims of the 1956 uprising.

The prime minister said that when the university students setting out from the Technical University, and the Budapest residents who joined them gathered, they did not yet know that they were revolutionaries; they became so only hours later, when the first shots were fired at the Hungarian Radio building. But they already knew something of themselves, he said: that with their silent march and their dignified procession they had become free Hungarian citizens, “and this could never again be taken from them.”

“No later retribution could take it from them, nor the tramping of Soviet boots, nor the prison years, nor the decades spent under oppression,” he said.

“Nor could they take away that strength which also fills us whenever we grow weary, whenever we lose faith in Hungary for even a moment — that strength which also carries us forward. For nothing is stronger than the will of free Hungarians and the courageous stand of free Hungarians,” the prime minister said.

Photo: MTI

The prime minister said that it was a matter of “shame and pain” that in seventy years, and even since the change of regime, the nation had failed to discharge one of its greatest debts: there was no single, worthy place dedicated in its entirety to the memory of the heroes and victims of 1956.

He said that, in homage to the heroes of the Revolution and Freedom Fight, the government undertook to create in the coming years a “worthy shrine of Hungarian freedom”, establishing a museum of 1956 that pays tribute to the victims, to those who fought, and to the nameless heroes.

Magyar said the martyrs of the revolution would never be forgotten: the innocents led to the gallows, the martyrs buried in unmarked graves, the courage of “the Pest lads and the Pest girls”, the thousands tortured in prisons and the hundreds of thousands driven from their homeland, the innocent victims of the firing squads, and the pain of Hungarian families torn apart.

“Their names and their sacrifice live forever in our hearts and in the memory of the Hungarian nation,” he added.

Photo: MTI

He said the proof of their victory was that Hungarians could celebrate with cheerfulness, pride and a sense of liberation. That cheerfulness, he said, proved that the Hungarian people had not been broken and had not bowed their heads, and that people could still look one another in the eye today, backs straight, proudly, with a smile.

“We know that the sacrifice was not in vain: the homeland is free, and we have a common future,” the prime minister said.

Magyar called the flag with a hole, born when the Rakosi coat of arms was cut out of the national colours, a world-famous symbol of the 1956 Revolution. Everyone understood it, he said, because it said the same thing in every language: this is our country, and we want to decide its fate. That is why it is still raised high with pride today, he said, because the hole in the middle of the flag is an everlasting symbol of Hungarian freedom.

Magyar described presenting awards to former ’56 university students as one of the most uplifting experiences of his life. Those who stood up for the homeland seventy years ago “are still among us”, he added.

Photo: MTI

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official Telegram channel!

The prime minister also declared that dividing the nation “is a sin”. He said there were still some who failed to understand that there were minutes and hours when “we are Hungarians only, without qualifiers, without regard to origin or political sympathy”; they could still decide whether bowing their heads to 1956 or their day-to-day political interests mattered more to them, he said.

Anyone arriving with respect and good will would be embraced as a friend, he said, “but we will not yield an ounce of our freedom.” The nation had grown into its own history and looked forward to its independent future “with heads held high and unshakeable faith”, he added.

Paying homage to every hero of 1956, the prime minister closed his address with the words: “Long live the free, truly independent Hungary.”

Most of those attending the ceremony arrived at Bem Square with a torchlight procession setting out from the Technical University, part of the Gloria Victis 1956 memorial series organised by the Rákóczi Association. The march commemorated the student assembly held at the Technical University on October 22, remembered as one of the defining events of the revolution, at which the students set out their demands point by point and decided that, in a gesture of solidarity with the Polish people, they would march to Bem Square the following day, October 23. Many of the marchers waved national flags and the pierced flags symbolising the revolution.

Photo: MTI

The Rakoczi Association wrote on its website that 15,000 secondary school and university students were taking part in its commemorative programmes. Some 3,500 of them, from 170 schools in Hungary and abroad, were arriving in Budapest between October 21 and 23 for the memorial events.

After the ceremony on Bem Square, the participants marched to Imre Nagy Square, where the prime minister lit the flame of the revolution.

World.title: Hungary to build a dedicated 1956 revolution museum, Magyar announces
World.content:
Prime Minister Péter Magyar has pledged to establish a museum dedicated to the heroes and victims of Hungary’s 1956 Revolution, saying the country has failed to honour this historic debt for 70 years.

Hungary will establish a dedicated museum commemorating the 1956 Revolution and its heroes, Prime Minister Péter Magyar announced in a speech in Budapest on 23 October, marking the uprising’s 70th anniversary.

Speaking at Bem József Square, Magyar said it was both shameful and painful that Hungary had not yet created a worthy national memorial devoted entirely to those who fought against Soviet-backed rule and those who lost their lives.

“We undertake to create, in the coming years, a worthy sanctuary of Hungarian freedom. We will establish a genuine museum of 1956 that pays tribute to the victims, the fighters and the anonymous heroes,” the prime minister said.

A museum to honour the heroes of 1956

Magyar stressed that, seven decades after the revolution, Hungary still lacked a dedicated place where the memory of the uprising could be preserved in its entirety.

He described the proposed institution as a long-overdue tribute to those who risked their lives for the country’s freedom, including the many ordinary people whose names never became widely known.

The prime minister arrived at Bem Square after walking along the Bem embankment from Budapest University of Technology and Economics. It was from the university that students began marching towards the city centre on 23 October 1956, helping set the Budapest uprising in motion.

“There is no force stronger than the determination of free Hungarian young people,” Magyar said, praising the students who took a leading role in the revolution.

‘Thirteen days that shook the world’

Reflecting on the events of October 1956, Magyar described the uprising as a historic turning point that shook the foundations of tyranny and left an enduring mark on world history.

The revolution began on 23 October and developed into 13 days of resistance against Soviet domination and Hungary’s communist regime. Although the uprising was crushed by Soviet military intervention, Magyar argued that it had made Hungarians free citizens in a way that subsequent repression could never entirely undo.

He also highlighted the courage required of those who joined the movement, noting that individuals had to decide for themselves what they were willing to risk for their country.

“Someone had to say that it was time to set off. Someone had to take the lead, and everyone had to decide individually what they would do for their homeland in its hour of need,” he said, expressing gratitude to the students and all the heroes of 1956.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official Telegram channel!

Magyar praises Polish-Hungarian solidarity

The prime minister also paid tribute to the longstanding friendship between Hungary and Poland, explaining that the choice of Bem József Square was particularly fitting because the square is named after a Polish-born general who became a hero of the Hungarian Revolution of 1848–49.

Magyar recalled how workers in the Polish city of Poznań had given Hungarians hope during protests in the summer of 1956. In the autumn, he said, the Hungarian uprising in turn inspired and encouraged the Polish people.

“Thus, in those days, the friendship between the two nations became courageous solidarity, active cooperation and life-saving assistance,” he said. He also paid tribute to the heroes of both nations.

A call to remember the victims and overcome divisions

Magyar called the 1956 Revolution an enduring symbol of Hungarian freedom, while stressing that celebrating the country’s spirit did not mean forgetting the tragedy that followed the uprising’s defeat.

He urged Hungarians to remember those who were executed or persecuted, the young revolutionaries known as the Pesti srácok (‘the boys of Pest’) and the girls who also took part, the innocent victims of the shootings, and families torn apart by repression.

Their memory, he said, demonstrated that the Hungarian people had not been broken and could still look one another in the eye with pride.

Magyar also used his speech to call for national unity, arguing that there are moments when Hungarians should put aside political loyalties and other divisions.

“Dividing this homeland is a sin,” he said, adding that people still had a choice between paying tribute to the heroes of 1956 and prioritising their immediate political interests.

He concluded by calling for a free and genuinely independent Hungary. The prime minister also invited the public to attend the anniversary celebrations at Kossuth Square, in front of Parliament, later that day.

World.title: ‘Collective Fear’: Pressure on Serbians with Disabilities to Vote for Ruling Party
World.content:
According to Serbia’s 2022 census, more than 356,000 people with disabilities in Serbia, or roughly 5.5 per cent of the population over the age of two.

For years, Serbian election authorities have been criticised for failing to ensure voting privacy for people with disabilities, such as those living with blindness or vision impairment who are not provided with braille ballot papers; international election observers have previously cited the inaccessibility of polling stations for people with disabilities.

Political pressure on socially vulnerable voters in Serbia has been documented before.

In a 2023 report, election watchdog CRTA identified networks of political influence within social welfare centres and collected accounts from employees describing the use of social assistance to secure political support, including votes and participation in party activities.

CRTA’s monitoring of the 2023 elections also documented a case in which beneficiaries of social welfare support were denied that support for supporting an opposition party.

According to 2021 data from the association Creative-educational centre, people with disabilities and their families are among those at highest risk of poverty, with over 70 per cent of families living below the poverty line and only 13 per cent of people with disabilities in work.

Many people with disabilities are dependent on state welfare support – financial as well as in healthcare support and services – and on associations that usually provide help with access to assistive devices, education, training and employment.

Out of a dozen people interviewed by BIRN for this story, five reported witnessing statements from representatives of these associations that could be interpreted as pressure to vote for the SNS.

A person from a disability organisation in southern Serbia said the recently appointed head of the organisation had asked others within the organisation to pledge their vote for the ruling party and its candidate for prime minister, ex-President Aleksandar Vucic.

“I was present at the assembly when she was elected president,” the person said. “Afterwards, she told several people to stay because she wanted to ask them something. She then took each of them outside individually, including my neighbour. When my neighbour returned, I asked her what she had been asked. She told me she had immediately realised what it was about – whether she was willing to pledge her support to Vucic and the SNS as a secure vote.”

Many of these organisations are dependent on funding from public coffers.

Another person from a Belgrade-based organisation said such pressure is commonplace.

“We receive threats that our funding will be cut,” the person said.

Associations linked to politics

World.title: Week in Review: Polls and Storms
World.content:
A two-year-long political and societal crisis is set to culminate in parliamentary elections set for October 25 in Serbia. But will the elections put an end to the crisis, or make it worse? In his opinion piece for Balkan Insight, Djorjde Trikos looks at how and why the tide in Serbia may be turning against the Serbian Progressive Party and its de facto leader, Aleksandar Vucic.

World.title: Proposed Law to Curb Powers of Hague-Based Court Returned to Kosovo Assembly
World.content:
This post is also available in this language: Shqip Bos/Hrv/Srp



Supporters of former Kosovo Liberation Army (KLA) leader and former Kosovo President Hashim Thaci take part in a march in support of him in Pristina, Kosovo, prior to the verdict, September 12, 2026. EPA/GEORGI LICOVSKI

Kosovo President Justina Shiroka Pula sent the amended Kosovo Specialist Chambers (KSC) bill back to parliament on Thursday for review on the request of the Democratic Party of Kosovo (PDK) which had proposed the bill, less than three weeks after its controversial approval.

The law, which aims to curtail the jurisdiction of the Hague-based court, came after weeks of street protests led by Kosovo Liberation Army (KLA) veterans, who rallied under the slogan “Not in my name” – a reference to the KSC judge’s choice of words, “In the name of the people of Kosovo”, when he read the verdict.

“The president received a formal proposal from the parliamentary group of the Democratic Party of Kosovo – the sponsor of the legislation – to allow the assembly to reconsider the law, specifically the provisions concerning the jurisdiction and mandate of the Specialist Chambers,” read a statement from the president’s office on Thursday.

“The president has reiterated her opposition to any attempt to distort the historical truth of Kosovo, to cast doubt on the liberationist nature of the war, or to equate the people who fought for freedom and survival with the regime that oppressed them,” the statement read.

The initial bill was passed after four former KLA leaders were convicted by the KSC for the war crimes of arbitrary detention, cruel treatment, torture and murder, committed between April 1998 and June 1999.

Hashim Thaci and Jakup Krasniqi were sentenced to 25 years in prison each and Kadri Veseli and Rexhep Selimi received 18 and 13 years, respectively, with credit for time served in detention from November 2020. The verdict can be appealed and their lawyers are working to challenge the conviction.

Given the uncertainty over whether the KSC will indict anyone else, the effect of the bill is uncertain, but the message it sent was clear, and the European Union was unhappy.

“The Law […] goes against Kosovo’s international obligations towards the EU,” read a statement from the EU after the law was initially approved. The EU finances most of the court’s operations.

In a speech at the Berlin Process Summit in Montenegro on Thursday, European Commissioner for Enlargement Marta Kos said that “weeks and months of defining moments” lie ahead for the Western Balkans and reminded Kosovo of its obligations under international law.

On Thursday, Perparim Gruda, a MP from PDK who was involved in drafting the recent KSC bill wrote on Facebook that “there is no error in the law amending the Law on the Specialist Chambers.”

The Kosovo Specialist Chambers is a hybrid court, part of Kosovo’s judiciary but located in The Hague and staffed by internationals. The court was established in 2015 under pressure from Kosovo’s Western allies. Hashim Thaci was one of the main Kosovar supporters of the establishment of the court.

Since the conviction of the former KLA leaders over a month ago, criticism of the KSC has continued unabated in Kosovo. On October 14, Kosovo’s Ombudsperson, Naim Qelaj, held an event in Pristina to demand external oversight of the KSC.

Qelaj claimed that the court “has not been subject to democratic monitoring and control by the institutions of the Republic of Kosovo, creating a lack of transparency and accountability towards the citizens and institutions of Kosovo”.

He said it should report to the Kosovo authorities and that the Ombudsperson institution should be able to have access to its work.

KSC spokesperson Angela Griep told BIRN that “according to the legal framework of the Specialist Chambers, the Kosovo Ombudsperson does not have any responsibility with respect to the Specialist Chambers. This responsibility falls exclusively with the Ombudsperson of the Specialist Chambers in accordance with the Kosovo Constitution”.

World.title: One Dead, Crew Members Missing After Ship Sinks off Romania
World.content:
A Romanian navy squad during NATO naval drill ‘Sea Shield 24’ on the Black Sea, off the coast of Constanta, Romania, 16 April 2024. Photo: EPA/ROBERT GHEMENT

Romanian maritime authorities launched a rescue operation on Friday morning about 24 kilometres off the coast after a vessel was reportedly struck by a drone.

Rescuers are continuing to search for three missing crew members, according to preliminary reports.

The circumstances of the incident remain unclear, including the origin of the drone and whether the vessel was deliberately targeted.

President Nicusor Dan reacted swiftly to the incident, saying that it “is another event in the process of escalation that Russia is pursuing in the Black Sea region.”

The sinking follows an incident on October 15 when two other commercial ships were hit overnight while anchored in the Black Sea near the mouth of the Danube-Black Sea Canal, a major shipping route used to transport Ukrainian goods. Ukraine’s Black Sea ports have been a frequent target of Russian attacks.

Similar incidents have also occurred in Bulgarian territorial waters, where drone strikes have reportedly left at least 23 sailors dead or missing.

The escalating tensions in the Black Sea have prompted NATO to announce increased surveillance in the region following recent attacks on commercial vessels.

Meanwhile, Romania has proposed that it join Bulgaria and Turkey, the other two NATO member states bordering the Black Sea, in establishing a joint military command to be led by the three countries on a rotational basis.

World.title: Alleged Police Violence Against Minors Alarms Albania
World.content:
In a video shared on Monday evening, a group of police officers can be seen rushing towards several young people and beating them with batons. Amid the blows, one of them can be heard shouting that he is only 13 years old.

BIRN was unable to independently verify the ages of the young people in the video, but similar footage showing police in Tirana using violence against protesters, including minors, has circulated widely in the media and on social media over the past week.

The footage has raised concerns about how the State Police is treating children and teenagers involved in the wave of protests against Prime Minister Edi Rama’s government.

World.title: Serbia Braces for Most Uncertain Elections in 14 Years
World.content:
On Sunday, Serbia is bracing for what could be its most uncertain and high-stakes elections in 14 years, with the ruling Serbian Progressive Party, SNS, facing a challenge that has emerged out of a two-year student-led protest movement.

Since 2012, Aleksandar Vucic and his party SNS have largely dominated the political and electoral landscape. This time, however, the election outcome is far less predictable, political analysts say, as the student movement has reshaped the opposition landscape and mobilised supporters well beyond the established parties.

“These are the first elections in a long time whose outcome is entirely uncertain,” Nebojsa Vladisavljevic, a professor at the Faculty of Political Sciences in Belgrade, told BIRN.

World.title: Democracy Digest: Czech Culture Ministry Cuts Funding for Velvet Revolution Anniversary
World.content:
Former Hungarian central bank chief detained; govt tries to solve budget dilemma

Hungary’s former central bank governor, Gyorgy Matolcsy, was detained on Wednesday on suspicion of economic fraud causing substantial financial losses and the use of forged documents. Under Matolcsy, the Hungarian National Bank spent lavishly on refurbishment projects and established several foundations that channelled money into dubious foreign investments and projects that seemed to benefit family and friends. Several hundred billion forints are alleged to have been diverted from the central bank during his tenure or lost through investments. Media estimates put the total losses at 400-500 billion forints (1.0-1.4 billion euros). The current governor, Mihaly Varga, a former finance minister, and his team had submitted more than 30,000 pages of documents to the special investigative committee on central bank affairs by the end of September. Matolcsy’s detention signals the new government and prosecutors are getting serious about making key figures in the previous administration accountable for financial losses incurred during their 16 years in power. Matolcsy, once former PM Viktor Orban’s cherished economy guru, became governor of the central bank in 2013 after serving as economy minister in 2010-2014. Matolcsy’s term ended in 2025. His son and people in his business circle were reportedly among the main beneficiaries of lavish renovations to the central bank building.

Hungary’s new government tabled its first draft budget, causing disappointment in various quarters. The finance minister warned that budget discipline is necessary to prepare the country for joining the euro, planned for 2030-2032. In the draft budget for 2027, the government has pledged to cut the deficit from the current 7.0 per cent of GDP to 4.9 per cent by the end of next year and to 2.9 per cent for the end of its term in office in 2030. Inflation is forecast at 3.0 per cent and GDP growth at 2.4 per cent. Both Finance Minister Andras Karman and PM Peter Magyar acknowledged that there is a need for further wage increases in several sectors, but those could only happen “step by step”. As for immediate measures, the government fulfilled its electoral promise of doubling childcare to 24,000 forints (66 euros) a month per child and raising the minimum pension from January 2027. The draft budget would increase corporate taxes for multinationals, aligning with the global minimum tax regulations, from the current 9 per cent to 11.25 per cent. The government is introducing a special wealth tax for assets over 1 billion forints, and will further tax energy companies and banks. Major investments are pledged for health care, transport and energy, mostly funded by the unblocking of frozen EU funds. Magyar argued in his two-hour speech to parliament that cutting the deficit is essential, pointing to France and Romania as examples of governments unable to halt the spiral in spending. “Powerful, major economies – including European economies – are struggling in a debt trap, with the burden of interest payments choking their economies,” he said. Most controversial is the promised 1.5-trillion-forint cut in public sector funding. The police said they were disappointed by the 15 per cent wage increase and teachers voiced concerns about the 25 per cent increase pledged by the government from 2027. Workers in the cultural sector staged a small protest against their 10 per cent rise. “There are also sectors where there are no wages increases at all,” Magyar pointed out to those complaining, while asking for more societal solidarity.

World.title: Four Croatian Aminess Campsites Win Prestigious ADAC Superplatz Award
World.content:
October the 23rd, 2026 – Four Croatian Aminess campsites have taken home the prestigious ADAC Superplatz award, further spotlighting the progress camping in Croatia has experienced.

The latest prestigious ADAC Superplatz award has been given to Aminess Style Camping Atea Resort on the island of Krk. Poslovni reports that the latest prestigious ADAC Superplatz award has been awarded to Aminess Style Camping Atea Resort on the island of Krk, as part of the jubilee 20th Croatian Camping Congress, thereby joining the camping resorts Maravea and Sirena in Novigrad and Avalona on the island of Pag, which already carry this label.

The latest awards come at a time when Croatian camping is further strengthening its already enviable international position. Croatia is increasingly profiling itself as one of the highest-quality European camping destinations, and Aminess, with its investments, innovations and high management standards, is confirming its position among the leading Croatian companies in the premium camping segment.

“Four campsites with the ADAC Superplatz label are confirmation of the quality of Aminess’s camping offer and its position at the very top of Croatian camping, but also an incentive for further investment in its development. We are particularly proud of Atea Camping Resort, in whose development we invested 32 million euros last year. Such awards show that investments, knowledge and the dedication of employees bring concrete results. Our ambition is to actively raise European camping standards by developing products that, in terms of quality, facilities and guest experience, compete with the best in Europe. Croatian camping is at the very top in Europe, and Aminess wants to actively contribute to its further development and strengthening of competitiveness,” said Mladen Knežević, President of the Management Board of Aminess.

The renovation of Aminess Atea Resort, worth a hefty 32 million euros, was completed in 2025, transforming the campsite into a five-star premium resort. The renovation included raising the quality of accommodation, arranging pitches and modern accommodation units, developing additional facilities for guests and introducing modern digital solutions. Special emphasis was placed on preserving the natural environment and increasing the share of green areas, while reducing accommodation capacities in order to provide guests with greater privacy, comfort and a higher-quality holiday experience. Achieving the highest quality standards, including the criteria for ADAC Superplatz, was one of the key goals of this investment.

ADAC Superplatz is otherwise one of the most prestigious awards in the entire European camping industry and is awarded by the German automobile club ADAC on the basis of very strict quality criteria. The award is therefore an important indicator of excellence, but also additional confirmation of the competitiveness of Croatian campsites on the demanding European market.

World.title: Croatian Studio Mipmap Developing Digital Version of HEAT Board Game
World.content:
October the 23rd, 2026 – The Croatian studio MipMap is currently developing the digital version of the award-winning and wildly popular HEAT board game.

The Croatian studio MipMap has joined forces with Asmodee, whose portfolio includes some of the world’s best-known board games. Sinisa Malus reports for Poslovni that the Croatian independent video game development studio Mipmap Digital, in cooperation with the international company Asmodee (whose portfolio includes some of the world’s most famous board games such as CATAN, Ticket to Ride and Dobble) is developing the official digital adaptation of the award-winning board game HEAT: Pedal to the Metal, published by Days of Wonder. The digital version of the game will be available on Steam as well as on devices running iOS and Android.

putting a digital spin on a 60s wonder

Set in the golden age of motor racing back during the 1960s, HEAT: Pedal to the Metal is a board game by Asger Granerud and Daniel Pedersen in which victory depends not only on speed, but also on timely decisions and judging how much the engine can be pushed. Players use cards to manage speed, successfully negotiate corners and compete against friends, computer-controlled opponents and players from around the world.

One of the main challenges for the talented Croatian development team was to transfer the experience of playing HEAT at the table onto screens of different sizes. The digital adaptation features three-dimensional depictions of four tracks located in the USA, France, Great Britain and Italy. Players will be able to race against computer-controlled opponents known as Legends, organise local races with friends, take part in championships that include garage upgrades, sponsorships and different weather and track conditions. Cross-platform play will also be available, along with private rooms and automatic player matching. The Legends expansion will be included free of charge from day one, and additional official expansions are planned after launch.

The cooperation between Mipmap Digital and Asmodee began with a simple conversation at the SPIEL Essen 2024 fair. The Croatian studio approached Asmodee representatives with the idea of a digital adaptation of HEAT, and the first meeting gradually grew into a collaboration with Days of Wonder on the development of the game. One of the main challenges for the development team was to transfer the experience of playing HEAT at the table onto screens of different sizes. The digital adaptation remains faithful to the rules and visual identity of the original game, while using the possibilities of the digital format for clearer presentation of information, camera focus on key moments of the race and automation of certain parts of the game.

a major partnership

“Two years ago, we went to SPIEL 2024 hoping to start a conversation about the possibility of a digital adaptation of HEAT. Returning to this year’s fair, now that the game is in development, is therefore particularly significant for us. HEAT has a very distinctive identity, both visually and in the way it is played, and we have worked closely with Days of Wonder to transfer everything that makes this game special into the digital version,” said Joško Mikuličić, director and co-founder of Mipmap Digital.

“We’re extremely pleased to be working with Croatia’s Mipmap. An exciting and distinctive board game like HEAT deserves the best possible digital adaptation. We’re more than sure that Mipmap, owing to its experience and passion for HEAT, will create an outstanding digital experience for players and further enrich the experience of playing this board game,” said Christian Dunn, Head of Interactive Content Licensing at Asmodee.

who are mipmap?

Mipmap Digital is otherwise independent Croatian video game development studio specialising in digital adaptations of board games. The studio was born out of a shared love of games and the well-known problem of board game enthusiasts: finding the time, place and company for joint play. Drawing on experience in video game development, the team decided to make favourite board games more accessible in digital form while retaining their distinctive characteristics.

Mipmap Digital’s portfolio includes digital adaptations of the board games Roll Player, Point Salad and Canvas, while HEAT: Pedal to the Metal is currently in development. Asmodee is one of the world’s leading companies in the board game industry, dedicated to connecting people through games and stories. With over 2,200 employees worldwide, the company has one of the largest portfolios of board games.
