A trial nearly eight years in the making embroiling businessmen, journalists, and both Labor and Liberal politicians has concluded following several weeks of deliberations in the West Australian Supreme Court. Property developer Greg Poland claimed he was defamed by this masthead following the publication of two stories in 2019, which were based on a covert recording sent to journalists by federal Liberal MP Andrew Hastie. Andrew Hastie arrives at the West Australian Supreme Court. Ross Swanborough The first story alleged Poland coached a contact on how to engineer a land swap deal with the WA government that would see “toxic soil” from a Metronet project dumped and buried in exchange for a sand mining operation. In the recording, which has since been publicly released, Poland can be heard discussing his relationship with then-Transport Minister Rita Saffioti and former Regional Development Minister Alannah MacTiernan, and that if you do a favour for either minister, they would “just steamroll anything through”.



The second article published, also related to the recording, discussed Poland’s claims that an attempt to increase WA’s lobster catch was his plan, but the state government, including then-Fisheries Minister Dave Kelly, had “botched it”. Since the publication of those stories, both the plaintiff and the defendants have been locked in a legal battle which culminated this week. All three state government ministers, Hastie, and others were called in to take the stand. The last person to provide evidence was former WA Liberal Leader Zak Kirkup, who in 2019 was working as the member for Dawesville. He admitted he had been sent the audio, but claimed he had not listened to it.



Poland’s lawyer Martin Bennett suggested Kirkup was “discussing the recording with Andrew Hastie because it was of political benefit if there was a secret deal with Labor Party ministers” – a suggestion that was denied. Two people then advised Poland’s solicitors that Kirkup had lied on the stand, and that he had, in fact, been “gleeful” after hearing the recording and that he had wanted to use it as a “political weapon”, with Bennett suggesting Kirkup’s evidence had been false. Bennett suggested it proved both Hastie and Kirkup had released the recording for their own political gain and requested to reopen the case with new witnesses, and to cross-examine Kirkup again. That request was ultimately denied by Justice Matthew Howard. Across Thursday and Friday, Bennett and Nine’s lawyer Matthew Lewis then delivered their closing submissions.



“The stories are not flattering to Poland at all, we agree,” Lewis told the court. “He engaged in overreach and exaggerated about his contact to Rita Saffioti and Alannah MacTiernan ... He has nailed his colours to his mast.” In written closing submissions, the defence stated Poland was “revealed at trial to be a dishonest and unreliable witness”. “He would say whatever he perceived would advance his interests. He was unconcerned to give the court an honest account of what occurred at the meeting,” it reads. “Parts of [his evidence] lacked any semblance of seriousness or sobriety … He was willing to improvise, embellish and alter his account as the situation demanded.”



One of Poland’s key contentions was the soil was not toxic, with Bennett telling the court that a publicly available document and a background note from then-Fisheries Minister Dave Kelly’s office and sent to journalists both supported that claim. However, Lewis argued that Poland himself used the word toxic in the recording, and that Bennett also used the word toxic in a letter to journalists on behalf of his client before publication. Lewis also said there were no imputations of corruption on Poland’s behalf because it was clear he would not have gained anything through the land swap deal. Bennett argued that was incorrect.



Written closing submissions from the plaintiff states that the defendants “seize on the proposition that critically the reader is told of no benefit of any kind being attributed to Mr Poland”. “That’s the lawyer’s analysis of the first article, not the reading of a hypothetical ordinary reasonable reader capable of reading in a real world (not ivory tower) sense,” it states. “It is quite plainly conveyed to the reader that Mr Poland, apparently Labor-aligned and in a position of apparent authority (as Deputy Chairman of the PDC, a role to which the reader is told he was appointed by Ms MacTiernan after Labor came into power in 2017) was using his position to arrange an unorthodox, valuable deal for a local businessman, that would benefit the Labor Government.” Nine’s counsel Martin Goldblatt and Matthew Lewis SC arriving at court. Colin Murty Bennett also said Poland had called both Saffioti and MacTiernan by their first names, which indicated a “level of closeness”.



Both politicians distanced themselves from Poland while providing their evidence and said he did not have the influence he claimed. Justice Howard agreed, telling Bennett, “I can call Madonna by her first name, it doesn’t mean I know her well.” He will now take time to review the evidence submitted by both sides and will deliver his verdict at a later date. It is likely the decision will not be revealed until 2027.

World.title: Asian flavours, fresh pastries and pub hits: Why Baillie Hill is Vic Park’s new food hub
World.content:
Review Eating outEast Victoria Park Asian flavours, fresh pastries and pub hits: Why Baillie Hill is Vic Park’s new food hub Max Veenhuyzen October 24, 2026 Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. 1 / 3 Pub classics - with good beer-battered chips - are a key part of the offering at The Berwick. Supplied 2 / 3 Parco Pizza specialises in sturdy wood-fired pizza. Supplied 3 / 3 Spiced carrot scotch egg with pickled papaya. Supplied Previous Slide Next Slide 14 / 20 How we score Baillie Hill Pub dining$$$$ A good meal doesn’t just get people out of their homes. It can also be the catalyst for luring old buildings out of retirement. Consider the city’s long abandoned general post office that’s now part of a formidable (and essential) CBD food and drink hub. At the other end of the Terrace, a popular brasserie has made its home in the former Royal Insurance Co headquarters. And let’s not forget the western suburbs boatshed and its unlikely second act.



Once upon a time, all these buildings lay dormant and underutilised, waiting for the kiss of true love – or a sideways glance from the right property developer – to wake them from their slumber, Sleeping Beauty-style. Baillie Hill received a recent makeover. Restaurant reviews, news and the hottest openings served to your inbox. Sign up One of the newer admissions to this congregation of the born-again is Baillie Hill: a dining precinct in East Victoria Park that opened in January at the site of WA’s first dedicated maternity hospital. If you’ve ever wondered what $25 million of combined state, federal and private sector funding gets you in terms of redevelopment work, wonder no more. While I can’t speak to what Baillie Hill looked like pre-facelift – embarrassingly, I didn’t know it existed, even though I’ve lived most of my life in the area – its current iteration is bright, welcoming and sympathetic to the space’s past as well as its present.



Federation-era detailing and red brick exteriors are a constant throughout, but the dining areas are spacious and open. Native waterwise plants are all around and there always seems to be landscaping happening. I’m not mad about any of the above. Cosmetic benefits aside, this makeover also created different spaces and venues that awaken throughout the day. The earliest riser among these is Beth’s Bakery which occupies the rotunda building that Baillie Hill’s namesake Elizabeth Baillie built in 1912. It’s the only venue that’s tenanted and not run in-house, but in partnering with the likes of Laurance Greenfield (Community Coffee Co) and baker Sam Blaikie (Goods), management have assembled a team that understands the café and bread caper. Around midday, the rest of the gang starts to stir. The Berwick, the precinct’s pub-style offering, is Baillie Hill’s most visible offshoot thanks to the umbrella-shaded tables and giant TV screen near the entrance. The cooking follows suit with modern-day public house hits including fish and chips that’s flaky and crunchy in the appropriate places; burgers; salt and pepper squid and other bar snacks du jour, plus wood-fired pizzas with puffy, gently blistered crusts slicked with a bright sugo. Grazie Parco Pizza. But most of the interesting stuff is happening at Milly’s Acre, the section of Baillie Hill that includes a semi-outdoor area next to the gardens, children’s play area and Greensleeves: a kiosk slinging good house-made gelato.



The complex is a likeable suburban hub. It’s here that you can best see – and taste – some of the Asian influences that new executive chef Aldren Teo brings to the QR code-equipped tables. Think rectangles of prawn sesame toast crowned with black and white sesame seeds; a Thai-inspired grilled beef salad wheezing with chilli; plus the terrific scotch egg clad with spiced carrot served with a mophead of turmeric-pickled shredded papaya. I also suspect Teo might have had a hand in developing the Vietnamese coffee-flavoured gelato at Greensleeves, too. As mentioned, QR code ordering is available: one of many concessions made by both owner and diner for making a venue this big run. See also fetching your own cutlery and the at-times confusing crossover between the menus in each venue and the rules on what you can order where. One solution is to head to the bar and place your order with staff directly. Not only does it allow you to, say, order the tacos at Milly’s Acre (they’re only served there) but get them delivered to your table at The Berwick: it also lets you peruse the end of bin wine specials too, that I can’t seem to find on the app.



More importantly, it’s a reminder that at the end of the day, the purpose of any pub is the pleasure of human connection. The low-down Atmosphere: a likeable suburban hub that’s quietly broadening the discussion about food and drink at the pub. Come during the week for specials like Monday night’s $39 meal deal. Go-to dishes: beer battered fish and chips ($32), spiced carrot scotch egg ($20), Thai beef salad ($33). Drinks: a comprehensive round-up of modern drinks culture including non-alcoholic beers and sodas on tap. Cost: about $75 for two people, excluding drinks. Good Food reviews are booked anonymously and paid independently. A restaurant can’t pay for a review or inclusion in the Good Food Guide.

World.content:
WorldEuropeRoyal family Meghan reveals allegations against her father were reported to police in 2018 India McTaggart October 23, 2026 — 11:53pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. The Duchess of Sussex has said she knew about allegations against her estranged father in 2018, after it emerged that he was being investigated by police for allegedly possessing child sex abuse images. Thomas Markle, who lives in the Philippines, is alleged to have an extensive collection of illegal material that was reportedly discovered by Thomas Markle jnr, the duchess’s half-brother. Meghan, the Duchess of Sussex, and her estranged father Thomas Markle sr. AP; Supplied In a statement on Friday, the duchess said: “I am deeply distressed at the news that has come to light in the last 24 hours, and my thoughts are with any children who may have been harmed. “In 2018, a letter was sent to the Metropolitan Police and Royalty and Specialist Protection. That letter was subsequently shared with me. It made troubling and disturbing allegations against my father, and I was given assurances that these were being investigated.



“I hope it can now be understood that, despite certain media publications’ distortion over the years, any distance from my father and my choice to not allow him to have contact with our children, was for one reason: to protect them. I trusted that the authorities were doing the same for other families. “Although the breadth of what has now been uncovered is more sickening than one could ever imagine, my sincerest hope is that justice will be fully served and that the priority remains the safety and protection of innocent children.” Sources close to the Sussexes told The Telegraph that the Royalty and Specialist Protection Unit within the Metropolitan Police shared the letter with the duchess, and she was assured that UK authorities were pursuing the investigation. The Telegraph understands the letter was sent to the duchess in the summer of 2018, after her wedding to Prince Harry in May. According to The Sun, Markle snr kept “hundreds, if not thousands” of underage sexual images in four large boxes that had been mixed up with family mementos at his home in the city of Cebu.



Meghan’s relationship with her father, a former Hollywood lighting director, became estranged around the time of her wedding to Prince Harry in 2018. AP Police in the Philippines are reportedly preparing to seize the evidence, and the FBI is said to be looking into opening an investigation in the US, where 82-year-old Markle snr resided after having a leg amputation last year. Markle jnr, 60, has submitted a sworn statement to police in the Philippines and told The Sun: “When I found this material I was horrified and I had no option but to report my dad. “I have supported, cared for him and helped him for years – but that stops now. I won’t speak to my father ever again unless I’m called to give evidence against him.” On Friday, Markle snr denied the allegations, telling The Daily Mail: “I’m shocked, I’m hurt and I’m very upset that my son is making these accusations against me. I could never do what I’m being accused of. It’s the worst thing anyone could accuse me of.



“This is bullshit. It’s just a bunch of lies. It’s sick. I have no idea why Tom is trying to destroy me with these lies.” The Sun’s report said that Markle jnr, who has been his father’s carer since he suffered a life-threatening stroke in 2022, had told friends he had been left a “shaking wreck” by the discovery. “I knew right away it was highly illegal and would land me in jail for a long time if I didn’t get rid of it. I felt betrayed, angry and disgusted, and realised I had to report him,” he said. He is said to have reported his discovery to the FBI Hotline and the US-based National Centre for Exploited and Missing Children in July, as well as to the state police in Pennsylvania, where his father was living. Markle jnr said that among old family home videos, books and mobile phones, he found “old books that turned out to be full of naked little girls”.



After enlisting a local IT expert to access the computer hard drives he found, Markle jnr said: “His desktop was full of row upon row of thumbnail pictures linking to the most sickening child abuse imaginable. The worst of the worst.” Related Article Royal family Meghan’s estranged father investigated over alleged child abuse images: report Details of the found documents allegedly included film negatives showing naked schoolgirls and “vile images” on the same hard drive as some of Markle’s work files and “core accomplishments”, including his professional CV and a download of the duchess addressing a women’s event at the United Nations. Markle’s daughter, Samantha Markle, denied the allegations and accused her brother of inventing the story. Speaking to The Daily Mail, she said: “There is no merit in these disgusting allegations whatsoever, and my brother is disgusting for making them up. He wants to destroy our dad. Shame on him.”



It was reported last year that the duchess, 45, has no plans to see her estranged father again. Markle and the duchess’s mother, Doria Ragland, divorced when the duchess was six. The pair have not spoken since 2018, when he worked with a paparazzi photographer near his home in Mexico to stage pictures of him being fitted for a suit before his daughter’s wedding. He has never met the Duke of Sussex, Prince Archie or Princess Lilibet. Writing in his memoir, Spare, Prince Harry said his wife was “mourning” the loss of her father. Markle has struggled with poor health, suffering two heart attacks on the eve of the duchess’s 2018 wedding, which prevented him from flying to the UK. In his absence, the King, then Prince of Wales, gave Meghan away. In December last year, his left leg was amputated below the knee during surgery to remove a blood clot, which left him “fighting for his life” at the time.



In August 2018, the duchess wrote begging her father to stop talking to the media, with extracts later published in The Mail on Sunday. The duchess remains close to her 70-year-old mother, who lives in California and would regularly visit the Sussexes’ home in Montecito before the couple relocated back to the UK with their two children. The Telegraph, London Support is available from the National Sexual Assault, Domestic Family Violence Counselling Service at 1800RESPECT (1800 737 732) or the Men’s Referral Service on 1300 766 491. World.title: Trump ordered to sit for deposition in defamation case against BBC
World.content:
WorldNorth AmericaTrump diplomacy Trump ordered to sit for deposition in defamation case against BBC David Fischer Updated October 23, 2026 — 11:45pm ,first published October 23, 2026 — 4:22am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

A US judge has ordered President Donald Trump to sit for a deposition in his $US10 billion ($14.2 billion) defamation lawsuit against the BBC by December 11. The order from federal magistrate Judge Enjoliqué Lett on Thursday (US time) came as lawyers for the British broadcaster complained that Trump had delayed his appearance in his own lawsuit. US President Donald Trump speaks at a campaign rally on Wednesday. AP Photo/Julia Demaree Nikhinson Charles Tobin, the lawyer for the BBC, said that with two months left in the discovery period, “we still haven’t been able to depose the plaintiff”. Meanwhile, it remained uncertain whether former special counsel Jack Smith would be allowed to sit for a deposition. Federal rules require current and former employees to receive permission from agency heads before testifying in court cases. Smith has requested permission but has not received an answer, and the judge ruled that the department must respond to him by November 2.



In arguments about Trump’s deposition, Tobin noted there had been an agreed-upon date of October 16, but Trump had cancelled it for a “matter of national importance.” He said the Republican president was, in fact, campaigning in Georgia that day. “He was participating in party politics and prioritised that over sitting for the deposition,” Tobin said. Related Article Donald Trump Trump sues BBC in $15 billion lawsuit over edited footage Lett said Trump must sit for a deposition by December 11, or face sanctions up to the possible dismissal of his lawsuit – unless the discovery period is extended by the presiding judge. Discovery, where lawyers for both sides exchange documents and other evidence, is scheduled to end on December 18, and the BBC’s lawyers want to make sure they have Trump’s deposition before that deadline. Lett said only the presiding judge assigned to the case can alter the trial schedule, and the defence said it would be open to scheduling the deposition at a later time if the trial schedule was also changed.



Trump, who has often avoided depositions, filed his lawsuit against the BBC last December. He accused the publicly funded broadcaster of defamation as well as deceptive and unfair trade practices related to a documentary, Trump: A Second Chance. The BBC acknowledged that filmmakers spliced together quotes from different sections of the speech Trump delivered to his supporters on January 6, 2021, before the storming of the US Capitol, to make it seem he was directly urging violence. The broadcaster apologised over the editing, and the head of the BBC and its top news executive both resigned. But the BBC has denied Trump’s claims that it defamed him. Trump’s lawyers also argued against recording his deposition on video, asking for only a court reporter. The judge ruled that the deposition could be recorded on video but only for attorneys, meaning it wouldn’t be released to the public. Former Justice Department special counsel Jack Smith, pictured in September. AP Photo/Allison Robbert To bolster its defence, the broadcaster subpoenaed former special counsel Jack Smith earlier this month. Trump’s lawyers argued, in a joint filing asking for a hearing on the matter, that there was no good reason for Smith, who is not a party to the case, to appear. The BBC has said Smith has extensive knowledge of what happened that day.



At issue in Thursday’s hearing, though, was whether Smith had received the legally required permission from the Department of Justice. Assistant US Attorney Matthew Feeley told the judge that Smith had sent a letter to the department saying he would not testify without permission, and the agency had not yet responded. Lett ordered the department to respond to Smith by November 2. It seems unlikely that the department would grant Smith permission, or that he would move forward without it. Earlier in the hearing, Tobin, the BBC lawyer, argued that Smith has not objected to being deposed for this case, meaning the only objection is coming from Trump. Tobin said the BBC is not trying to relitigate the events of January 6, but Smith is one of the leading experts in what happened that day, and his deposition could lead the BBC to evidence that could help their case. “We can argue later on whether his testimony is admissible,” Tobin said, “but we are entitled to that deposition.” Trump’s lawyer, Alejandro Brito, said Smith has no personal knowledge of Trump’s January 6 speech or Trump’s state of mind when he gave it. All of Smith’s knowledge about the case is secondhand, Brito argued, and the special counsel’s report, along with Smith’s testimony before Congress, is all public and available to the BBC’s lawyers.



Editor's pick US midterms On the road in Ohio: Why Trump is on the defensive in this crucial state The judge agreed that the BBC should be allowed to see records for the total number of applications for membership at Trump’s Mar-a-Lago resort in Florida from January 6, 2020, through January 6, 2026, as well as the total cost of membership and initiation fees for new applicants. Tobin said one aspect of any defamation case is showing actual damages, and the popularity of Mar-a-Lago is a significant indicator of Trump’s reputation. The BBC’s lawyer described the private club as “a place where he exhibits his reputation in front of people who are important to him”. Brito argued that Trump does not actually run Mar-a-Lago, and that his reputation is not associated with the club. AP

World.title: AFLW round 11 LIVE: ‘I don’t know if it gets much lower than this’: Magpies suffer goal-less loss to Power
World.content:
Collingwood’s horror week got worse as they were kept goal-less in a 48-point loss to Port Adelaide at Alberton Oval on Friday night, which leaves them second-last on the AFLW ladder.

Compounding a miserable week in which they learned captain Ruby Schleicher is returning to her native Western Australia, Collingwood kicked their lowest-ever AFLW score by three points with the one bright spot a 29-disposal game from young star Ash Centra.

Violet Patterson of the Magpies and Ashleigh Woodland of the Power compete for the ball. AFL Photos via Getty Images

The 48-point winning margin easily eclipsed Port’s previous best this season of 21 and they equalled their biggest team score of the campaign.

AFLW commentator Kate McCarthy didn’t spare the Magpies, who have also faced questions around how seriously the club’s hierarchy treats their women’s side while the loss came in the club’s 100th game in the AFLW.

World.title: ‘Don’t know what he was thinking’: How Labuschagne left his fate twisting in the wind
World.content:
SportCricketAustralian cricket ‘Don’t know what he was thinking’: How Labuschagne left his fate twisting in the wind Daniel Brettig Updated October 24, 2026 — 3:01am ,first published 6:16pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Gqeberha: A narrow gap between two grandstands at St George’s Park is the margin by which Marnus Labuschagne finds himself on the edge of losing his Test place as South Africa eye the series victory that would emboss their status as world champions. Proteas captain Temba Bavuma has flagged the importance of his team embracing the title of world No.1, something he felt they did far more effectively in Gqeberha. Labuschagne, meanwhile, is fighting for Test cricket survival this week as the Australian selectors ponder their options with the series locked at 1-1 and the final Test starting in Cape Town on Tuesday. Loading As a strong wind whipped across the ground on the fourth afternoon of the second Test, Labuschagne had established a partnership with Travis Head and just evaded the tightest of lbw decisions on review. The sunny uplands of a long awaited-big score beckoned. But the spin bowler Labuschagne was contending with was Simon Harmer, an Eastern Province local with deep knowledge of the coastal breezes that occasionally stir into something more like the gales that battered the ground that afternoon.



The western stand, which recently had a roof upgrade ahead of next year’s ODI World Cup, provided some shelter from the wind. So too did the instantly recognisable Duck Pond End terrace, which adorns the St George’s Park logo. Having played here many times before, Harmer recognised the gap between those two stands as a source of pushback for airborne shots. With Marco Jansen posted at a deepish mid-on, he tossed the ball higher and dared Labuschagne to hit up. What followed was the moment that put Australia, and Labuschagne, in considerable trouble. “I don’t know what he was thinking,” Harmer said with a laugh. “Obviously I’ve played a lot of cricket at St George’s Park and it funnels through that corner of the old stand and the Duck Pond, and a lot of times you think you’ve got enough of it, but it just gets held up in the wind. “I’m sure he’ll be disappointed in hindsight, especially when they were looking to draw the Test.” Marnus Labuschagne immediately regretted his shot selection after being dismissed in Australia’s second innings of the second Test against South Africa in Gqebera. Kayo



“Those are the nuances of playing here in St George’s,” Bavuma said. “You can see a shortish boundary … you can underestimate the fact that the wind plays a factor. He didn’t get all of that ball, Marnus, and the wind did what it did. “It held it, and you probably had the guy with the safest hands in the team; Marco Jansen, to catch it. Those are the small things [about] playing here at St George’s. If you haven’t played, they can get you.” Bavuma, who gave his team a chance with a sublime 179 after the hosts had slipped to 6-110 early on day three, spoke with empathy about Labuschagne’s lengthy run of handy but insubstantial scores. “I think I’m probably the last person to speak in terms of getting starts and not going big, but I guess he’s within that phase, right?” Bavuma said. “As a cricketer, that’s probably the frustrating thing as a batter when you are getting to 30 and 40, and you’re not able to go and get the big scores. I mean, he’s doing all the hard work. The narrow gap between the two grandstands at St George’s Park, Gqeberha, South Africa. Daniel Brettig



“From what I’ve learned, it’s more a mental thing, and I think only he will know what’s happening in his head when he gets into those moments. He’s definitely going to be thinking about it when he gets to 30 and 40. “I think the moment he sees himself getting past those moments, that’s when he’ll kind of get his confidence and belief.” Bavuma acknowledged that his men had been chirpier and more aggressive in Gqeberha. “We were just probably just looking at things a lot more internally in terms of what has allowed us to play well, and I think part of it is being aggressive in situations, not necessarily having to have a word with our opposition, or look for fights, but be aggressive in how we approach it. Loading



“Look for opportunities to make the play for the team, and be ruthless in doing so. There’s obviously certain individuals within the team who enjoy a little argy bargy, and I mean, you allow those guys to go about doing that within the rules. Yeah, there was a little bit more verbal chatter about it.” Partly, this was because the South Africans spoke after the Durban Test loss of being more comfortable with the pressure that comes from winning last year’s WTC final at Lord’s. “I think sometimes, as a team, we forget that the target is on our back, and everyone wants to have a go at us. Everyone wants us to show our mettle as the current world champions, and everything that we do is under the microscope. “So I think our performance, the game up in Durban was a realisation of that, but also a realisation of what it means coming up against super-strong opposition.



“From a pride point of view, from a belief point of view, we’ve definitely strengthened that by being able to perform like that from a pressure point of view and expectation point of view, that’s probably going to keep increasing individually, but within a team. “And I guess the case for us is just to keep embracing that, keep going towards that pressure, rather than kind of allowing it to hit us in the face.” Related Article Analysis

Australian cricket Australia’s patched-up batting has reached boiling point. It must change for Cape Town Bavuma added that there had been plenty of introspection to get to 1-1, a feeling Labuschagne will know well this week. “You definitely have many conversations,” he said. “I think when you front up to the media, you try to keep a steely face. But when you’re there alone in your room, you can’t kind of lie to yourself. So, I mean, you do the whole thing. You analyse you batting innings, and you look at it from a technical point of view.



“I think from a mental point of view, you kind of tune yourself to making sure that you’re ready for battle. You’re out to compete, and if the opportunity is there, you wanna make the play for the team. “For me, it was a lot of that from a mental point of view. Spent the time in the nets as well to kind of try find something, some sort of rhythm or feeling that I was confident I could go into the game with.” News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Monday.

World.title: A covert tape, political feuds and toxic soil: Eight-year defamation battle reaches end
World.content:
NationalWAWA courts A covert tape, political feuds and toxic soil: Eight-year defamation battle reaches end Holly Thompson October 24, 2026 — 3:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

A trial nearly eight years in the making embroiling businessmen, journalists, and both Labor and Liberal politicians has concluded following several weeks of deliberations in the West Australian Supreme Court. Property developer Greg Poland claimed he was defamed by this masthead following the publication of two stories in 2019, which were based on a covert recording sent to journalists by federal Liberal MP Andrew Hastie. Andrew Hastie arrives at the West Australian Supreme Court. Ross Swanborough The first story alleged Poland coached a contact on how to engineer a land swap deal with the WA government that would see “toxic soil” from a Metronet project dumped and buried in exchange for a sand mining operation. In the recording, which has since been publicly released, Poland can be heard discussing his relationship with then-Transport Minister Rita Saffioti and former Regional Development Minister Alannah MacTiernan, and that if you do a favour for either minister, they would “just steamroll anything through”.



The second article published, also related to the recording, discussed Poland’s claims that an attempt to increase WA’s lobster catch was his plan, but the state government, including then-Fisheries Minister Dave Kelly, had “botched it”. Since the publication of those stories, both the plaintiff and the defendants have been locked in a legal battle which culminated this week. All three state government ministers, Hastie, and others were called in to take the stand. The last person to provide evidence was former WA Liberal Leader Zak Kirkup, who in 2019 was working as the member for Dawesville. He admitted he had been sent the audio, but claimed he had not listened to it.



Poland’s lawyer Martin Bennett suggested Kirkup was “discussing the recording with Andrew Hastie because it was of political benefit if there was a secret deal with Labor Party ministers” – a suggestion that was denied. Two people then advised Poland’s solicitors that Kirkup had lied on the stand, and that he had, in fact, been “gleeful” after hearing the recording and that he had wanted to use it as a “political weapon”, with Bennett suggesting Kirkup’s evidence had been false. Bennett suggested it proved both Hastie and Kirkup had released the recording for their own political gain and requested to reopen the case with new witnesses, and to cross-examine Kirkup again. That request was ultimately denied by Justice Matthew Howard. Across Thursday and Friday, Bennett and Nine’s lawyer Matthew Lewis then delivered their closing submissions.



“The stories are not flattering to Poland at all, we agree,” Lewis told the court. “He engaged in overreach and exaggerated about his contact to Rita Saffioti and Alannah MacTiernan ... He has nailed his colours to his mast.” In written closing submissions, the defence stated Poland was “revealed at trial to be a dishonest and unreliable witness”. “He would say whatever he perceived would advance his interests. He was unconcerned to give the court an honest account of what occurred at the meeting,” it reads. “Parts of [his evidence] lacked any semblance of seriousness or sobriety … He was willing to improvise, embellish and alter his account as the situation demanded.”



One of Poland’s key contentions was the soil was not toxic, with Bennett telling the court that a publicly available document and a background note from then-Fisheries Minister Dave Kelly’s office and sent to journalists both supported that claim. However, Lewis argued that Poland himself used the word toxic in the recording, and that Bennett also used the word toxic in a letter to journalists on behalf of his client before publication. Lewis also said there were no imputations of corruption on Poland’s behalf because it was clear he would not have gained anything through the land swap deal. Bennett argued that was incorrect.



Written closing submissions from the plaintiff states that the defendants “seize on the proposition that critically the reader is told of no benefit of any kind being attributed to Mr Poland”. “That’s the lawyer’s analysis of the first article, not the reading of a hypothetical ordinary reasonable reader capable of reading in a real world (not ivory tower) sense,” it states. “It is quite plainly conveyed to the reader that Mr Poland, apparently Labor-aligned and in a position of apparent authority (as Deputy Chairman of the PDC, a role to which the reader is told he was appointed by Ms MacTiernan after Labor came into power in 2017) was using his position to arrange an unorthodox, valuable deal for a local businessman, that would benefit the Labor Government.” Nine’s counsel Martin Goldblatt and Matthew Lewis SC arriving at court. Colin Murty Bennett also said Poland had called both Saffioti and MacTiernan by their first names, which indicated a “level of closeness”.



Both politicians distanced themselves from Poland while providing their evidence and said he did not have the influence he claimed. Justice Howard agreed, telling Bennett, “I can call Madonna by her first name, it doesn’t mean I know her well.” He will now take time to review the evidence submitted by both sides and will deliver his verdict at a later date. It is likely the decision will not be revealed until 2027.

World.title: Asian flavours, fresh pastries and pub hits: Why Baillie Hill is Vic Park’s new food hub
World.content:
Review Eating outEast Victoria Park Asian flavours, fresh pastries and pub hits: Why Baillie Hill is Vic Park’s new food hub Max Veenhuyzen October 24, 2026 Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. 1 / 3 Pub classics - with good beer-battered chips - are a key part of the offering at The Berwick. Supplied 2 / 3 Parco Pizza specialises in sturdy wood-fired pizza. Supplied 3 / 3 Spiced carrot scotch egg with pickled papaya. Supplied Previous Slide Next Slide 14 / 20 How we score Baillie Hill Pub dining$$$$ A good meal doesn’t just get people out of their homes. It can also be the catalyst for luring old buildings out of retirement. Consider the city’s long abandoned general post office that’s now part of a formidable (and essential) CBD food and drink hub. At the other end of the Terrace, a popular brasserie has made its home in the former Royal Insurance Co headquarters. And let’s not forget the western suburbs boatshed and its unlikely second act.



Once upon a time, all these buildings lay dormant and underutilised, waiting for the kiss of true love – or a sideways glance from the right property developer – to wake them from their slumber, Sleeping Beauty-style. Baillie Hill received a recent makeover. Restaurant reviews, news and the hottest openings served to your inbox. Sign up One of the newer admissions to this congregation of the born-again is Baillie Hill: a dining precinct in East Victoria Park that opened in January at the site of WA’s first dedicated maternity hospital. If you’ve ever wondered what $25 million of combined state, federal and private sector funding gets you in terms of redevelopment work, wonder no more. While I can’t speak to what Baillie Hill looked like pre-facelift – embarrassingly, I didn’t know it existed, even though I’ve lived most of my life in the area – its current iteration is bright, welcoming and sympathetic to the space’s past as well as its present.



Federation-era detailing and red brick exteriors are a constant throughout, but the dining areas are spacious and open. Native waterwise plants are all around and there always seems to be landscaping happening. I’m not mad about any of the above. Cosmetic benefits aside, this makeover also created different spaces and venues that awaken throughout the day. The earliest riser among these is Beth’s Bakery which occupies the rotunda building that Baillie Hill’s namesake Elizabeth Baillie built in 1912. It’s the only venue that’s tenanted and not run in-house, but in partnering with the likes of Laurance Greenfield (Community Coffee Co) and baker Sam Blaikie (Goods), management have assembled a team that understands the café and bread caper. Around midday, the rest of the gang starts to stir. The Berwick, the precinct’s pub-style offering, is Baillie Hill’s most visible offshoot thanks to the umbrella-shaded tables and giant TV screen near the entrance. The cooking follows suit with modern-day public house hits including fish and chips that’s flaky and crunchy in the appropriate places; burgers; salt and pepper squid and other bar snacks du jour, plus wood-fired pizzas with puffy, gently blistered crusts slicked with a bright sugo. Grazie Parco Pizza. But most of the interesting stuff is happening at Milly’s Acre, the section of Baillie Hill that includes a semi-outdoor area next to the gardens, children’s play area and Greensleeves: a kiosk slinging good house-made gelato.



The complex is a likeable suburban hub. It’s here that you can best see – and taste – some of the Asian influences that new executive chef Aldren Teo brings to the QR code-equipped tables. Think rectangles of prawn sesame toast crowned with black and white sesame seeds; a Thai-inspired grilled beef salad wheezing with chilli; plus the terrific scotch egg clad with spiced carrot served with a mophead of turmeric-pickled shredded papaya. I also suspect Teo might have had a hand in developing the Vietnamese coffee-flavoured gelato at Greensleeves, too. As mentioned, QR code ordering is available: one of many concessions made by both owner and diner for making a venue this big run. See also fetching your own cutlery and the at-times confusing crossover between the menus in each venue and the rules on what you can order where. One solution is to head to the bar and place your order with staff directly. Not only does it allow you to, say, order the tacos at Milly’s Acre (they’re only served there) but get them delivered to your table at The Berwick: it also lets you peruse the end of bin wine specials too, that I can’t seem to find on the app.



More importantly, it’s a reminder that at the end of the day, the purpose of any pub is the pleasure of human connection. The low-down Atmosphere: a likeable suburban hub that’s quietly broadening the discussion about food and drink at the pub. Come during the week for specials like Monday night’s $39 meal deal. Go-to dishes: beer battered fish and chips ($32), spiced carrot scotch egg ($20), Thai beef salad ($33). Drinks: a comprehensive round-up of modern drinks culture including non-alcoholic beers and sodas on tap. Cost: about $75 for two people, excluding drinks. Good Food reviews are booked anonymously and paid independently. A restaurant can’t pay for a review or inclusion in the Good Food Guide.

World.content:
WorldEuropeRoyal family Meghan reveals allegations against her father were reported to police in 2018 India McTaggart October 23, 2026 — 11:53pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. The Duchess of Sussex has said she knew about allegations against her estranged father in 2018, after it emerged that he was being investigated by police for allegedly possessing child sex abuse images. Thomas Markle, who lives in the Philippines, is alleged to have an extensive collection of illegal material that was reportedly discovered by Thomas Markle jnr, the duchess’s half-brother. Meghan, the Duchess of Sussex, and her estranged father Thomas Markle sr. AP; Supplied In a statement on Friday, the duchess said: “I am deeply distressed at the news that has come to light in the last 24 hours, and my thoughts are with any children who may have been harmed. “In 2018, a letter was sent to the Metropolitan Police and Royalty and Specialist Protection. That letter was subsequently shared with me. It made troubling and disturbing allegations against my father, and I was given assurances that these were being investigated.



“I hope it can now be understood that, despite certain media publications’ distortion over the years, any distance from my father and my choice to not allow him to have contact with our children, was for one reason: to protect them. I trusted that the authorities were doing the same for other families. “Although the breadth of what has now been uncovered is more sickening than one could ever imagine, my sincerest hope is that justice will be fully served and that the priority remains the safety and protection of innocent children.” Sources close to the Sussexes told The Telegraph that the Royalty and Specialist Protection Unit within the Metropolitan Police shared the letter with the duchess, and she was assured that UK authorities were pursuing the investigation. The Telegraph understands the letter was sent to the duchess in the summer of 2018, after her wedding to Prince Harry in May. According to The Sun, Markle snr kept “hundreds, if not thousands” of underage sexual images in four large boxes that had been mixed up with family mementos at his home in the city of Cebu.



Meghan’s relationship with her father, a former Hollywood lighting director, became estranged around the time of her wedding to Prince Harry in 2018. AP Police in the Philippines are reportedly preparing to seize the evidence, and the FBI is said to be looking into opening an investigation in the US, where 82-year-old Markle snr resided after having a leg amputation last year. Markle jnr, 60, has submitted a sworn statement to police in the Philippines and told The Sun: “When I found this material I was horrified and I had no option but to report my dad. “I have supported, cared for him and helped him for years – but that stops now. I won’t speak to my father ever again unless I’m called to give evidence against him.” On Friday, Markle snr denied the allegations, telling The Daily Mail: “I’m shocked, I’m hurt and I’m very upset that my son is making these accusations against me. I could never do what I’m being accused of. It’s the worst thing anyone could accuse me of.



“This is bullshit. It’s just a bunch of lies. It’s sick. I have no idea why Tom is trying to destroy me with these lies.” The Sun’s report said that Markle jnr, who has been his father’s carer since he suffered a life-threatening stroke in 2022, had told friends he had been left a “shaking wreck” by the discovery. “I knew right away it was highly illegal and would land me in jail for a long time if I didn’t get rid of it. I felt betrayed, angry and disgusted, and realised I had to report him,” he said. He is said to have reported his discovery to the FBI Hotline and the US-based National Centre for Exploited and Missing Children in July, as well as to the state police in Pennsylvania, where his father was living. Markle jnr said that among old family home videos, books and mobile phones, he found “old books that turned out to be full of naked little girls”.



After enlisting a local IT expert to access the computer hard drives he found, Markle jnr said: “His desktop was full of row upon row of thumbnail pictures linking to the most sickening child abuse imaginable. The worst of the worst.” Related Article Royal family Meghan’s estranged father investigated over alleged child abuse images: report Details of the found documents allegedly included film negatives showing naked schoolgirls and “vile images” on the same hard drive as some of Markle’s work files and “core accomplishments”, including his professional CV and a download of the duchess addressing a women’s event at the United Nations. Markle’s daughter, Samantha Markle, denied the allegations and accused her brother of inventing the story. Speaking to The Daily Mail, she said: “There is no merit in these disgusting allegations whatsoever, and my brother is disgusting for making them up. He wants to destroy our dad. Shame on him.”



It was reported last year that the duchess, 45, has no plans to see her estranged father again. Markle and the duchess’s mother, Doria Ragland, divorced when the duchess was six. The pair have not spoken since 2018, when he worked with a paparazzi photographer near his home in Mexico to stage pictures of him being fitted for a suit before his daughter’s wedding. He has never met the Duke of Sussex, Prince Archie or Princess Lilibet. Writing in his memoir, Spare, Prince Harry said his wife was “mourning” the loss of her father. Markle has struggled with poor health, suffering two heart attacks on the eve of the duchess’s 2018 wedding, which prevented him from flying to the UK. In his absence, the King, then Prince of Wales, gave Meghan away. In December last year, his left leg was amputated below the knee during surgery to remove a blood clot, which left him “fighting for his life” at the time.



In August 2018, the duchess wrote begging her father to stop talking to the media, with extracts later published in The Mail on Sunday. The duchess remains close to her 70-year-old mother, who lives in California and would regularly visit the Sussexes’ home in Montecito before the couple relocated back to the UK with their two children. The Telegraph, London Support is available from the National Sexual Assault, Domestic Family Violence Counselling Service at 1800RESPECT (1800 737 732) or the Men’s Referral Service on 1300 766 491. World.title: Trump ordered to sit for deposition in defamation case against BBC
World.content:
WorldNorth AmericaTrump diplomacy Trump ordered to sit for deposition in defamation case against BBC David Fischer Updated October 23, 2026 — 11:45pm ,first published October 23, 2026 — 4:22am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

A US judge has ordered President Donald Trump to sit for a deposition in his $US10 billion ($14.2 billion) defamation lawsuit against the BBC by December 11. The order from federal magistrate Judge Enjoliqué Lett on Thursday (US time) came as lawyers for the British broadcaster complained that Trump had delayed his appearance in his own lawsuit. US President Donald Trump speaks at a campaign rally on Wednesday. AP Photo/Julia Demaree Nikhinson Charles Tobin, the lawyer for the BBC, said that with two months left in the discovery period, “we still haven’t been able to depose the plaintiff”. Meanwhile, it remained uncertain whether former special counsel Jack Smith would be allowed to sit for a deposition. Federal rules require current and former employees to receive permission from agency heads before testifying in court cases. Smith has requested permission but has not received an answer, and the judge ruled that the department must respond to him by November 2.



In arguments about Trump’s deposition, Tobin noted there had been an agreed-upon date of October 16, but Trump had cancelled it for a “matter of national importance.” He said the Republican president was, in fact, campaigning in Georgia that day. “He was participating in party politics and prioritised that over sitting for the deposition,” Tobin said. Related Article Donald Trump Trump sues BBC in $15 billion lawsuit over edited footage Lett said Trump must sit for a deposition by December 11, or face sanctions up to the possible dismissal of his lawsuit – unless the discovery period is extended by the presiding judge. Discovery, where lawyers for both sides exchange documents and other evidence, is scheduled to end on December 18, and the BBC’s lawyers want to make sure they have Trump’s deposition before that deadline. Lett said only the presiding judge assigned to the case can alter the trial schedule, and the defence said it would be open to scheduling the deposition at a later time if the trial schedule was also changed.



Trump, who has often avoided depositions, filed his lawsuit against the BBC last December. He accused the publicly funded broadcaster of defamation as well as deceptive and unfair trade practices related to a documentary, Trump: A Second Chance. The BBC acknowledged that filmmakers spliced together quotes from different sections of the speech Trump delivered to his supporters on January 6, 2021, before the storming of the US Capitol, to make it seem he was directly urging violence. The broadcaster apologised over the editing, and the head of the BBC and its top news executive both resigned. But the BBC has denied Trump’s claims that it defamed him. Trump’s lawyers also argued against recording his deposition on video, asking for only a court reporter. The judge ruled that the deposition could be recorded on video but only for attorneys, meaning it wouldn’t be released to the public. Former Justice Department special counsel Jack Smith, pictured in September. AP Photo/Allison Robbert To bolster its defence, the broadcaster subpoenaed former special counsel Jack Smith earlier this month. Trump’s lawyers argued, in a joint filing asking for a hearing on the matter, that there was no good reason for Smith, who is not a party to the case, to appear. The BBC has said Smith has extensive knowledge of what happened that day.



At issue in Thursday’s hearing, though, was whether Smith had received the legally required permission from the Department of Justice. Assistant US Attorney Matthew Feeley told the judge that Smith had sent a letter to the department saying he would not testify without permission, and the agency had not yet responded. Lett ordered the department to respond to Smith by November 2. It seems unlikely that the department would grant Smith permission, or that he would move forward without it. Earlier in the hearing, Tobin, the BBC lawyer, argued that Smith has not objected to being deposed for this case, meaning the only objection is coming from Trump. Tobin said the BBC is not trying to relitigate the events of January 6, but Smith is one of the leading experts in what happened that day, and his deposition could lead the BBC to evidence that could help their case. “We can argue later on whether his testimony is admissible,” Tobin said, “but we are entitled to that deposition.” Trump’s lawyer, Alejandro Brito, said Smith has no personal knowledge of Trump’s January 6 speech or Trump’s state of mind when he gave it. All of Smith’s knowledge about the case is secondhand, Brito argued, and the special counsel’s report, along with Smith’s testimony before Congress, is all public and available to the BBC’s lawyers.



Editor's pick US midterms On the road in Ohio: Why Trump is on the defensive in this crucial state The judge agreed that the BBC should be allowed to see records for the total number of applications for membership at Trump’s Mar-a-Lago resort in Florida from January 6, 2020, through January 6, 2026, as well as the total cost of membership and initiation fees for new applicants. Tobin said one aspect of any defamation case is showing actual damages, and the popularity of Mar-a-Lago is a significant indicator of Trump’s reputation. The BBC’s lawyer described the private club as “a place where he exhibits his reputation in front of people who are important to him”. Brito argued that Trump does not actually run Mar-a-Lago, and that his reputation is not associated with the club. AP

World.title: AFLW round 11 LIVE: ‘I don’t know if it gets much lower than this’: Magpies suffer goal-less loss to Power
World.content:
Collingwood’s horror week got worse as they were kept goal-less in a 48-point loss to Port Adelaide at Alberton Oval on Friday night, which leaves them second-last on the AFLW ladder.

Compounding a miserable week in which they learned captain Ruby Schleicher is returning to her native Western Australia, Collingwood kicked their lowest-ever AFLW score by three points with the one bright spot a 29-disposal game from young star Ash Centra.

Violet Patterson of the Magpies and Ashleigh Woodland of the Power compete for the ball. AFL Photos via Getty Images

The 48-point winning margin easily eclipsed Port’s previous best this season of 21 and they equalled their biggest team score of the campaign.

AFLW commentator Kate McCarthy didn’t spare the Magpies, who have also faced questions around how seriously the club’s hierarchy treats their women’s side while the loss came in the club’s 100th game in the AFLW.

World.title: Gateway to city should be a square to remember
World.content:
Letters NationalVictoriaLetters Gateway to city should be a square to remember October 23, 2026 — 8:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Photo: Megan Herbert To submit a letter to The Age, email letters@theage.com.au. Please include your home address and telephone number. No attachments, please include your letter in the body of the email. See here for our rules and tips on getting your letter published. Former New York mayor Bill de Blasio and city planner Carlos Moreno had positive things to say about Melbourne, but both agreed that Federation Square needs a makeover.

Having attended the opening session of the Melbourne Assembly at the square, I can only agree that it is looking tired and forsaken – there are few open cafes or restaurants and the aluminium cladding is looking weathered and cheap. As a gateway to the city the Taxi pub building remains a nondescript disappointment and access to the river is obstructed.

That’s not to say it isn’t a marvellous asset for the city – where it works, it works well. But it shouldn’t be regarded as set in stone (or aluminium) – it should be thought of as a work in progress adapting to the city’s needs. We should heed the advice of our objective visitors and take the opportunity to make Federation Square the world-beating icon it could be.

Bruce King, Malvern East The health benefits of tree canopy

Heatwaves kill more Australians than bushfires, floods and storms combined, yet we are sleepwalking into a scorching El Nino summer (“Experts sound health alarm over hot summer”, 22/10). Trees are one of our best defences, cooling streets and homes, and the Victorian government’s 500,000 new trees across Melbourne are welcome. But every development that bulldozes established trees undoes that work, and our overall tree canopy keeps shrinking.

Protect the trees we have. Build homes with light-coloured roofs that reflect heat, and add proper cooling. Open cool refuges for those most at risk. And make sure our hospitals are ready for the surge. Heat is a silent killer, and we need to start talking about it.

Larni Dibben, Glen Iris Labor’s housing narrative is troubling

The narrative surrounding the demolition of Melbourne’s 44 public housing towers is deeply troubling, particularly given the gusto with which the Labor government has pursued this policy. The article “Hundreds of market rate rentals but no public housing” (17/9) highlights the contradiction at the heart of this issue. Labor has shifted substantially from its historical position on the left towards a political centre increasingly shaped by the imperatives of capitalism, at the expense of public housing, welfare and education. These are fundamental responsibilities of a government that previously claimed to represent working people.

Travelling regularly through the CBD, I see growing numbers of people experiencing homelessness. At a time of escalating housing insecurity, the demolition of public housing raises serious questions about our collective priorities and the kind of society we are prepared to accept. I can no longer vote for a party whose policies appear so far removed from the social values it once represented. While the Greens do not align with all my views, they at least offer a clear commitment to addressing many of these concerns.

Rozalind Drummond, North Carlton



THE FORUM The right priority

The Snowy Hydro upgrade is now estimated to cost up to $25billion (″⁣Huge setback as Snowy 2.0 cost blows out to $25b″⁣, 23/10). For this investment, the country gets an important power generation facility that has very little ongoing environmental impact, and will operate for 100 years.

The estimated cost of the AUKUS deal is $368 billion, a figure that will probably increase dramatically. For this spend our country becomes a potential nuclear target, and gets an arguably 20th-century military deterrent, which will be obsolete before it is paid for. I know which investment seems good value to me.

Mike Francis, Fitzroy Words matter

ASIO boss Mike Burgess has repeatedly conveyed concern about the use of violent rhetoric in public discourse.

It starts in parliament with the normalisation of extreme rhetoric in parliamentary debate, or what passes for debate today. Question time especially is characterised more by point scoring, personal insults and mindless character assassination than by any genuine attempt to debate policy. Many (most) politicians today appear to have lost the capacity to debate, reliant on dot points and staying on message. Genuine intellectual engagement rarely happens.

Democracy worldwide is under threat and Australia is no exception. ″⁣Words matter,″⁣ says Burgess. It’s time our parliamentarians acknowledge this and resolve to ″⁣debate with respect and disagree with restraint″⁣.

Difference and diversity are our future.

Neil Hudson, East Melbourne Error of his ways

After the release of jailed American Stephen Hubbard, according to Donald Trump, “The United States, out of respect for President Trump, was not required to give anything in return – an unprecedented situation for Russia.” (″⁣Russia releases retired US teacher″⁣, 23/10).

Of course, this ignored the removal of sanctions on Russia and the purchase of diesel to bolster Russia’s war machine. This is nothing, according to Trump – but the rest of the world knows otherwise.

Alan Inchley, Frankston Touch of madness

How amazing that it is only recently that the risk from touch screens in cars is receiving the attention it deserves (“Experts hit alarm button on touchscreens risk”, 23/10). I have been arguing for years that they are a dangerous distraction to driving. There should be no need for studies and data gathering on the topic as anyone who has driven a modern car knows how distracting touch screens are.

We are banned from using mobile phones while driving for good reasons, but in many ways screens are a worse distraction. Any function that is accessed while in motion should be operated via a button or a dial. The reasons car makers prefer screens is that are much cheaper to design and install and they look modern. Virtually every car designed this century comes with a dangerously distracting touch screen.

It’s time to go back to the days of common sense car designs or ahead to driverless cars.

Tony O’Brien, South Melbourne



Cuts are coming

The public finance guru ″⁣who did the numbers for Kennett and Andrews″⁣ is canvassing ″⁣belt tightening″⁣ (″⁣State heading for big bill″⁣, 23/10). As a former public servant who barely survived Kennett’s mayhem, I can only read that as meaning one thing for public servants, and that’s voluntary and involuntary retrenchments.

I expect the first action of a Liberal/One Nation government will be to establish an ″⁣audit committee″⁣, which will announce that the finances are ″⁣much worse than we thought″⁣.

David Fry, Windsor Tax the rich

Dear Premier Carroll, please do not sell any more assets owned by Victorians. The proposed sale of the vegetable market will just add a profit margin, add to inflation and continue the reckless and destructive neo-liberal policies that have reduced Australia – and the world – to their current parlous conditions. Tax the rich, not the poor.

Ian Porter, Kensington Offshore operations

Many of us, myself included, assume that most companies providing services to Australians are Australian. I recently had a billing issue with my energy provider. Imagine my surprise to learn that the person trouble-shooting my issue was based in South Africa and that the company providing my energy was Chinese-owned.

Ewa Haire, Moonee Ponds Don’t cut taxes

It is disingenuous (Letters, 22/10) to interpret Ross Gittins’ opinion piece (21/10) that a 15 per cent GST will do nothing to balance the budget as a criticism of excessive government spending. It is quite clear that the reason the Grattan plan would not assist budgetary repair is that it recommends (unnecessarily in my view) that the largest share of revenue gain from an increased GST should go to tax cuts, not to government spending on income support for lower-income households as your correspondent implies.

As other correspondents have explained recently, Australia, by international standards, is a low-tax country. Further reducing taxes will not address the budget deficit and will handicap the ability to supply the education, healthcare, aged care and housing services that the electorate wants and needs.

Terry Burke, Cape Paterson Living with the cuckoos

Reports that Starlink has degraded the service provided to the Ukraine military such that they are less likely to intercept Russian drones should be a wake-up shout to the Australian government and military.

What is being done to reduce any reliance that we have on Starlink for our defence? Anyone who thinks that this could not happen to us because of treaties or that our ″⁣friends″⁣ would never do that to us is living in cloud cuckoo land.

David Robertson, Wheatsheaf



Don’t raise rates

Is the Reserve Bank part of the solution to our current woes or is it part of the problem? If the economy falls into recession, many will think the bank has failed the community. Increasing interest rates to high levels has many adverse effects, including increased unemployment, and an even larger intergenerational gap between young and old in so many areas. Also, increased disenchantment in these uncertain times can result in a downward pressure on innovation and productivity.

A 2 per cent to 3 per cent inflation rate would, of course, be good to have but is it really feasible in times like these?

I would suggest that interest rates should now be regarded as at a peak. Further increases will add to frustration and anger. Overseas, that has led to upheavals in democracies, which we want to avoid here.

John Kent, Mornington No taste

Pauline Hanson said the video about Jacquie Lambie’s vaginal prolapse ″⁣wasn’t as tastefully done as it could have been″⁣. Would she please explain how you can tastefully mock or trivialise someone’s vaginal prolapse?

Angela O’Connor, Glen Iris Sage advice

At a wedding in 1968, which I can still clearly see, the minister at the altar meets the gaze of the young couple after declaring them “man and wife”.

Looking at them over the top of his glasses, he kindly says he has three words of advice for them: “Watch. Your. Words”.

This is now a long time ago, but his advice could continue to be heeded and spread to all humanity. Words, said and written, are powerful and they truly matter especially in these troubled times.

Helen Clements, Mount Waverley Behave, you’re not MPs

When my year 10 students were acting up I would say (rather forcefully) to them, “Behave yourselves! Where do you think you are, parliament?“

Mary Rice, Greensborough Photo: Matt Golding



AND ANOTHER THING Foreign affairs

David Shoebridge says the Greens do not support giving military aid to Ukraine. That puts him in the same bracket as Donald Trump.

Greg Hardy, Upper Ferntree Gully An ″⁣entente cordiale″⁣ between Russia and the US based on lies, deception and self-interest where the betrayal of allies barely gets a mention. Donald Trump will go down in history, just not in the way he imagines.

Claude Miller, Castlemaine Vladimir Putin a “humanitarian″⁣. Did I miss something, US special envoy Steve Witkoff?

David West, Essendon Furthermore

Faced with a choice between a Labor frying pan and Coalition or One Nation fire at the state election next month, voters might be wise to stick with the frying pan (“Voters signal end for Labor”, 22/10).

Lawrie Bradly, Surrey Hills



To your letters correspondent (PM, act on gambling, 22/10) I’d say: Don’t bet on it.

Marlene Krelle, Surrey Hills With the predicted El Nino drought, we won’t need Pauline Hanson to drain the swamp (″⁣Experts sound health alarm over hot summer″⁣, 22/10).

Alan Boltman, Blackburn South I was shocked to see a photo of the data centre in West Footscray dwarfing the adjacent residential houses. How was planning permission ever given? Buildings of this size should be in paddocks far away. And do we really need them?

Alec Dean, Soldiers Hill The person trapped in their flooded car (“ABC reporter saves man as car sinks”, 23/10) was lucky. All vehicles should be designed with a way of opening a window manually from the inside. I carry a brick under the seat.

Graham Patterson, Briar Hill In what profession can you fail all your major KPIs, yet still receive your maximum salary? The Australian men’s first XI.

David Cayzer, Clifton Hill Finally

After the horror of the past week I rejoined The Cloud Appreciation Society. I urge readers to look to the skies and ground themselves.

Margaret Skeen, Ocean Grove

World.title: Auckland’s Cornwall Park to introduce carpark fees
World.content:
One of Auckland's most popular parks is planning to implement paid parking to manage overwhelming crowds, RNZ can exclusively reveal.

The independent trust that manages Cornwall Park confirmed to RNZ that, from 1 December 2026, it would charge between $2.50 and $5 an hour to park in some areas of the Epsom parkland and along Pūriri Drive.

On weekdays, parking would be $5 an hour after an initial two-hour free period and capped at $35 a day.

Weekend and public holiday parking would be $2.50 an hour after the initial free period and capped at $20 a day.

Cornwall Park Trust chief executive Murray Reade said the park had become increasingly busy over the years and many people who came to the park struggled to find a parking spot.

"Parking demand at Cornwall Park continues to grow, particularly during weekends, major events, and peak seasonal periods.

"Finding a park can be challenging during busy times, and visitors regularly tell us that parking availability is becoming more difficult. During peak periods, high-demand parking areas can become heavily occupied, making it harder for visitors to find a space."

Reade said it had struck a balance by keeping parking for the first two hours free and providing 300 free all-day parking spaces on Grand Drive and Bollard Avenue.

"We've deliberately structured the pricing to support the way people use Cornwall Park. Most recreational visits remain free, while reduced weekend and public holiday rates support families, groups, and recreational visitors.

"Paid parking is one tool that will help improve parking turnover, support fair access, and make parking more readily available for visitors."

He said about 70 percent of the two million visits to the park each year lasted less than two hours.

He said the revenue generated through paid parking would go towards the park's ongoing maintenance and preservation and improving the visitor experience.

World.title: Chief of Defence resigns over 'inappropriate relationship'
World.content:
The Chief of Defence Air Marshal Tony Davies has resigned over questions of integrity, Defence Minister Paul Goldsmith says.

The issues make his role no longer tenable and it has been referred to the Inspector General of Defence.

"Air Marshal Tony Davies has informed me that he'll be resigning from his position as Chief of Defence Force, effective immediately.

"The reasons regarding his decision relate to integrity matters, that he did not previously disclose. We both agree his position is no longer tenable.

"I will be recommending to the Governor-General that she accepts Mr Davies' resignation."

In a statement, Davies said the matters involve an "inappropriate relationship".

"The resignation is for personal reasons, and results from errors of judgement made by me in the past, for which I am taking responsibility. The errors of judgement were contrary to the values of the Defence Force.

"These matters revolved around an inappropriate relationship I had when in a position of unit command, and I regret not disclosing this when I had the opportunity to do so."

The Defence Force said arrangements were underway to transition responsibilities to the vice chief of Defence Force, Rear Admiral Mat Williams, who will serve as acting chief of Defence Force.

Former Defence Minister Ron Mark, who is standing for New Zealand First again this election, said the circumstances surrounding the resignation needed to be thoroughly investigated - including what was known about the matter and when.

Mark said the resignation pointed to a possible failure of Defence Force processes.

World.title: Fetū Samoa thrash Wales in 14-try World Cup romp
World.content:
Fetū Samoa sprung back from their first-up loss to Australia last weekend to claim their first win at the Rugby League World Cup, thrashing Wales 76-0 in Sydney on Friday night.

They created history in the process, recording their highest win at a world cup.

A dominant first half set the pace for the Samoans, who ran in seven tries in the first 35-minute spell to lead 40-0.

That was topped off by an almost faultless goal-kicking by playmaker Pauline Piliae-Rasabale, who kicked six out of the seven conversion attempts she took.

In the end, the Samoans had piled on 14 tries to nil, 10 of which were converted.

Captain Evania Isa'ako said post-match the team played well and deserved the win.

"Really proud of the effort the girls put in tonight," she said.

"All our debutants that debut at this world cup, really proud of them.

"They really put their best foot forward."

Player of the match Amber Hall said they had worked hard after the loss to Australia.

"I guess after last week we worked pretty hard to get here today and the girls put it on and how good.

"It's been pretty good; we had talked about all the women that had come before us."

Having been unable to score a single point against the Jillaroos in round one last weekend, the Samoan women turned on the firepower in the first 10 minutes of Friday's clash.

Two early mistakes ruled by the referee meant Samoa did not complete their first two sets.

But once Laikha Clarke crashed through to score close to the left post after a good Samoa attack in the seventh minute, the floodgates opened.

Piliae-Rasabale kicked the conversion and Fetū Samoa were up 6-0.

Wales tried to piece moves together but it was ruthless from the Samoans who just kept applying the pressure, showing power and strength from their forwards and an entertaining backline that ran the ball at every chance.

Samoan forwards Annetta Nu'uausala, Mary-Jane Taito, Laikha Clarke, Leilani Wilson, Ivana Lolesio and Tavarna Papalii kept the ball tight and ran through the Welsh defensive line, setting up play deep inside their opponents' half.

One such move in the 12th minute saw Piliae-Rasabale feed Tyra Ekepati, who stepped in and out before diving over the line in the right corner for the team's second try.

Then it was Destiny Mino Sinapati's turn two minutes later before Ekepati got her second for the night.

Amber Hall of the Sydney Roosters, playing her third World Cup, burst her way through after coming off the bench, to score Samoa's fifth try, before the 2026 NRL-W Rookie of the Year, Newcastle Knights' Mercedez Taulelei-Siala, dotted down for her try in the 31st minute.

Hall was the provider again in the last seconds of the first half, running through the Welsh defensive line, before setting up Ivana Lolesio for the team's seventh try, as Samoa led 40-0 at the breather.

Dominance continues

The second half saw Wales getting some possession early, trying to get some territorial gain.

But Samoa's defence stood out, keeping Wales in their own half.

They went straight back to where they left off in the first half, with captain Isa'ako, a former World Cup winner with Australia, picking up the ball and diving over the line to claim her try.

Hall was at it again a few minutes later with another strong run through, before she offloaded to Monica Tagoai, who stepped in and dived over to score Samoa's ninth try.

The try of the match would have been Sinpati's second, after she had collected the kick from Wales near Samoa's tryline before running through from one end of the field to the other to score.

Then it was Taulelei-Siala's turn to claim her second for the night, after Nu'uausala ran through the defense and offloaded.

Eighteen-year-old Freedom Crichton Ropati scored her first try for Samoa with 11 minutes to play after she finished off another Samoan attack.

That was followed by 19-year-old Ekepati, who finished off another exciting Samoa move, before Tavarna Papali'i sent the Weslh defence the wrong way with her dummy and ran over to score her team's final for the night.

Samoa dominated the run metres, recording 2,136m against Wales' 596m.

World.title: Fire and Emergency New Zealand chief executive Kerry Gregory resigns
World.content:
The chief executive of Fire and Emergency New Zealand has resigned.

Kerry Gregory's resignation was announced by Fire and Emergency New Zealand (FENZ) board chairperson Raveen Jaduram on Friday afternoon.

Jaduram said Gregory had resigned "effective immediately" from his role.

"Mr Gregory says that, in the light of of the Minister of Internal Affairs' recent public statement that she did not have confidence in him, it has become untenable for him to remain in his role.

"The Board wishes to acknowledge and thank Mr Gregory for his 36 years of dedicated service, including a very lengthy period as an operational firefighter, and wishes him well for the future."

Darry Purdy would remain as acting chief executive and Megan Stiffler as national commander.

Friday's announcement came after RNZ lodged enquiries about Gregory's employment status earlier this week.

Minister of Internal Affairs Brooke van Velden, said she was advised of the resignation by the board on Friday afternoon.

"I expect the Board to manage the leadership transition appropriately and ensure the organisation remains focused on delivering for firefighters and communities."

Before Gregory's resignation he had been on extended leave for more than a month.

FENZ declined to say whether Gregory was on paid or unpaid leave.

The New Zealand Professional Firefighters Union said Gregory's resignation should be the catalyst for massive and sweeping change for FENZ.

The union's national secretary Wattie Watson said Gregory's position was untenable.

NZ Professional Firefighters Union nation secretary Wattie Watson. (File photo) RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

"This is incredible it took more than a month to happen quite frankly. I think there needs to be a proper full investigation. Those that have been enabling him to undertake the damaging policies and in his words vision that he had also need to come under strong scrutiny," she said.

Watson said Fire and Emergency was in a "dire situation".

"This should herald in wide sweeping changes. In the very least the board now needs to stop the changes that he was pushing through including the restructure, including the attacks on emergency response," she said.

"We would welcome the opportunity to meet with them to reset not only the bargaining but where this organisation needs to head."
